  • Industry observers note that it’s essential to recognize that the learning process is a process, a gradual evolution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past problems beginning in 1975. This article about Pasasana first appeared in the September-October 2002 concern of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Pasasana is the first pose in the Second Series of Ashtanga Yoga. To start this series, you need not only the physical ability to learn the poses but, more importantly, the correct attitude. If you take away anxiety about having to do challenging poses, take away “I-have-to-do-Second-Series” ambition, and release the fear of never achieving Pasasana, you create space for the willingness to persist, an attitude that helps you continue to try even in the face of difficulty.

Industry observers note that it’s essential to recognize that the learning process is a process, a gradual evolution. Given that we live in an age of instant gratification, the idea of slowing down and relishing gradual progress can frighten our results-oriented minds. But the desire to be somewhere other than where we are only hinders progress toward the goals to which we aspire.

Sources indicate that this interference of the ego is one of the ways in which perception becomes clouded. The clouding of our perception is known as avidya, or the lack of knowledge. Indian yoga teacher T. K.V. Desikachar describes the four “children” of avidya in his book Religiousness in Yoga (University Press of America, 1980). The first child, asmita (ego), always says “I know” or “I am right.” Raga (greed), the second child, wants everything immediately, whether or not the time is right. Under raga’s influence, if you want to move on to a difficult pose, you do, whether you are ready for it or not. The third child, dvesa (aversion), avoids or discards anything that seems difficult. The fourth child is abhinivesa (“clinging to life”). In our experience, this appears as fear not just of death but also of the death of a habit, a mind-set, a sense of achievement—of anything to which we’re attached. Fear has an infinite number of faces: fear of looking inadequate, fear of exploring the unknown, and fear of failing, to name only a few.

Avidya often rears up in the practice of yoga. All its forms feed our misinterpretation of reality, which is usually the source of our discomfort. The first step in finding release from avidya is recognizing the moments when we become entrapped in it. Then we build a sustaining, satisfying practice by learning to work through asmita, raga, dvesa, and abhinivesa. As we do this and begin to live in the truth, we become quiet inside. Like a child who knows they are loved, we walk through life with confidence.

For 99 percent of us, Pasasana is one of those poses best learned with the consistent hands-on help of a teacher and with the aid of props. It is not a pose that most of us will inhabit easily. Many students practice for years before they can do Pasasana with their heels on the floor and their wrists clasped. Because of the often slow progress and the help required in working on this pose, it provides an ideal landscape for avidya to take root and flourish. Suddenly we feel we are a less accomplished student because we need a prop or a hand to help us into the pose. For many students, the reaction to this feeling comes in the guise of avidya’s aforementioned children: stubborn insistence that we already know how to approach the pose; over-eagerness to leap blindly into an advanced expression of the pose that we’re not ready for; aversion to working with a prop, or deliberate resistance that maintains ignorance because we are scared to find out what we don’t know.

In my efforts to empower students, I give them all the tools I think are appropriate, including props. Props can be a crutch, but if they are used with intelligence, they can lessen the frustration in a pose, and this facilitates learning. To me, developing confidence in a pose through the use of a prop is learning. Sitting on a block while the body learns to open and strengthen is not a crime; dislocating a shoulder or tearing apart a knee is.

Pasasana is a perfect pose to illustrate the value of props. What is the point in trying to wrap the arms in Pasasana if your roots, your feet, are not planted firmly on the ground? Without a solid foundation, belief that you understand the pose is illusory, and your practice of Pasasana will feed into the cycle of avidya rather than serving as an opportunity for the experience of Truth.

For students beginning Pasasana, I often suggest a preparatory version in which we eliminate the wrap of the arms. We remove this difficult element of the pose in order to develop strength in the legs, challenge the Achilles tendon, and set the stage for proper twisting. To come into this Pasasana prep, stand at the front edge of your mat in Samastitihi (Equal Standing). Join the inner edges of your feet together. Spread the toes apart and feel the four corners of each foot making even contact with your mat. From the arches of your feet, lift through the core of the body. Gently draw the sides of the hips in toward the midline. This creates stability and steadiness.

Without a firm foundation, your poses can feed a cycle of ignorance, not an experience of truth.

Now begin to bend your knees. As you squat, keep both knees pointing straight ahead, and keep both the heels firmly rooting into the ground. Do not press the knees together, as this will cause the groins to tighten. With the groins soft, allow the inner thighs to descend toward the ground. Attempt to lower the thighs to a 90-degree angle. Breathe smoothly and evenly. Keeping your heels on the ground, take the left hand to the outside of the left thigh. Using the left hand as leverage, bend your right arm and bring your right elbow to the outside of your left leg. Pause for a moment and make sure that your breath has not become forceful. Stay calm on the inside; let go of struggling and forcing. To safeguard the knees and keep the hips properly level, do not let your elbow push the knees to the right. Also, keep the knees in line with each other: Do not let the right knee move in front of the left one. Use the left hand to help you move the right elbow more deeply down the leg, so that the right armpit and thigh come together like pieces of a puzzle.

To deepen the twist, move it into the upper back by leveraging the elbow and thigh against each other. Draw your right kidney area into your body and drop your shoulders way down away from your ears. Reach the top of the sternum away from your navel and spread across the collarbones. Again use the left hand to bring the right elbow farther down the leg. If the armpit and thigh make contact with each other, straighten your right arm and place the hand on the ground. (If not, continue to work with a bent arm, elbow at the side of the leg.) Line your fingertips up with your toes. Press down through whatever is on the floor. These are your roots. Begin with the feet: Press them deeply down, as though you could dig holes in the floor. Let the arches of your feet act as suction cups that draw energy up the legs. Move the shinbones in the direction of the calves and use the calves to deepen the rooting of the heels into the floor. This will stabilize the pose and help protect the knees.

Recent findings suggest that now press the palm of the right hand into the floor and drop both shoulders away from the ears. Reach your left arm high and straight up toward the ceiling. Spread tremendously through the arms.

As you work in the twist, begin low in the spine and continue into the upper back. Move the bottom tips of the shoulder blades deep into the body as the shoulders release down the back. As the shoulder blades draw in, resist the temptation to round and collapse the chest. Instead, let the action of the shoulder blades fuel the opening of the chest. The right arm and left leg act as leverage for the chest to make its ascent up out of the belly. From the twisting of the upper back, reach back with the left hand and attempt to clasp the right inner thigh. Do this by rotating the left shoulder back and moving the left elbow away from the body. Turn the head and gaze straight over the shoulder.

Breathe smoothly. Be mindful of the hips: Keep the side hips firm and do not let the left hip pop out to the side. The hips and knees should still be facing straight forward (Figure 1). After a few breaths, release and repeat the pose on the other side.

If it’s hard for you to sink to a right angle with the heels on the ground, your Achilles tendons will need to lengthen. I strongly discourage the use of a prop under the heels. In this case, a prop is a crutch, not a learning tool: It hinders the lengthening of the Achilles, which is an essential component of Pasasana.

According to recent reports, now let’s go to a wall to work with another preparation for Pasasana. The wall allows us to twist into the pose with the heels on the floor even if the Achilles tendons have not lengthened enough to permit a grounded balance in the middle of the room.

Stand sideways to the wall. Be sure the outside edge of the left foot and thigh are an inch or two away from it. Begin to squat, lowering your buttocks as close as possible to the floor. Again, keep the heels on the ground and the knees in line with each other. On an exhalation, hook the right elbow on the outside of the left thigh as far down the leg as possible. Place both hands on the wall for balance. Perhaps you can now lower the hips a little closer to the floor (knees in line, of course).

Using the hands on the wall, begin to twist from the lowest part of the spine. Press the hands into the wall and isometrically pretend to drag them down. This action will aid you in lengthening the spine, which is always the first rule of twisting. Work to bring the right side of your rib cage into the body and forward toward the wall. Let the spine move up toward the top of the head and create maximum extension from the navel to the sternum. Release the shoulders by letting the trapezius muscles cascade down the back. Slide the shoulder blades down and into the body. Move the top of the sternum farther up toward the ceiling (Figure 2). As you work to open the chest, use the grounding of the feet into the earth like a springboard. The energy of the feet, the lift of the arches, and the corresponding vitality in the legs give the pose a feeling of lightness. Hold the pose for a few breaths, then release and do the other side.

Use the grounding of the feet like a springboard: The corresponding lift of the arches and vitality in the legs will give the pose a feeling of lightness.

It has been revealed that A third Pasasana variation teaches the wrap of the arm by using the aid of the wall for balance. For this variation, stand with the buttocks either against the wall or slightly away from the wall, and squat deeply. (Experiment to find exactly the right place for your feet.) As in the first preparation, begin by bringing the right elbow to the outside of the left leg. Move the elbow deeply down the leg to initiate this action from the back rather than just from the arm. Take the left hand behind you to the wall for balance. Use the left hand at the wall to move the left shoulder blade down the back. Drawing the left upper arm bone into its socket, move from the shoulder blade as you rotate the shoulder head straight back.

Recent findings suggest that now wrap the right arm way down and around the shinbones and rotate the palm open. Release the right shoulder down away from the ear, thus setting the right upper arm bone in its socket. Working once again from the shoulder blade, resist the right shoulder’s tendency to round forward by rotating it back against the left leg. You are attempting to climb the right hand past the top of the right thigh all the way up to the right side of the waist (Figure 3). To do this, the twist in the chest has to deepen. This is a critical part of the pose. If the hand does not reach far enough up the thigh, not only will the clasp be difficult but also the chest will round in order to compensate.

In a recent development, achieving the wrap is by no means contingent upon having long limbs. For most of us, it is a result of the opening of the chest in the twist. Yes, if you have long arms the wrap is going to be much easier. But those of you in this category must make sure you are using your chest and not relying solely on your genetic good fortune.

After you’ve held this variation for a few breaths, release and repeat it on the other side.

In our next Pasasana preparation, we’ll concentrate on the clasping of the hands. To do this, get a block and move away from the wall. The block provides support similar to that of the wall, but now you have more room to work the wrap and clasp of Pasasana.

Sit on the block with your feet together and a few inches forward of the block. Root your sitting bones deep into the block and—of course—keep the knees in line with each other. Draw the right elbow down the left thigh, bringing the right armpit to the left leg. Work the twist, turning the right side of the back forward and around as though you are wringing out your torso like a wet towel. From the action of the right ribs into the body, begin to open the chest. Rotate the left shoulder back and down as you move the bottom tips of the shoulder blades deep into the body. Create the feeling of a backbend in the upper back.

Now slide the right arm far down around the shins and turn the palm open counterclockwise. Reach the hand as far around the leg as you can. As the chest opens and the shoulders move down the back, begin to reach for the clasp. Ideally, the right palm remains open and faces away from your body, and the left wrist falls into the right hand, securing the clasp. Once the clasp is in place, you have greater leverage to deepen the twist. (Those of you unable to clasp can use a towel between the hands or continue to work with the previous variation at the wall.) Keep turning the right side of the back toward the left thigh as though you could expose the entire front of your body to the left wall. Once again slide the shoulders down the back and then move the thoracic spine into the body.

Spin the wheel of your chest by rolling both shoulders back even farther (Figure 4). Breathe smoothly, which can be a challenge in a deep twist. As the breath steadies, so does the attention, and the mind quiets. When you feel calm on the inside, reconnect with the ground through your feet: Press them down firmly as you move your shinbones back and descend the weight of the calves into the heels. Attempt to lift your buttocks off the block. Do this gracefully. Discover the connection between the rooting of the feet and the energy that then ignites inside the body. This energy carries all the way up into the chest so that the body remains light and balanced over the feet. After a few breaths, repeat the pose on the other side.

In a recent development, when you can easily clasp the hands behind the back in the Pasasana preparation on the block, it is time to let go of all props and work in the center of the room. You may find that some of the variations were actually harder then [than] the final pose. In the variations, the work on each component part of the pose is very specific. As you isolate parts of the pose, you often find that you can actually work harder and more deeply, which provides a greater challenge and more learning.

As you isolate parts of the pose, you often find that you can actually work harder and more deeply, which provides a greater challenge and more learning.

To come into Pasasana, stand at the front edge of your mat and join together the inside edges of your feet. Move the sides of the hips toward the center of the body, letting the core of the body rise. Let the knees graze each other as you slowly bend them and track them directly in line with the second toes. Lower your buttocks as close to the heels as possible, keeping the heels on the ground and the shinbones moving back. Take the left hand to the side of the left thigh and work the right elbow down the leg. Keep the outer sides of the hips firm. Let the heels dig down through your mat. As you root the heels, lift the sternum up and away from the navel.

Now begin to wrap. In order to make the clasp, you may need to lift the buttocks up a little. Once you’ve made the clasp, work with the shins and calves to make the heels as heavy as possible. Again, you may need to lift the buttocks to achieve this. As the heels continue to press the floor, work to bring the buttocks down as far as possible (Figure 5). After five breaths, release the pose and repeat on the other side.

Recent findings suggest that our yoga poses serve as metaphors—and mirrors—for our lives. The attitudes that hinder us when we approach difficult poses are probably the attitudes that hold us back elsewhere in life. When we encounter these negative attitudes, first we must recognize them as such and then we must look closely to learn how they arise from avidya. The more tools we have at our disposal to help us see clearly, the more promptly we can cut through the clouds. In fact, often it is the embrace and integration of our difficulties that deepen our connection to ourselves. A meeting with our own shadow, our own weakness or pride or fear, can be a painful encounter on our journey toward wholeness; yet these meetings teach us compassion, humility, and wisdom. When we reach a difficulty that we cannot surmount with our familiar habits, we are forced to let go of rigid beliefs that no longer serve us.

According to recent reports, one place I often see this struggle is in students and teachers who, in the name of tradition, disregard ideas that come from a system other than their own. On the opposite side of the scale are practitioners who are disregarding tradition completely, showing no respect for any existing system. But aversion of either kind is simply a form of self-sabotage. Obviously, any practice that stems from a long lineage can be a fountain of knowledge. With all the information available to us, we must use our intelligence and intuition as we balance tradition and innovation. Can we allow ourselves to become free from what we think we know and discover what we do not know? If we take steps to free ourselves from avidya in all its forms, we can make choices progressively more grounded in health, well-being, and wisdom.

Can we become free of what we think we know and discover what we do not know?

Industry News: Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

📅 24 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that as a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times.
  • When shopping for new road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that as a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a newly introduced helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

When shopping for new road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Recent findings suggest that helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

In a recent development, so, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Currently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

Sources indicate that “The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

According to recent reports, virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a latest helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

In a recent development, editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

Industry observers note that “Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

All of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

The Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

For a fresh brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the manufacturer grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically massive lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

The Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

In a recent development, in our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina mentioned it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

It has been revealed that P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Industry observers note that unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

It has been revealed that of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Fresh England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Sources indicate that turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable. (Photo: Challenge Family).

We know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves. Either it’s too cold outside or it’s too beautiful a day to pass up a bike ride. Or perhaps there’s a storm 100 miles away that might suddenly decide to blow right over the aquatics center. But the truth is, if your workout is interesting enough, you’ll have all the excuses you need to get yourself into the pool, not out of it.

It has been revealed that and we’re not just talking about adding in a random drill here and there. Gamifying your swim workout, whether through solo exercises or team activities, helps make a workout enticing enough that you’ll want to do it over and over again. Adding an element of play to your swim can make it more challenging, productive, and fun all at once.

Before we get into a handful of our favorite games and drills, we asked Sage Hopkins, head coach of Women’s Swimming & Diving at San José State University, for his tips on how to make swimming more enjoyable. With these tools in your arsenal, you might not skip your pool workouts anymore, but actually look forward to them instead.

According to recent reports, first, Hopkins stresses how crucial it is to hear laughter echoing across the pool deck. This might not be possible if you’re training alone, but if you have a training buddy who always keeps you smiling, make it a priority to meet with them more regularly. Hopkins also encourages using music to establish an upbeat atmosphere; that might look like playing a pump-up song on your way to the pool, or investing in a pair of swimming headphones to keep the tunes going lap after lap.

In a recent development, once you know your purpose, Hopkins says, it’s easier to figure out what kinds of activities will make swimming more meaningful and enjoyable. Those who enjoy the camaraderie aspect of swimming and triathlon will enjoy team games like sharks and minnows.

Industry observers note that even simple details like naming a set, Hopkins says, can add a thrill to swimming. If there’s a test set you’re always dreading, give it a quirky or amusing name to make it seem less intimidating. You could use the most challenging triathlon you’ve ever lined up for as inspiration (The Wales One Hundreds, for instance, or the Norseman No Breathers).

Now, without further ado, let the games begin!

You don’t need any fancy clubs to play a round of swim golf — just enough glycogen in your head to add numbers. Hopkins suggests this drill for data-driven triathletes because it’s easy to keep track of your progression over time. Essentially, you add the number of strokes with the number of seconds that it takes you to complete a certain distance (such as 50 yards) to get a “score.” You’ll then repeat that distance several times within a single set, trying to keep your score as low as possible. This game helps improve your distance per stroke and ultimately conserve energy.

In a recent development, healthy suspense invites bursts of dopamine and curiosity into your workout, and it also means that there’s no one to blame but fate for back-to-back sprint sets. Make sure to write the following rules down on a whiteboard or protected piece of paper to reduce confusion.

Start by grabbing a set of waterproof playing cards, and assign a technique to each suit; for example, spades might call for kicking, hearts for drills, diamonds for swimming, and clubs for pulling. Next, assign a distance to groups of numbers (for instance, 2s and 3s might mean 50s, while 4s and 5s might mean 100s, and so on). Keep your jacks, queens, kings, and aces in a separate pile because they’ll dictate the number of repeats (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively).

So, for example, pulling a 5 of clubs alongside a queen would require you to grab your pull buoy for 2×100. Pulling a 2 of hearts alongside an ace would mean a 5×50 drill.

According to recent reports, another way to bring a measure of unpredictability to your workout is to roll a single die four times to determine your next set. The first roll determines your technique (5s could require kicking), the second your effort level (perhaps 4s always mean sprints), the third your distance (1s could mean 50s), and the fourth your number of reps (anywhere from 1 to 6).

Sources indicate that if you were on a summer swim team as a kid, chances are high you played many games of sharks and minnows. The game starts out with one “shark” who tries to tag all the other “minnows” as they swim from one side of the pool to the other. Each swimmer who gets tagged turns into a shark for the next round. You can complicate this game by instituting an underwater safety zone.

If you have an area of the pool to yourself, form teams, set up goals on opposite walls with pull buoys, grab a ball, and play water polo. This is an excellent way to make vertical kicking, sprinting, and treading water more exciting. It also facilitates team bonding.

It has been revealed that head to the deep end for this game to work on endurance as you tread water and practice vertical kicking. If the lifeguards allow it, you can play water volleyball over the flags with an inflatable beach ball. Your pool might even have a water volleyball net, and some versions float so that you can move them as required.

According to recent reports, hopkins recommends “call it sets,” inspired by Bob Steele, to work on pacing and fine-tuning your internal clock. Essentially, you and your training partners will swim a set of 100s, and before each repeat, each one of you will predict the time you expect to hit. Whoever is closest to their estimates wins the set.

Chase sets are a fun way for training groups with seemingly disparate ability levels to unite, says Hopkins. Slower swimmers are allowed a head start, while faster swimmers are tasked with trying to catch them. Chase sets are ideally employed for speedwork, not drills.

Industry observers note that casino night is extraordinarily fun for large teams and helps highlight everyone’s unique talents. First, two or three swimmers who are roughly equivalent in speed line up at the blocks. Then, the other teammates line up behind the swimmer they predict will win.

Recent findings suggest that from there, you’ll use cards or dice to determine the “event” that the swimmers will be competing in (see general rules above in the solo workouts). Whoever has picked the winning swimmer gets a rest break while the rest of the team completes a penalty swim (a 50 sprint, perhaps). If you have one seemingly unbeatable swimmer on the team, you can assign them a permanent handicap.

#9638. Does Running Build Muscle?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1290 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Does Running Build Muscle?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Running obviously builds your endurance.
  • In a recent development, running also builds strength.
  • Recent findings suggest that but does running build muscle?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Running obviously builds your endurance. While one mile (or five miles) might feel really hard when you first start running, those distances become much easier the more you get out there.

In a recent development, running also builds strength. As you power up hills or hit a finishing kick, you realize you have the force required to pick up the pace.

Recent findings suggest that but does running build muscle? Can you change your body composition simply by clocking more miles?

Industry observers note that the short answer is yes. But there’s more to the story. Here’s what to know about running and its affect on muscle mass.

Research indicates running can produce muscle growth. For example, a 2015 research review, published in the journal Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews, found that aerobic exercise can increase skeletal muscle and whole muscle size, particularly in sedentary individuals. (This means those just starting to run are more likely to experience the muscle-building benefits.) Those study authors suggest aerobic exercise as a mechanism to stave off the muscle loss that comes with aging.

Likewise, a 2017 study published in the International Journal of Exercise Science found that running induced muscle growth in the vastus lateralis muscle (one of the quadricep muscles) in 12 recreationally active university students. The participants completed about 25 sessions of high-intensity running (four sets of four minutes of running at 90 to 95 percent of heart rate max, with three minutes of active rest in between) for 10 weeks.

According to recent reports, this muscle growth likely stems from the way running loads the body—more specifically, the lower body. “With running, the majority of the muscle work or contraction is eccentric, which is the hardest load on the body,” Joe McConkey, a Boston-based exercise physiologist and USATF-certified running coach tells Runner’s World. Eccentric contractions occur when a muscle lengthens under load or tension. For example, during the lowering phase of a squat, the quadriceps (front of thigh) muscles eccentrically contract.

When running, “the act of landing, where you’re absorbing two to four times your body weight, is done eccentrically. That’s the major stimulus for muscle growth during running, particularly for beginners,” McConkey notes.

Recent research highlights that aerobic exercise may have more of an effect on maintaining muscle mass, rather than building it. That’s especially true if you stick to a similar routine, without adding intensity.

That said, new runners, compared to those who have been running for a while, are more likely to see the most noticeable changes in muscle mass and strength just by virtue of running more often or for longer for the first time (or the first time in a long time).

Also, even though runners who consistently do steady-state runs won’t build more muscle mass, their muscles can start to look more defined as body composition changes due to increasing mileage, adds McConkey.

If you’ve been running a long time, you’ve also probably already built strength in the slow-twitch muscle fibers that primarily power your long distance running, Janet Hamilton, C.S.C.S., owner of Running Strong, tells Runner’s World.

All runners can develop more strength—in terms of power and muscle ability—and likely more muscle by tapping into their fast-twitch muscle fibers, which have less endurance than slow-twitch fibers but exert more force. “These don’t really get called upon until either a) there’s an activity that requires more strength than slow-twitch fibers can muster or b) the slow-twitch fibers are fatigued and you keep going,” notes Hamilton.

To recruit more of those fast-twitch fibers, you need to do something that requires greater power output. Think about the massive leg muscles of a sprinter: “Any high-powered, short bout of exercise—so long as it is progressive in nature (i.e. harder, faster, higher than what you have already adapted to)—will increase the size of fast-twitch fibers, and thus increase muscle mass,” notes McConkey.

In summary, to promote muscle growth, you need a bigger challenge on your muscles and a variety of challenges, otherwise running will offer more maintenance than progression.

Sources indicate that to support your muscle-building efforts, consider the general exercise recommendations for each week: at least three cardio workouts, two strength workouts, and at least one flexibility workout. Incorporating these all into your routine will not only support your muscles, but make you a more well-rounded athlete.

One crucial component of that muscle-building plan is weight training. Strength workouts create micro-tears in your muscles that, during recovery, build back bigger and stronger. You also need enough protein in your diet to help with this process.

It has been revealed that when it comes to running, though, an easy way to build fast-twitch fibers and muscle mass is through hill workouts. “Running up a hill requires more muscle power than running on level ground,” says Hamilton. You may not be lifting a weight, but you’re carrying your own weight up an incline against the force of gravity—its own kind of resistance training.

Speed workouts will also engage fast-twitch muscle fibers. “If you’ve been doing nothing but easy effort, marathon-pace runs, incorporating short to moderate intervals at a faster, 5K pace is going to require you to exert more force every time your foot hits the ground,” notes Hamilton. “And that’s how you speed up—you generate a greater push-off.”.

It has been revealed that to build more muscle on your runs, check out these workouts below. The mileage, effort, and total distance will depend on your running fitness, but each workout can be scaled up or down to meet you where you are in your training.

Recommended Experience: No experience necessary! Anyone can accomplish this training initiative.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: This proposal is for a new runner who is just getting back into exercise.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a upcoming runner who has been exercising regularly for at least a year, or someone who has completed a few 5Ks or 10Ks and can complete 6 miles in one workout. This blueprint peaks at 28 miles in a week with a 12-mile long run.

According to recent reports, get the PlanRecommended Experience: For runners comfortable exercising for at least an hour at a moderate effort. This proposal peaks at 32 miles in a week with a 14-mile long run.

Industry observers note that get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a consistent runner used to regularly working out four to five times a week. The plan starts with a 10-mile long run and peaks at 44 to 47 miles a week with a 22-mile long run, helping you average under a 9:10 per mile come race day.

#9637. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1297 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree.
  • Sources indicate that if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month.
  • But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

Sources indicate that if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

In a recent development, before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the glitch in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Recent findings suggest that let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

Recent findings suggest that on one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Sources indicate that those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference revealed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

On a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar concerns early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the concern. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The company has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

Sources indicate that if you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

According to recent reports, the major problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Industry observers note that alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

Industry observers note that and yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

It has been revealed that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but rapidly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#9636. 4 Winter Running Habits to Keep Building Endurance in the Off-Season—No Treadmill Required

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1513 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

4 Winter Running Habits to Keep Building Endurance in the Off-Season—No Treadmill Required

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When days get shorter, temperatures get colder, and you no longer have a race on the horizon, the motivation to run consistently can seriously start to wane.
  • But prioritizing your aerobic fitness all year means you don’t have to start from scratch when it comes time to train for a race again, says Brant Stachel, an Ontario-based USATF-certified endurance coach at Fast and Free Performance Coaching.
  • Recent findings suggest that whether you’re a longtime treadmill hater in need of more exciting options or you simply don’t have access to one, we tapped experts for their best alternatives that allow you to maintain your endurance without hopping on the belt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When days get shorter, temperatures get colder, and you no longer have a race on the horizon, the motivation to run consistently can seriously start to wane.

But prioritizing your aerobic fitness all year means you don’t have to start from scratch when it comes time to train for a race again, says Brant Stachel, an Ontario-based USATF-certified endurance coach at Fast and Free Performance Coaching. “Anytime you’re taking big swaths of time off, you have to go back into rebuilding mode where you spend weeks getting back up to the fitness that you previously had,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re a longtime treadmill hater in need of more exciting options or you simply don’t have access to one, we tapped experts for their best alternatives that allow you to maintain your endurance without hopping on the belt. Follow these habits to keep your aerobic engine revved in the off-season.

Recent findings suggest that the minimum amount of training you need to do depends on your fitness level and your current (or most recent) training load. “If you’re somebody who’s running five to seven days a week, you probably still want to do three to four days a week,” Stachel suggests.

Industry observers note that even one to two days a week can keep you from starting completely from scratch in the spring season, indicates Danielle Kroot, DPT, certified run coach and physical therapist based in Portland, Maine. “It’s also keeping your tissues and muscles exposed to that type of load so that there’s not this shock to your system when you start training for a race again, and can help decrease injury risk,” she adds.

Keep in mind it usually takes six weeks of consecutive low-mileage weeks to really lose fitness gains, states Andrea Dell, an RRCA-certified run coach, so taking a few weeks off (especially if you’re recovering from marathon season) won’t do any harm; it’ll actually help you recharge.

Sources indicate that unless you’re training for marathons year-round, you’re likely periodizing your training, Stachel says, which means cycling through off-seasons, shorter distances, and maintenance mode in between major race training cycles. He explains that periodizing your training is really important for staying well-rounded and building adequate speed, strength, and endurance—all factors that make you a stronger, faster runner.

In a recent development, winter is a great time to analyze any gaps or weaknesses in your fitness, especially following a fall marathon season, Stachel indicates. Look at your recent training cycles and factor in what didn’t work for you. You might address strength and injury prevention after dealing with nagging calf pain, or consider focusing on speed workouts you didn’t get to hit as much during a marathon season, like mile race pace, 3K, and 5K pace efforts, he adds.

According to recent reports, strength work builds stability, power, and durability for better performance, and can help you handle mileage and speed. Building more strength in the off-season will translate to more speed, power, and injury prevention when you decide to ramp mileage back up.

Off-season strength should generally target major muscle groups runners rely on most, like the calves, glutes, and quads. Both Dell and Kroot recommend focusing on deadlift variations, squat variations, lunges, calf raises, step-ups, and plyometric movements.

Generally, you want to choose weights that make you feel like you could do only two more repetitions; that signals that the weight is heavy enough, Kroot explains.

“Even if you’ve got those five-pound weights hanging out in your basement, you can see how many squats you can do until you feel close to exhaustion,” Stachel adds.

If you have limited equipment at home, each expert recommends combining movements, such as doing a 15-minute stair climb, followed by bodyweight burpees or planks.

GET YOUR STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

It has been revealed that one particularly snowy winter, Stachel broke up his 90-minute run into five different sections, utilizing the equipment at his local gym and combining running and cross-training in one session. He ran 15 minutes to his local gym, went on the elliptical for 20 minutes, biked for 20 minutes, went on the treadmill for 20 minutes, then ran 15 minutes home. “The idea of simply going on a treadmill for 90 minutes was mentally numbing,” he indicates.

Stachel explains that while it’s best to complete a 90-minute run through running alone to stay specific to your sport, you have to find a workout you can stick with. “The best winter workout is the one you’ll actually repeat and build on next week,” he notes.

In the off-season, cross-training is your friend, Stachel says. Even if you don’t have any injuries, it’s a good idea to add some form of alternative aerobic-focused movement to your routine such as swimming, aqua jogging, elliptical, or cycling. “Then it doesn’t seem like a shock to the system when that first snowfall drops and you’ve got a week where you can’t go outside and run,” he adds. Stachel explains that gym memberships can be especially helpful for this reason.

Stachel’s go-to workout: a tempo session on the elliptical. “This has the closest carryover to running in terms of cardiovascular function,” he indicates. “It also loads the tissues because you’re more upright, whereas on the bike you don’t get that.”.

Recent findings suggest that you can do any run interval workout on the elliptical or another cross-training machine, Stachel notes, but the general rule is to take your typical outdoor recovery time and cut it in half. For example, if you give yourself two minutes to recover between tempo intervals outside, take one-minute recoveries on the elliptical. This might look like three 10-minute bouts at tempo pace with one minute of easy efforts in between.

If you don’t typically go to a gym, Dell and Kroot recommend stair workouts, at-home workout videos that provide follow-along Zumba or high-intensity interval workouts, and jumping rope.

Recent findings suggest that each expert recommends making an effort to still get outside as much as possible, even if it’s once or twice a week, or more during weeks when your local weather cooperates. Bundling up for the occasional outdoor run keeps training exciting, and helps your body stay adjusted to the roads.

Here are a few of their tips for making the most of those outdoor runs.

Industry observers note that oftentimes the best way to stay consistent with running in the off-season is to find safe, paved places to run when roads might be wet or covered in snow. Stachel recommends asking other runners in your community or talking to runners at your local run store to find the best routes in your area.

Recent findings suggest that “Every city I’ve been to or coached in during the winter has had some hidden gem that’s plowed for some reason,” Stachel claims. This might be a municipal building, a local mall, hospital, or other parking lots. “Those little tips and tricks can make it all the more fun,” he adds.

Recent findings suggest that good gear becomes your armor for bracing cold winter runs. “If you’re out there and you’re underdressed, you’re miserable the entire time. If you’re overdressed, then you’re sweating through your clothes and your heart rate’s high and then you’re frustrated,” Dell says.

It has been revealed that to dress according to winter weather, use the Runner’s World what to wear tool, which highlights you how to layer based on different weather patterns. Dell also recommends investing in a good pair of fleece-lined tights or joggers, as well as ear covers and gloves. Stachel also recommends microspikes that you can strap onto running shoes for better traction on wet or snowy surfaces.

In a recent development, view the off-season as an opportunity to rise to another challenge, Stachel notes. “There are so many times that as athletes, we feel hardcore for doing things. You could probably figure out a way to feel really hardcore for navigating a crazy winter or running,” he says, noting that a sense of empowerment comes from training through a season that many people don’t train through.

In a recent development, “Winter doesn’t change what builds endurance, it just changes how you collect it,” states Stachel. You might spend more time hacking your training and moving workouts indoors, or bundling up to run outside.

By spring, you can expect an “epic” racing season that feels rewarding and full of satisfaction because of all the hard work you put in during winter months, Stachel notes. Then, you will likely find the urge to continue training every winter because you know you’ll feel rewarded when the spring comes and you’re much closer to hitting your paces and PRs.

In a recent development, kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and presently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

In a recent development, if a cyclist is able to work strength training into their fitness routine, especially throughout the off-season, then the ceiling for potential power and speed goes up. The challenge is, as cyclists we just want to ride our bikes—driving to a gym, spending an hour or more in the weight room, then driving home is that much less time we’ll get in the saddle.

I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season. The TRX Suspension Strap System is a versatile, compact, and burlier-than-expected piece of gym equipment. I’ve had the same pair since I was certified almost 10 years ago and they are still in great shape—even after loads of personal use as well as using them for in-home training sessions with clients.

It has been revealed that one of the major reasons I continue to use the TRX system in my own workouts is because I can do a full-body strength workout, in a fraction of the time it takes me in the weight room, and I can do it all with one piece of equipment at home. All the TRX system needs is a way to mount it and enough room to do the exercises on the list.

Here, we’ll dig deeper into what TRX Suspension Straps are, why I recommend them to cyclists specifically, and give you a workout to jumpstart your season.

It has been revealed that TRX Suspension Straps are a suspension-based training tool designed to be used for bodyweight exercises. They were initially created by Randy Hetrick, a former U.S. Navy SEAL. He wanted to create a piece of fitness equipment that could offer full-body training and fit into a backpack—several iterations later, TRX was born. TRX Suspension Straps are basically a set of adjustable nylon straps that have handles to grab and cradles for feet. Most of the exercises you start with will have both hands on the handles, but as you progress you will start to add exercises with your feet in the cradles instead. The unique thing about this piece of equipment is that it can equally push a high-level athlete as well as offer things like balance improvement exercises. TRX bands can take simple exercises like a plank or a squat and offer modifications to make the exercise easier or create challenging progressions to make the exercise (much) harder. That makes them valuable for cyclists just starting out on a strength-training program or for those of us who have been doing it for years. The other great thing is they pack down really well. I have personally put them in the bottom of a carry-on bag on many trips over the years. You can set them up on everything from a traditional wall anchor to tree limbs and doorjambs. During my in-home personal training days, I had even set them up poolside for a great outdoor session with a client.

Sources indicate that cyclists benefit from some level of strength training off the bike. It’s one of the best ways to build speed, power, and durability. (Our Strength Training for Cyclists program, which is free to members, is packed with training prepares, strategies, and expert advice, making it a great place to get started or to elevate your current workouts.) With the TRX system, you can get all the benefits of strength training in with a tool that’s super effective. I like it because you can use it for moves that work your whole body, like an atomic push-up, which is when you perform a pushup with your feet in the bands, or something that isolates a muscle group, like a calf raise. Building a strong and sound core is a key to developing stability through the body.

It has been revealed that one great thing about the TRX straps is that almost every exercise you do will help improve core stability. Increasing that stability will allow for better energy transfer through your body as you ride. The straps also are incredible for mobility and stretching, allowing you to get deeper into and out of stretches. They do this by allowing you an extra point of stability when your hands are holding the handles or cradles at the end of the straps.

Industry observers note that if you are setting these up in your home gym, you will need a way to mount the straps. They come with a carabiner attached to the straps, but that has to get clipped to something. I typically use a double-length nylon sling used for climbing because I had a few of these lying around that I retired from my climbing rack. TRX also makes specific straps, wall anchors, and even doorjamb anchors to set the straps up on just about anything you can think of. Pro tip—make sure the anchor you use for the straps is strong enough to hold more than bodyweight.

I have been using my own set of the TRX Straps for over a decade now and they show few signs of wear. During my time as a personal trainer, I used the suspension straps for everyone from elite athletes to people in their seventies and eighties just looking to improve balance and mobility. They can handle everything from explosive training days to core and stability training. For cyclists that are looking to build a stronger core, here are a few of my favorite exercises.

You can find our complete expert-recommended workout here. The exercises, demonstrated by Susane Pata, TRX senior master instructor, will build the strength, stability, and mobility cyclists need. You can do the warmup moves anytime you want to wake up your muscles before a ride, and the stretches to loosen up when you’re done.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that shaunneka Hewitt is the founder of the YouTube channel Move with Shaunneka and has more than a decade of yoga teaching experience. Her approach is rooted in the belief that movement should feel good and allow you to slow down and listen to your body, which is exactly the aim of this seated yoga practice before bed.

According to recent reports, maybe you’re not one to curate the “perfect” nighttime routine. After all, what even is that? Your typical evening might consist of working until you can barely keep your eyes open or doomscrolling in bed until you essentially pass out mid-swipe. But technically, you already have a nighttime routine, whether it’s intentional or not. So you might as well make it work for you.

Sources indicate that that doesn’t mean your pre-sleep schedule needs to include Himalayan-salt-lamp lighting and bubble baths. It can be much simpler. When you steal just a few minutes from the end of your day for checking in with yourself, as opposed to checking out, you give your entire body a break from the busy day. Practicing even a few minutes of seated yoga before bed is one way to reintroduce your body to the idea of rest after a long day of, well, not resting.

According to recent reports, these stretches are inspired by the longer holds of yin yoga, and if you have the time, by all means, linger in each shape for 3 to 5 minutes. There’s no Savasana, with the hope that your final resting pose happens in the comfort of your bed as you drift off to sleep.

Sources indicate that sit on the mat and draw the soles of your feet together, letting your knees lower to the sides. Reach the crown of your head toward the ceiling, then hinge forward with a flat back so your chest is over your legs in Butterfly Pose (Bound Angle Pose). For more of a stretch, use your elbows to gently press your thighs away from you. Breathe here, then slowly return to an upright position.

From Butterfly legs, keep your left leg bent and straighten your right leg to the side with your toes pointed toward the ceiling. Slowly fold forward straight ahead, lowering your fingertips or forearms to the mat in a variation of Half Butterfly Pose. Relax your neck and let your head hang as you breathe here, then slowly roll up to an upright position.

In a recent development, from Half Butterfly legs, shift your weight into your left leg as you bend your right knee behind you at about a 90-degree angle and draw the sole of your right foot toward your right glute. Draw the sole of your left foot toward your right knee in Deer Pose (also known as 90/90). Inhale and twist toward your right; exhale and lower your fingertips or forearms to the floor outside your right thigh in Deer Pose Twist. Breathe here, then slowly roll up.

It has been revealed that from Deer Pose, press your hands or fingertips into the mat to frame your left leg and draw your left foot closer toward your hips. Straighten your right leg behind you in Pigeon Pose. Inhale and reach the crown of your head toward the ceiling; exhale and fold forward over your left leg, resting your hands or forearms on the mat. Breathe here.

Repeat Butterfly Pose, Half Butterfly Pose, Deer Pose Twist, and Pigeon Pose on the opposite side.

Industry observers note that sit on the mat with your legs extended in a wide V shape and your toes pointed toward the ceiling. Press your heels into the mat. Inhale and reach the crown of your head toward the ceiling; exhale and fold forward, lowering your hands or forearms to the mat in Wide-Legged Forward Bend. Relax your neck and let your head hang as you breathe here, then slowly roll up.

Sit on the mat and straighten your legs in front of you, about hip-width apart. Slowly fold forward, resting your hands on your thighs, shins, or on the mat on either side of your legs in Seated Forward Fold. Relax your neck and let your head hang. Breathe here, then slowly roll up.

Industry observers note that come to your hands and knees. Walk your hands forward and slowly lower your forehead until it’s resting on the mat or a block in Melting Heart or Puppy Pose. Breathe here.

From Melting Heart, come to your hands and knees. Separate your knees and lower your hips toward your heels. Walk your hands between your legs and toward the wall behind you as you lower your shoulders onto the mat. Turn your head toward one side so one cheek is resting on the mat in a Child’s Pose variation. Breathe here.

After you come out of Child’s Pose, continue with your own version of a nighttime routine, eventually making your way to bed.
