Self-care might be a personal undertaking, but that doesn’t mean you can’t give your people tools they’ll find useful along the way. A well-chosen wellness gift is typically a blend of thoughtfulness and innovation, something that delivers support, creativity, and a little extra mindfulness to everyday routines.

Our chosen gifts of the year are YJ editor-tested and approved, buzzed about by friends and family, and generally coveted by wellness enthusiasts. They include analog tools that encourage presence as well as gadgets that support your body and mind. And because we’re all about self-care, it’s okay if one of your recipients is you.

Here, 10 wellness gifts to help make your holiday shopping a touch more intentional.

Sources indicate that yoga blocks are not one-size-fits-all, or at least they don’t have to be. With its lower-than-usual profile, Manduka’s slender block is perfect for those who want slightly deeper, but still supported stretches. And for some, the elongated shape is just a better fit for hand size and posture. The blocks are made of lightweight, grippy cork, and might just be the perfect gift for the yogi that has everything (but also knows they need nothing).

This smart ring supports anyone who is so over any sort of tracking technology. I tested the Pulse Mindfulness Ring—which pulses to remind you to breathe deeply, focus, or whatever other intention you choose—and found the lightweight, stylish accessory to be a helpful and minimalistic tool for maintaining presence throughout the day. If your giftee’s goal is less about personal optimization and more about simple reminders to enjoy life, Pulse is worth slipping on.

Recent findings suggest that any tool that helps the body feel relieved, relaxed, and de-puffed is a gift we can get behind. Sliding this oversized gua sha tool over lotioned or oiled limbs is one of my favorite self-care moments. Lymphatic drainage is an actual thing, but even if all that this giant gua sha is doing is giving me a good old-fashioned massage, I offer it my gratitude. If you or someone you know enjoys a multi-step evening routine, add this to the holiday list.

Industry observers note that yes, you can give the gift of a regulated nervous system. The Open app is a wonderland of breathwork, meditation, mindfulness, even yoga and movement classes. It’s also really, really pretty, which let’s be honest, is an important aspect of an app that’s designed to calm you down. I’ve admittedly fallen off my streak, but for a few months I was meditating daily (and happily) with Open. An Open credit pack allows you to gift that to someone else. Basically, for the person who wants to elevate their mindfulness routine but isn’t sure where to start, there’s an app for that.

Sources indicate that I hold a lot of tension in my shoulders; I also work at a laptop all day everyday, which might have something to do with my tightness and pain. At the end of a massage a few years ago, the masseur very seriously told me to invest in a Theragun to help loosen some of my long-held knots. The mini version of the tool is lightweight and easy to grip, making at-home massage sessions simple. For what it’s worth, my shoulders have definitely loosened up.

Sources indicate that sitting in stillness, tuning in to your breath, and letting your thoughts float by is the work of a lifetime—and notoriously difficult. If a regular yoga practice aims to limber up your body so you can sit for longer stretches, a good set of meditation pillows can help make the prospect even more comfortable. This pretty, eco-friendly cushion makes meditation all the more aspirational. Who knows? This could be the start of your giftee’s mindfulness journey, or the thing that helps the sometimes-meditator develop a more consistent sitting session.

Whether your loved one is a deck collector or just getting into their spiritual card game, they’ll appreciate learning something latest (or cementing their astrological knowledge) on the daily. Rather than skipping self-imposed limits while you’re out and about—or working at your desk—Brick requires physical contact with the phone to lift restrictions. The gift of technological boundaries is truly one that keeps on giving.

Is this entirely due to this therapy bag? Probably not. But if there’s a lover of wellness and innovation in your life, I guarantee they will appreciate taking in this at-home, full-body red light at their leisure.

When it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

Recent findings suggest that but the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate swiftly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

To be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health issues (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”.

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition plan. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

You might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

The salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

With no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you plan to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

In a recent development, if you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is right now facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.).

In a recent development, with 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Recent findings suggest that instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

Despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

According to recent reports, led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

Sources indicate that made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”.

Recent findings suggest that the flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

As a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.

Running Faster vs Running Longer: Which Should I Focus On First?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Runners have two main paths to choose from when it comes to running goals: run faster or run longer.
  • According to recent reports, should you focus on running faster to build power and strength, or should you go the distance to test your physical and mental stamina?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Runners have two main paths to choose from when it comes to running goals: run faster or run longer. Both will make you a stronger, fitter athlete—but training for one looks a little different than the other.

According to recent reports, should you focus on running faster to build power and strength, or should you go the distance to test your physical and mental stamina? There’s no right or wrong answer, but understanding the differences between these two approaches can help you make the most of your training.

Like so many questions in running, the answer depends on your current fitness level and your goals. But for most fresh runners, it’s generally better to start training to run longer.

According to recent reports, “I think sometimes runners are quick to jump into trying to run all-out, whatever their goal race is, instead of just working toward being able to feel okay completing the distance first,” indicates Ruth Atkinson, VDOT-certified McKirdy Trained running coach based in Dallas. That means you probably want to think about the distance you want to cover first, whether you’re vying for your first 5K or have some shorter distances under your belt and are considering a half marathon or marathon.

According to recent reports, there’s a saying in running: Start where you are. In other words, don’t put a time goal on a race when you start training. Instead, start training, see how your fitness improves as you get closer to race day, then set a time goal. Some research even indicates that building up your easy mileage will lead to better long-distance run performance compared to focusing on speed workouts: A study published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021, involving 84 male runners, found a correlation between volume of easy runs—not tempo runs, not interval training—with world-class long-distance running performance scores.

It has been revealed that one of the most important benefits of gradually increasing your volume is training your tendons, ligaments, joints, and bones to withstand the repetitive impact of running without overtaxing them, which might lead to overuse injuries. “Starting with distance gives your body a chance to catch up to the muscular capacity you need to develop to stay healthy and move forward,” claims New York-based Nike running coach Rebeka Stowe. It’s generally easier and faster for beginners to build aerobic capacity compared to muscle strength, so you have to give your muscles enough time to build that strength.

Once you have a solid aerobic base—the foundational fitness you need to sustain your training—you could shift to more of a speed focus.

It has been revealed that not all running has the same effects on your body. When you’re training for distance, most miles will be at a low-intensity effort. (When it comes to rate of perceived exertion, this would be about a 4 out of 10 effort, or lower, with 10 being all out.) That easy, conversational pace may not feel challenging—although it will help you develop mental toughness by teaching you how to push through fatigue and discomfort as the miles add up—but it’s stimulating notable physiological adaptations that will improve your performance at faster paces.

For starters, you’re improving your cardiovascular capabilities. “Your heart is a muscle,” says Stowe. “By running at a slower pace, you’re building that muscle’s capacity to pump blood to the rest of your body so it can handle higher intensity work later.” As your heart’s stroke volume increases with training, it beats less frequently to supply the same amount of blood to the body—meaning it’s becoming more efficient.

Slower runs also train your slow twitch (type I) muscle fibers, which allow you to sustain your pace over longer distances. These muscle fibers have a higher density of mitochondria and greater capillary density, both of which help you maintain your energy level.

In fact, aerobic exercise increases the number of mitochondria in your cells, according to research published in the American Journal of Physiology—Endocrinology and Metabolism, and can increase capillary density by more than 25 percent, an older study in Journal of Atherosclerosis and Thrombosis found. The more mitochondria you have, the more energy you can produce, and the greater your capillary density, the better blood flow to your working muscles. Both of those benefits translate to improved performance at faster speeds.

Speed work, on the other hand, acts almost like strength training, developing your muscles as you work against increased ground reaction forces.

In a recent development, “Challenging your body to run at a faster pace is going to call on more muscle fibers,” notes Stowe. In this case, you’re working fast twitch (type II) muscle fibers, which are best suited for short, explosive efforts. These fast-twitch fibers also come into play at the end of a race for your finishing kick.

Picking up the pace also improves your cardiovascular capacity, but in a different way than easy running. Working at a higher intensity increases your VO2 max, “the maximum amount of oxygen that your body can use during exercise,” explains Atkinson. “The more you practice running at this pace, the easier it will be to translate that into holding faster paces for longer periods of time.”.

Training for speed will also improve your lactate threshold—the intensity level at which lactate accumulates in the blood faster than you can remove it, leading to fatigue—so you can improve your endurance at faster paces.

Sources indicate that to gain these benefits, you can base the pace needed off of your 5K time. If you don’t know your race pace for that distance, you can just go out and run 3.1 miles as hard as you can—it should be an 8 or 9 effort level on a scale of 1 to 10. VO2 max pace is a bit faster than 5K pace, while lactate threshold pace is a bit slower than 5K pace. (Keep in mind speed workouts aren’t always built around just these specific paces. A good training plan will have you holding speeds from mile pace or faster all the way up to marathon pace and slower, depending on your goals.).

Speed training also positively affects the density and structure of your bones, and may potentially prevent age-related bone loss, according to a research review published in 2023 in Sechenov Medical Journal—further bulletproofing your body against overuse injuries.

Another benefit of speed training: It requires a lot less time than building volume, which helps runners who are balancing training with other obligations.

Industry observers note that when you train for distance, your workouts will focus on gradually building up the time or mileage you run. Long runs at a conversational pace will be the cornerstone of your plan, along with some moderate-intensity runs and recovery days.

According to recent reports, “If you’re running four days a week, you’d have one day of speed and three easy days with higher volume, including a long run,” says Atkinson. Your speed workout would typically include longer intervals at goal pace, adds Stowe. “You should do a good majority of your speed volume at half marathon or marathon pace so that you become more efficient—and more comfortable—holding that pace,” she explains.

Industry observers note that the goal, when you’re training to run longer, is to improve your aerobic endurance and teach your body to handle the physical demands of extended activity. As you progress, you’ll increase your weekly mileage to build the stamina you need to go the distance.

It has been revealed that training for speed generally aims to improve your pace over shorter distances. You might run shorter, more intense workouts but with more recovery time between efforts. Let’s say you’re training for a fast 5K race: “You would ease into it by doing 200-meter and 400-meter reps at goal 5K pace, because you’re not going to be able to sustain that pace over longer distances yet,” says Stowe. “As your training continues, you progress to 800s, mile repeats, even 2K repeats—you can work your way up to holding that goal pace in smaller chunks.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re still running four days a week, your training plan might include three easy runs and a speed workout, or two days with speed and two that are easy, Atkinson claims. Your focus will be on maximizing your cardiovascular capacity, running form, and the ability to push your body to sustain those faster efforts. “The quality of your workouts will be a little bit harder, which means the quantity will be a little bit less to keep everything balanced,” she explains.

A good training plan incorporates speed and volume, because your body has different energy systems that respond to different stimuli.

“Think of it like a recipe,” notes Stowe. “If you’re supposed to mix salt and sugar into something but you forget to do one, you’re not going to get the desired outcome. The taste is going to be off, right? If you want to optimize your outcome, you have to have speed and volume as part of your training, so you’re developing all of your systems.”.

Starting with distance will help you build the foundation you need to develop speed. “If you spend a dedicated amount of time increasing your volume, you’re going to build a pretty robust aerobic system,” states Atkinson. “When you add speed work to that, you’re learning how to turn your legs over faster and become more efficient at faster paces. Then, you have the aerobic system in place to be able to hold the faster paces you can now run.”.

Industry observers note that for most runners, it’s a cycle. You may spend four to six months training for distance, and then two to four months working on speed; then you layer endurance back in and combine the two.

Industry observers note that both speed and distance training have their own set of benefits, and you can always mix and match, choosing what fits your current goals and lifestyle. Whether you’re training to run faster or longer, each step will bring you closer to becoming the strongest version of yourself.

#9617. Are These 5 Popular Running Recovery Strategies Hype or Legit?

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2288 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Are These 5 Popular Running Recovery Strategies Hype or Legit?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recovery is not the most exciting part of a runner’s training program—after all, it’s literally just the rest you take in between workouts—but ensuring high-quality recovery is essential if you want to maximize the gains of exercise and generally feel better after a butt-kicking run.
  • When good recovery is your goal, you’ll find no shortage of tools and strategies that promise to deliver exactly that—from cold plunges and saunas to foam rolling, compression gear, and more.
  • But as with many things in the wellness world, not everything that’s trendy is actually beneficial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recovery is not the most exciting part of a runner’s training program—after all, it’s literally just the rest you take in between workouts—but ensuring high-quality recovery is essential if you want to maximize the gains of exercise and generally feel better after a butt-kicking run.

When good recovery is your goal, you’ll find no shortage of tools and strategies that promise to deliver exactly that—from cold plunges and saunas to foam rolling, compression gear, and more.

But as with many things in the wellness world, not everything that’s trendy is actually beneficial. So which recovery tactics are truly legit—and which ones are overhyped? We investigated five popular running recovery strategies to learn what’s worth your while… and what you could likely skip.

Recovery is when you give your body a break so that it can absorb the training you’re doing, Grace Horan, an exercise physiologist at the Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS), tells Runner’s World.

There are four foundational elements to recovery, according to Horan: sleep, hydration, nutrition, and maintaining an appropriate training load (basically, keeping your easy runs easy and avoiding large spikes in training volume or intensity).

Industry observers note that other recovery tools can be used on top of that foundation—and we’ll dissect five of them in this article—but it’s important to first make sure that your foundation is solid, Horan says. In particular, sleep and nutrition are the most important, Horan says. If you aren’t locked in with those two, “all of the other recovery methods almost can go out the window,” Horan says.

Recovery is part of what Horan calls the “adaptation equation”: stress plus recovery equals adaptation.

Stress is all your training runs and workouts. Recovery includes the four foundational elements, along with any other recovery tools used on top of that. And adaptations are physiological changes that occur in response to training, such as improved endurance, increased aerobic capacity, and more strength and power in your muscles, Susan Kwiecen, PhD, principal scientist with the Gatorade Sports Science Institute and author of numerous publications on exercise recovery, tells Runner’s World.

Basically, you’re not getting stronger and more fit from training alone, but instead when you combine training with quality recovery.

According to recent reports, these adaptations, says Kwiecen, are “ultimately what allow runners to become fitter and perform better over time.” And recovery—when done right—can enhance these adaptations by helping them happen better and faster. Recovery can also help you maintain performance by reducing soreness and managing fatigue, which allows you to run again as swiftly as possible.

Keep in mind: “there’s no single best strategy for recovery,” Kwiecen says. “It depends really on the runner’s goals.”.

Ah, the cold plunge. Most runners have a love-hate—or a straight-up hate-hate—relationship with this recovery tool. That’s because hanging out in frigid water is not very enjoyable in the moment. But is the discomfort worth it if your goal is recovery?

Recent findings suggest that possibly… with an asterisk. “The literature reveals that cold plunges, ice baths, and cryotherapy in general can reduce soreness and help improve perceived recovery,” says Kwiecen. And if you feel less sore thanks to cold plunging, you may be able to perform better either that day or the next day. For that reason, cold plunges can be useful when your priority is rebounding between races or hard training sessions, Kwiecen says.

But here’s the catch: Regularly jumping in a cold plunge post training could reduce some of your fitness adaptations. Research shows this concern is most pronounced after resistance training, Kwiecen indicates. The cold temps can reduce blood flow to your muscles, which can decrease the opportunity for protein synthesis, ultimately blunting hypertrophy (muscle growth) and strength gains, Horan explains. Cold plunging may diminish endurance adaptations, too, Kwiecen adds.

So if you’re in a phase of training where your goal is to get stronger, “using cold plunges might not be the best idea,” Kwiecen indicates. Instead, they’d be better shelved for the end of a training block, when you’re no longer interested in gaining strength but simply want to feel as recovered as possible for your race.

Horan’s take: Cold plunges are not a recovery strategy that people should go out of their way to do, especially because the experience of cold plunging is “not super pleasant.” She personally doesn’t partake in cold plunging because “there are other recovery methods that are a little bit more gentle and a little less jarring that will have a very similar effect on perceived soreness and perceived recovery,” she explains.

That said, if you’re already an ice bath enthusiast, continuing the habit wouldn’t make or break your recovery or your training adaptations, Horan notes.

If you do choose to cold plunge, pay attention to how your body reacts. Shivering, in particular, is a sign to end your session stat. “As soon as you start to shiver, you’re reversing all of the possible [recovery] benefits of cryotherapy,” Kwiecen explains.

It has been revealed that foam rolling can elicit a mixed bag of emotions from runners. Some athletes swear by their roller for reducing soreness and boosting mobility—and others try it and don’t feel any different, so they stop using it, Horan says.

Whatever camp you fall into, here’s the truth: “Rolling is definitely a low-risk option that can make runners feel looser and more prepared to train,” Kwiecen indicates. “It probably won’t ease muscle damage, but it can definitely help improve a runner’s mobility or comfort—both of which make it easier to complete planned training in the future.”.

Sources indicate that horan personally loves foam rolling and does it after every run: “It’s low risk. It’s inexpensive. It does a few things reasonably well,” she says. That includes increasing range of motion and reducing feelings of soreness and general tightness after a run.

These benefits can be especially helpful for runners who are in an intense training block—for example, people nearing the end of marathon training. For some people, heavy training can really increase tightness in the fascia and muscles, Horan explains, in which case foam rolling can be an easy antidote.

Also cool: A foam rolling session doesn’t need to be long to be effective. “It’s something that you can get done in five minutes or less,” Horan says. She recommends runners focus their foam rolling on the quads, glutes, calves, and hamstrings (though she adds that stretching the hamstrings is potentially more effective than foam rolling them). Spend about 30 seconds to 1 minute per side of each muscle group, she advises.

For each muscle group, roll up and down the major muscle belly (rather than near the tendons) and pause when you find a spot that feels super tight, Horan says. From there, contract the muscle you’re foam rolling, which helps the foam rolling penetrate deeper into the myofascia, she explains. For example, kick your heel to your butt multiple times to contract the quad, or point and flex your foot to contract your calves.

Many runners foam roll after their workouts. But it can also be a helpful tool in your warmups to help you feel loose and move efficiently during a long run or race, Kwiecen notes.

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—which you can find over-the-counter as Advil, Motrin, Aleve, or Aspirin—are a type of medication that some runners take to ward off post-exercise discomfort.

Recent findings suggest that the purpose of these drugs is to reduce pain and inflammation, Kwiecen claims. And that can be helpful… when there is a valid medical reason, Horan says. But Kwiecen and Horan agree NSAIDs shouldn’t be a routine recovery strategy from running—a stance supported by other experts and research.

According to recent reports, part of that is because the stress of training triggers an inflammatory response in most people, Horan says. That might sound bad, but it’s actually a good thing: This specific type of inflammation is a normal, natural reaction to exercise that “needs to take place for us to adapt optimally to the stress that we’re giving our body,” Horan explains. Taking NSAIDs suppresses that inflammatory response, which can ultimately minimize our gains from training, she explains.

Plus, taking NSAIDs to mitigate pain you’re feeling from running can cause you to continue training through an matter that would be better solved with rest, training modification, and potentially getting evaluated by a medical provider, Kwiecen points out. “Reducing pain and improving recovery are not the same thing,” she notes.

Recent findings suggest that bottom line: Runners shouldn’t rely on NSAIDs as a recovery strategy. If you’re an athlete who thinks you need this medication for another reason, Horan recommends consulting with your doctor on the pros and cons.

It has been revealed that compression garments—in the form of socks, pants, and pneumatic compression boots—are a popular choice for runners looking to accelerate their recovery after long or hard runs. But do they work?

In a recent development, this is another recovery strategy that does have legit benefits… but also comes with an asterisk. Horan generally likes compression garments, saying they can help boost a runner’s comfort, perceived recovery, and blood flow post exercise. Research also demonstrates that using compression gear can help you feel less sore, Kwiecen adds. But here’s a caveat: You need a certain level of compression in order to achieve that reduction in soreness—and it can be difficult to get that from commercially available products, Kwiecen says. As she puts it: “Compression garments are tricky.”.

That stated, they’re a pretty low-risk strategy, meaning they likely won’t harm your recovery in any way, Horan notes. “There are people that will wear their pneumatic compression boots after every single run, and if they love it, then I think that’s great,” she says. At the same time, some compression garments—particularly the pneumatic boots—can be pricey, and by no means are they essential to a quality recovery. As Horan puts it: “I don’t think people need to go out and buy $500 boots if it’s not something that they already love.”.

Unlike cold plunges or tight compression gear, saunas are one of those recovery strategies that feel good in the moment (and often afterward, too). “People love a sauna—myself included,” says Horan. They can help usher in a sense of relaxation and may also reduce feelings of soreness, Horan says.

Industry observers note that beyond those recovery benefits, saunas could also help stimulate adaptations that benefit endurance performance, Kwiecen adds. More specifically, sauna sessions count as heat exposure, which spurs the production of heat shock proteins, Kwiecen explains. “These proteins protect and repair cells when they’re under stress,” she says. This means sauna sessions can help the body adapt to heat, “which can be beneficial when preparing for races in warm conditions,” Kwiecen says. Horan agrees that sauna sessions can help runners acclimate to heat if used regularly.

Industry observers note that that said, saunas do have their limitations: They aren’t going to erase muscle damage or speed up recovery, Kwiecen claims. Even so, Horan sees them as a “great” option for runners who enjoy them and have the time for them in their schedule.

Recent findings suggest that just be careful about jumping into a sauna immediately following a long run, especially if you’re already dehydrated, Horan says. That’s because you’ll likely sweat in the sauna, which will cause you to become even more dehydrated. And proper hydration, like we mentioned, is an essential component to good recovery.

According to recent reports, also, for general safety, don’t spend a ton of concentrated time in the sauna. Unlike the cold plunge, there’s no reverse shivering response for the sauna, Kwiecen says. As a general rule of thumb, though, cap your sessions at 10 to 12 minutes (or get out sooner if you start feeling unwell). As long as you follow these general guidelines, “if you’re well-hydrated and you really like to be in a sauna, I say go for it,” Horan says.

Runners should steer clear of using NSAIDs as a routine recovery tool, in part, because they can blunt fitness adaptations and cause runners to train through pain, which can increase injury risk. As for the other four strategies mentioned here—cold plunges, saunas, foam rolling, and compression gear—Kwiecen’s stance is that “if it makes you feel better, go for it.” That’s because when you feel better, chances are you’ll perform better the next time you go out for a run. “It’s all super subjective,” Kwiecen indicates, adding that not many recovery modalities have strong science-backed benefits beyond the feeling of less soreness.

Also keep in mind: The “right” recovery strategy may change throughout your training cycle and overall running journey. “Matching the recovery strategy to the runner’s goal is important,” Kwiecen indicates. For example, because cold plunging can blunt strength gains, it may not be the best choice when your goal is to get stronger—but perhaps it does have a time and place right before a massive race, when your main priority is minimizing soreness.

Recent findings suggest that whichever recovery strategies you choose to use, remember to first prioritize the fundamentals. “Nothing,” says Horan, “will ever, ever, ever beat sleeping enough, eating enough, drinking enough water, and avoiding really sharp spikes in intensity or volume load.”.

How Yoga Supported Me Through Cancer (In Ways That Had Nothing to Do With Movement)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “You’ll need surgery,” my doctor mentioned.
  • Moments before, she had informed me that I had endometrial cancer, and it felt as if an anvil had landed on my chest.
  • In a recent development, yoga was the practice I turned to whenever life got big.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “You’ll need surgery,” my doctor mentioned. “After that, no yoga.”.

Moments before, she had informed me that I had endometrial cancer, and it felt as if an anvil had landed on my chest. My mind flooded with questions I couldn’t yet articulate. Somewhere in that static, I tried to recall exactly what she said about the diagnosis. And wait, no yoga?

In a recent development, yoga was the practice I turned to whenever life got big. And this was huge. As my doctor explained the “good news” was that we caught the cancer early, and if all went well I wouldn’t need chemo, I tried to focus. She stated I’d likely need a full hysterectomy, followed by months of recovery with limited movement. My heart sunk. How was I supposed to navigate cancer without the thing that always helped me navigate all the other things?

In a recent development, I immediately stepped into a fresh rhythm, my calendar filling with appointments for testing, bloodwork, and specialists. I wrote down hospital addresses and watched as needle after needle entered my veins. I freaked out as bills racked up and I had to repeatedly check in with my insurance firm because things were insanely complicated. I tried to let go of control where I could and take charge where I needed. It was exhausting.

At each appointment, I had to tell the cancer story all over again. As I traveled around New York City, I secretly hoped I’d find someone who would tell me this was all a mistake. It felt like my body had betrayed me or that I was suddenly in skin that wasn’t my own.

Most of the time I left a doctor’s office and went straight to a yoga class. I needed to feel my feet underneath me, to soothe my mind and heart with deep breaths. I told myself I was going to practice yoga as much as I could in the months leading up to surgery, almost as if I could stockpile it in my bones. It was often the only time I felt at home in my body.

Yoga provided a hum of consistency. There, on the mat, I felt that familiar alchemy of turning my anxieties over to the practice. I breathed. I moved. During these months of consultations and biopsies and test results, yoga was the only time I felt okay, sometimes even good, in my body.

According to recent reports, yet sometimes in Down Dog, it felt like my entire heart turned into a teardrop, heavy with emotion. I cried in Child’s Pose, processing the layers of emotions associated not just with the cancer but the fact that I’d be losing a part of my body.

Sources indicate that other times, I was hit with denial, fear, and shock. How had this happened? I was only in my 40s, and the most common age range for endometrial cancer was the 60s. Sometimes, lying in Corpse Pose, I’d let myself think about the truth underlying cancer, feeling my mortality. I was staring impermanence in the face.

Yoga was a place to feel all the things. Yet more often than not, I ended practice feeling awash with a rare calm I no longer took for granted. I wished I could escape into the post-yoga glow forever. I was clinging! Still, I wished there was a way.

The day of my surgery finally came, and it was time to say goodbye to my cancer, my uterus, and, at least for a while, yoga.

That morning, sitting in my hospital gown on a gurney waiting to enter the OR, I tried to stay centered, but my body took over. I broke out in a cold sweat. Nausea rolled through me and my breath caught in my chest. The room swirled.

Recent findings suggest that “You’re having a panic attack,” my doctor remarked, placing her hand on my back. I inhaled and exhaled for a count of five, over and over, instinctively practicing box breathing while trying not to jostle the many tubes hooked to me. My body knew this language. It eventually began to calm down.

In the days after surgery, my pelvis blared with pain. I couldn’t even sit up on my own in bed without wanting to pass out. Lying motionless and still feeling discomfort, I began to understand what the doctor had meant by taking a break from the poses. I couldn’t just unroll my mat and fall into Child’s Pose.

But I was starting to sense the ways yoga was still with me, even approaching me in this moment of pain and need.

In a recent development, while stuck in bed, I thought of the yoga teaching of purusha and prakriti. Purusha is the witness self, the spirit, the part of us that watches our experiences. Prakriti is the material world, including the body. As I cared for myself, taking my medications on a complicated rotation and hobbling around throughout the day to avoid blood clots, I realized I could watch my body yet also dwell in a different part of myself. I felt a small space between my body self and my witness self, and this space felt like a lifesaver.

Industry observers note that propped up by pillows, I listened to a recording of a yoga nidra guided meditation. The voice brought my awareness to various parts of my body that I hadn’t contemplated in months. One of my teachers, Dharma Mittra, had described yoga nidra as closing the open tabs on your computer, or your thoughts, while keeping the computer, or your consciousness, on.

Sources indicate that now I closed down one thing at a time, mentally minimizing the cancer, the pain, even the act of healing, and felt into the parts of me beyond that. I breathed and observed.

In a recent development, I felt inside me a quiet resilience I’d spent years getting to know and grow on the mat. I was in a forced state of slowing down, and here I saw a glimmer of an unprecedented intimacy with my life that no Netflix binge would blot out.

As I began to move through healing, I realized even pursuing treatment had been ahimsa, or non-violence practice, toward myself. I began to understand that my body hadn’t betrayed me. It was still my friend, just someone going through something, and my practice had been to try to be kind to it, advocate on my own behalf.

Industry observers note that coming to terms with cancer and the impermanence of my body had been a kind of satya, or honesty, practice. Walking the healing path and heading into surgery had been a sort of act of surrender, ishvara pranidana. Somewhere along the way I’d released into a kind of trust and faith that I would be carried by a higher power.

It has been revealed that I realized there was so much of the yoga practice already deeply within me beyond the poses. It was a relief: yoga wasn’t going anywhere. Neither was I. The practice’s philosophy and lessons were an invisible scaffolding supporting all aspects of my life. I even felt a sense of joy remembering I was more than my body.

Yoga was strengthening me just when I most needed it. It was teaching me about myself, a kind of svadhyaya, or self-study.

It has been revealed that yoga didn’t “save” me. It didn’t distract me from the realities of my situation. What it did was provide me with tools and a framework for navigating those realities and remaining acutely present with myself throughout the better part of a year. I had built these tools over decades of practice, and they were indeed inside me, deeper than I even knew.

I’d given myself to yoga years earlier. Now, it was giving back to me.

In a recent development, A few months after my surgery, I went to yet another post-op appointment. I was tired of being poked and prodded, but as my doctor checked my stitches, I stepped into the role of witness again, more consciously this time.

It has been revealed that “You’re cancer-free!” she remarked, reviewing the final pathology report. “You’re now a cancer survivor. You can go back to yoga now.”.

I didn’t tell her, but I’d been practicing all along.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman).

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

It has been revealed that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a new fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my significant shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

In a recent development, after finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

Recent findings suggest that “I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev stated, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”.

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

Industry observers note that “Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he remarked. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”.

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

According to recent reports, “There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the intends because of those doubts.”.

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

Recent findings suggest that “That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that strategy. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”.

Industry observers note that sticking to the proposal slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

“It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”.

Recent findings suggest that and for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Industry observers note that physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

Sources indicate that “To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

“It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’.

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

Industry observers note that “You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”.

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

It has been revealed that it worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

According to recent reports, “I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before big races.”.

Sources indicate that the day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

Recent findings suggest that “When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”.

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

Industry observers note that “I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”.

That feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

“It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”.

Thankfully for him, time went by rapidly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

Industry observers note that after that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”.

According to recent reports, recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”.

Starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a upcoming world’s best time, the specter of the Substantial Island tempered his elation.

“It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”.

One of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his fresh, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev quickly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a big difference in how hot I feel.”.

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of upcoming cooling strategy.

“It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”.

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

Sources indicate that “So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”.

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”.

When you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

“We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”.

According to recent reports, A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

“Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he said, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”.

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev quickly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

“I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”.

The bike offered another potential saving.

It has been revealed that “My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”.

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”.

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”.

For now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev indicates he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

Industry observers note that “Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”.

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

“He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”.

Altra holds a special place in my heart because one of the first shoes I reviewed after I was hired at Runner’s World was the brand’s now-discontinued Instinct/Intuition 4.5. Altra was founded in 2009 by high school running buddies Golden Harper and Brian Beckstead. Turns out the Instinct/Intuition was pivotal to Altra establishing itself in the running industry. It was the first model Altra rolled out in 2011.

Since my introduction to Altra, I’ve witnessed its evolution; the brand formerly known for strictly selling zero-drop shoes (when forefoot and heel cushioning are equal) has added models with a 4mm drop. This move has drawn the zero-drop-curious to the Altra way.

Looking for a zero-drop daily trainer → Altra Torin 9 (Men’s/Women’s).

In need of stability → Altra Experience Form (Men’s/Women’s).

Curious to try low-drop → Altra Experience Flow 3 (Men’s/Women’s).

Shopping for a low-drop trail shoe → Altra Experience Wild 3 (Men’s/Women’s).

Racing a marathon → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s).

Logging long runs → Altra Fwd Via 2 (Men’s/Women’s).

Wanting a true racing flat → Altra Escalante 5 (Men’s/Women’s).

A lover of gnarly trails → Altra Lone Peak 9+ (Men’s/Women’s).

Balanced Cushioning, which refers to the shoe’s heel-to-toe drop, or lack thereof. Altra designs most of its shoes with no drop, meaning your foot sits flat rather than sloping downward from heel to toe. According to Altra, this can help promote your natural stride and encourage a lower-impact landing—because the heel isn’t as beefed up, you’re less likely to land on it.

Altra also introduced its 4mm line of shoes so runners can ease into zero-drop with an offset that’s approximately two stacked nickels.

According to recent reports, the first time I ran in Altras, I couldn’t help feeling like I was wearing clown shoes. Unbox a pair of Altras and you’ll see that the forefoot is much wider than on other shoes; the enlarged, anatomical toe box allows the foot to expand and gives the toes room to splay. Altra now has three different foot shapes: original (the widest), standard, and slim (the narrowest).

Wide-foot runners and runners with bunions appreciate the roominess in the toe area. But all runners can benefit from wearing Altra’s foot-shaped trainers. A narrow toebox that cramps your toes can negatively affect your performance (and set you up for injuries).

The manufacturer uses three main cushioning materials in its shoes: Ego, Ego Max, and Ego Pro.

Ego: Compared to traditional EVA, this foam provides a springier feel and more durability.

Ego Max: A foam made of compression-molded EVA and tuned for a softer feel than Ego, but it isn’t as responsive.

Ego Pro: Altra’s top-shelf foam made of thermoplastic elastomers (TPE) formed in a supercritical fluid process. It’s the brand’s lightest and most responsive cushioning material.

P35X: Altra’s newly introduced and improved version of Ego foam that’s lighter and more efficient.

Altra’s stability tech is its guide rail, which is a layer of dense midsole foam that is raised on the medial side. The guide rail serves as a “bumper” that helps counter overpronation during your stride.

Altra’s women’s shoes are built on a women’s-specific last to match the biomechanics of female feet. These shoes are narrower through the heel and midfoot and better accommodate women’s generally longer arches.

Since my introduction to Altra as a newly introduced hire at Runner’s World in 2018, I have tested several models by the brand, appreciating the shoes’ generous toe room on my wide feet. I have tested all of the shoes in this buying guide and delved into the feedback of our 350-plus shoe testers. These local runners present an inclusive testing pool, ranging in gait patterns, arch heights, and experience levels.

*All weights are for men’s 10 and women’s 8.

The Torin has undergone a revamp with its ninth iteration—but rest assured, all these changes are welcomed upgrades.

Sources indicate that the shoe has a fresh Vibram outsole, which inspired our testers to take the shoe off the road and onto the trail. “I felt that the shoe performed best on a packed dirt/trail surface where it felt like it had a great traction and springy push off. Those trail runs were at a 7:00 to 7:30 pace,” noted tester Steven Blasi.

It has been revealed that on the road and off, the Torin 9 is bouncier and softer too. Altra’s P35X midsole makes for a more cushioned ride without silencing ground feel. The support makes the shoe a great entry into zero-drop for newbies.

Lastly, the fit is more accommodating. The non-gusseted tongue provides a roomier fit for those with high insteps.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

According to recent reports, the Experience Form provides stability when you need it with Altra’s guide rail. Acting as a “bumper” on the medial side, the feature lends support to overpronators and neutral runners, alike.

“I liked the overall stability and comfort of the shoe,” said Anthony Dentino, a heel-striker who runs with a neutral gait. “The shoe was firm but provided excellent cushioning throughout, especially in the heel. Because of its weight, this is not a shoe that I would suggest for speedwork or racing but it is an excellent training shoe.”.

Another favorite feature was the shoe’s hardiness and trustworthiness in inclement weather.

“I wore them multiple times in the rain and on some snowy surfaces, but felt like they provided good traction every time,” remarked overpronator Alyssa Dever. “Not only that, they did not soak through easily in the rain, and kept my feet warm in cold temperatures (some sub-20-degree runs).”.

Shop Men’s at rei.com Shop Women’s at rei.com.

Altra Experience Form Video Review.

If switching to zero-drop still sounds like taking a major leap, you can opt for running in the Experience Flow 3 before you go for a spin in the Torin 8. The Experience Flow has a 4mm offset, which is approximately the same depth of two nickels stacked on top of each other. The heel lift is subtle, allowing you to ease into running in a low-drop shoe.

Testers loved the versatility of the shoe, appreciating its supportive Altra Ego midsole. For some, it hit that Goldilocks sweet spot of feeling not too firm, nor too soft.

“I loved that it was a not a minimalist shoe, but wasn’t the huge cloud cushion kind either,” mentioned tester Chris Greg. “It was a happy medium between the two where I felt connected to the ground but was offered plenty of support to make my 5-mile runs smooth.”.

Others described the cushioning as having just the right amount of “squishiness.”.

“I really loved how much cushioning these shoes had,” said tester Mary Hartnett. “It made my runs feel so much easier and ‘squishier’ compared to other shoes I’ve used. This extra softness was a huge help during my training because I actually felt excited to put them on every morning, and my feet didn’t feel as tired afterward.”.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

We’ve loved the Experience Wild since its first iteration. The shoe is outfitted for technical trails, offering protection with a toe sweep, gaiter attachment points, and a grippy MaxTrac outsole that can handle loose, uneven terrain. It’s also a great option for those who run on bridle paths and groomed rail trails. The Experience Wild 3 is flexible, has an accommodating wide fit in the midfoot and toe area, and a padded tongue that makes the fit snug and enclosed, so pebbles and sand can be kept out.

The biggest update to the Experience Wild 3 is the mesh upper, which provides a more secure fit and more breathability.

“V3 takes the shoe to the next level with a redesigned upper that fits more generously but doesn’t make you feel like you are swimming around, a more plush cushioning that absorbs firmer ground yet remaining stable, and a lug pattern on the MaxTrac outsole that I felt was superior to each of the previous models in terms of grip,” remarked tester John Mikovits.

The Experience Wild 3+ ($165) is also available and has a Vibram Megagrip outsole.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

Industry observers note that the Vanish Carbon 3 feels like a true super while preserving Altra’s fit and feel. The racing shoe is the first in its line with a 4mm offset; the Altra shoe team realized their super shoe needed a drop so they wouldn’t be outmatched by competitors. Altra’s running economy tests revealed the Vanish Carbon 3 had 2.6 percent better running economy compared to the Vanish Carbon 2.

A carbon plate is sandwiched between FastRce, which is pure PEBA. The plate has a split big toe to allow for engagement and power. All this is housed in an upper with Altra’s signature roomy toebox that provides generous wiggle room for your toes to splay.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

As of updating this buying guide, I only just laced up in the Fwd Via 2 after meeting with Altra at the Runner’s World Shoe Summit before the NYC Marathon. The original Fwd Via was an instant favorite from first run. The shoe has a rocker profile and high cushioning, making the low heel-to-toe drop easier to get used to if you’re a zero-drop virgin. It’s great for long runs and recovery runs, and has a generous bed of foam for run/walkers.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

It’s been two and a half years since the release of the Escalante 4—but the Escalante 5 makes that length of time worth the wait.

It has been revealed that nothing has dramatically changed with the Escalante 5: same roomy toebox, same breathable knit upper, same Ego midsole, and same 24 mm stack height. Instead of fully revamping the shoe, the Altra team refined it with a few tweaks.

The strobel and sockliner are made of TPEE for even more comfort. In this way, you still get plenty of ground feel in this minimalistic, lightweight trainer, but with added comfort and support. The outsole also has more rubber to enhance traction and durability.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

In a recent development, the Lone Peak 9+ is the first iteration of the shoe with a Vibram Megagrip outsole. This makes the shoe have outstanding traction on wet or dry surfaces. RW Tester feedback confirms Vibram Megagrip’s traction on uneven, slippery terrain.

Mentioned tester Shelby Brett, “I greatly appreciate that the lugs on the shoe are significant and that they go in multiple directions, again adding to my confidence underfoot.”.

It has been revealed that the shoe has a durable ripstop upper and an extra eyelet for a more locked-in fit. Testers loved the ground feel of the Lone Peak 9+, saying the shoe had the perfect balance of cushioning and protection. Another highlight was that spacious toebox.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

Do I need to ease into zero-drop shoes?

Sources indicate that we recommend starting slow and short if it’s your first time running in zero-drop shoes. Shoes with a drop have more cushioning in the heel. If you’re a heel-striker, you may need to run in a zero-drop shoe with a higher stack height to provide more support under the heel area. Try Altra’s 4mm shoes first to become accustomed to a lower-drop shoe.

What is the difference between Altra’s guide rail and Brooks’s guide rails?

Altra’s guide rail runs along the medial side of the shoe, acting as a bumper and preventing your foot from collapsing during sharp turns or if your feet roll inward during your gait cycle (overpronation).

Brooks’s guide rails are on the medial and lateral sides of the shoe. Like Altra’s guide rail, the guide rails also provide stability when you need it, making the shoes supportive for overpronators and neutral runners. The guide rails act as bumpers, helping align the knee and ankle.
