Minimum points needed: ~75,000 Aeroplan points (70,000 base + 5,000 stopover). Build this through Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, or Bilt transfers.

For the FI-minded traveler, this is a high-ROI, low-cash-cost adventure that fits perfectly into a strategy of saving aggressively while experiencing the world nearly free.

## Why This Is Rated Moderate — And How to Handle It This sweet spot earns a **moderate difficulty** rating — not because the math is complicated, but because the booking process has more moving parts than a simple domestic award. **What makes it moderate:** 1. **Complex routing with a stopover** — Aeroplan's online tool doesn't always handle multi-city stopover bookings cleanly. You may need to call Aeroplan to finalize the itinerary, which adds a step and requires you to have your routing clearly planned before you dial. 2. **Partner award availability** — You're booking seats on ANA, Singapore Airlines, or other Star Alliance carriers, not Air Canada. Partner space is real and accessible (this scores a 4/5 for availability), but it requires searching specifically for it on aeroplan.com and sometimes triangulating with partner airline websites. 3. **Points transfer timing** — You need points in your Aeroplan account before completing the booking, which means coordinating a transfer after confirming space exists. Chase's instant transfer largely solves this problem. **Three tips to make it manageable:** - **Use aeroplan.com's multi-city search first** to understand what routing options exist before calling. Come to any phone call with a primary and backup itinerary already researched. - **Book 6–12 months out** using the 355-day window. More availability, more flexibility, less stress. - **Do one transfer before you need to** — move a small amount of points to Aeroplan just to practice the process and verify your accounts are linked. If you've successfully booked a domestic business class award before, this is a natural next step. The complexity is manageable, and the reward — business class across two ocean crossings with a Tokyo stopover — is absolutely worth the extra 45 minutes of work.

Recent findings suggest that identify your final destination and choose a stopover city that lies along a logical routing. Popular stopover cities include Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), Tokyo (ANA hub), Frankfurt (Lufthansa hub), and Zurich (Swiss hub). The stopover city must be a connection point that Aeroplan considers valid for your route.

In a recent development, on aircanada.com, use the multi-city search option. Enter your origin to the stopover city as the first segment, and the stopover city to your final destination as the second segment. Set business class and search. The system will show you combined availability and pricing with the stopover included.

Recent findings suggest that once you confirm availability, transfer the required points from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant to 24 hours), Amex Membership Rewards (1-3 days), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Transfer only after confirming both segments have availability.

Recent findings suggest that follow the booking flow on aircanada.com, selecting both segments. The system will recognize the stopover and price it as a single one-way award. Confirm the total mileage cost matches the one-way rate for your destination — the stopover should add zero additional miles.

With up to 45 days at your stopover city, plan accommodations and activities. Consider using hotel points for your stopover stay — Hyatt points in Istanbul or IHG points in Singapore pair well with an Aeroplan stopover. The stopover is the bonus trip, so treat it as a mini-vacation within your larger journey.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on one-way awards. This is more than enough time for a genuine visit to your stopover city. You can stay as briefly as 24 hours (anything less is considered a connection, not a stopover) or as long as 45 days before continuing to your final destination.

Sources indicate that no. The free stopover on a one-way award is included at no additional mileage cost. Your total point cost is determined by the origin-to-final-destination pricing, not by the number of stops along the way. A flight from Upcoming York to Bangkok with a stopover in Istanbul costs the same as New York to Bangkok direct.

Aeroplan prices round trips as two one-way tickets. Each one-way award allows one free stopover, so a round-trip booking can include up to two stopovers — one on the outbound and one on the return. This effectively turns a round trip into a four-destination itinerary.

Lufthansa, Swiss, Austrian, and THAI Airways impose significant fuel surcharges on award tickets that can add $100 to $400 per segment. To minimize out-of-pocket costs, route through carriers with no or low surcharges: Turkish Airlines, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines (on most routes), and United. Check the fare breakdown before confirming your booking.

Industry observers note that this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Aeroplan's free stopover on one-way awards is a genuinely unique feature that no other major North American loyalty program offers. The ability to spend a week in Istanbul, Singapore, or Tokyo as a free add-on to your business class award makes Aeroplan one of the most valuable programs in the travel rewards ecosystem. Combine this with access to 26+ Star Alliance carriers, online booking for stopover routings, and 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, and Bilt, and you have a program that delivers outsized value for the ChooseFI community. Build a transferable points balance, identify your dream two-destination trip, and let Aeroplan's stopover rule turn one award into two vacations.

Canyon’s PACE Cockpit Has a Clever Answer to One of Integrated Bars’ Biggest Problems

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Integrated cockpits can be light, aerodynamic, and good-looking.
  • I’ve given Canyon’s PACE system plenty of criticism in my reviews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Integrated cockpits can be light, aerodynamic, and good-looking. They can also make simple jobs harder than they need to be. Adjusting your position can mean cutting a steerer tube. Replacing a broken handlebar can mean buying a whole newly introduced cockpit. And routing brake hoses through everything can turn a small change into a long afternoon.

I’ve given Canyon’s PACE system plenty of criticism in my reviews. It’s proprietary, and integrated systems come with real compromises. But after swapping the drops on the Endurace CF SLX 9 I have in for review, I want to give Canyon credit for a thoughtful design choice.

The main section of the PACE cockpit is called the T-Bar. Canyon’s system lets you adjust cockpit height by up to 20 mm in 5mm increments, without cutting the steerer. The cockpit is also made up of three pieces, with the drop sections bolted to the T-Bar. That offers a couple of advantages.

First, it makes the bar width adjustable. The T-Bar has three width positions, 25 mm apart, for a total range of 50 mm. The actual widths depend on the drop shape. See the table below.

The bolt-on drops also let Canyon offer five shapes with different dimensions. If the drops that come on your new Canyon don’t suit you, you can swap them for another option.

Sources indicate that my Endurace review bike came with the Compact drops. They have a 108mm drop, width settings from 390 to 440 mm, and 8 degrees of flare. I prefer a narrower bar with a deeper drop and more flare, so I switched to Canyon’s Control drops. They have a 120mm drop, adjust from 370 to 420 mm, and feature 17 degrees of flare.

*U.S. prices at the time of writing. Bar tape and fixing screws are included.

Here’s what I needed to do to make the swap: unwrap the bar, loosen and slide off the controls, remove the old drops, install the newly introduced ones, then tighten everything and rewrap the bar. Canyon includes fresh bar tape with the replacement drops.

Canyon also includes a clever cardboard tool that helps you evenly align your controls. I loved it!

According to recent reports, with most one-piece integrated cockpits, switching to a different bar shape or replacing a broken drop means replacing the whole assembly. Depending on the bike’s routing, that may also mean disconnecting or replacing brake hoses and bleeding the brakes.

On the PACE, the brake hoses run behind the drop sections rather than through them, so I didn’t have to disconnect or cut them. That meant no brake bleed, no risk of ending up with a hose that’s too short, and no replacing the entire cockpit.

That also matters if you crash and break a drop. With a one-piece handlebar and stem, a broken bar can mean replacing the whole assembly. With PACE, you can replace the damaged section.*.

*If you break a drop, check the PACE T-Bar, or stem, for damage, too. Replace it if necessary.

In a recent development, the system can also make bike travel less nerve-racking. If your bar tape is set up so the controls can slide on and off without rewrapping, you can unbolt the drops and let them hang out of the way. The bike packs a little narrower, and the handlebar ends are less exposed to side impacts. I’ve had bars damaged in transit more times than I can count, so I appreciate this feature.

Recent findings suggest that PACE is still proprietary, and those concerns don’t disappear because one part of the system is clever. But integrated cockpits often force riders to accept limited adjustability, few shape options, and costly replacements. Canyon has found a useful way to make its handlebar easier to fit, repair, and travel with. For that, it deserves some credit.

The Top 11 Women’s Running Shoes That Have the Comfiest Fit, Coziest Cushioning, and Most Responsive Ride

Editor’s Note, November 12, 2026: End-of-year sales have already taken off. Our Best Stability Shoe, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, is now on sale with 19% off. (We are currently testing the newest model, the Adrenaline GTS 26.) Our Best for Speedwork Shoe, the Adidas Adizero Evo SL, is also discounted with 20% off.

We are in a upcoming era of running shoes, from stacked super trainers to plated racers to gravel models decked out with bike-inspired treads.

The industry formerly criticized for “shrink it and pink it,” i.e., the practice of making smaller-size men’s shoes and slapping pink on them and calling them women’s shoes, has gone to great lengths crafting footwear that’s women-specific.

Sources indicate that brands are taking care to produce shoes that accommodate the average woman’s foot shape: wider in the midfoot area, narrower around the heel. But don’t think this list is free of pink shoes. The traditionally feminine colors have been reclaimed by brands like Nike (turns out it’s flashy and easier to spot neon pink Alphaflys). Here you’ll find trainers of every color for all types of women’s feet and women runners.

Shopping for a daily trainer → Brooks Glycerin 23On a budget → Latest Balance EllipseMostly a run/walker → Hoka Clifton 11On the path to recovery → Hoka Bondi 9Adding in speedwork → Adidas Adizero Evo SLLogging long runs → Nike Vomero 18Racing a marathon → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3An overpronator → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25Suffering from bunions → Altra Torin 9Running on rail trails → lululemon WildfeelNew to technical terrain → Altra Experience Wild 3.

Industry observers note that runner’s World has been around for almost 60 years, providing news, fitness tips, and, of course, gear recommendations for runners. Our product guides for essentials like running shoes and shorts come from our hardworking test team, who put the latest and greatest running gear through their paces day in and day out. These selections come from Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen, who blazes the trails and is an ultramarathon beast, and me, Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer. I have written about running gear for a decade and hold an even longer Boston Marathon streak, beginning in 2013.

We picked these shoes based on feedback from the runners who are part of our 300-runner-strong team of local wear-testers and the expertise of our editors. We evaluated every shoe over the course of at least 100 miles, paying attention to overall performance, comfort, ride, longevity, and value.

Recent findings suggest that to ensure our shoe recommendations are truly comprehensive and trustworthy, we grabbed a wide array of shoe types to put through our rigorous testing. This involved evaluating them across diverse terrains, including challenging trails, smooth tracks, varied road surfaces, and—of course—treadmills. Our massive wear-test team allows us to gather feedback from individuals ranging from sprinters to marathoners, runners of different weights and body types, those with different foot strikes, shoe needs, and biomechanics. By combining varied surface testing with a diverse runner pool, we learn a ton about each shoe’s performance and suitability for a wide range of consumers and individual experiences. Based on our extensive testing, the options below are currently the best running shoes for women.

In our testing, we found the Glycerin 23 excelled as a daily trainer over the Ghost 18 among women testers. The formerly max-cushioned Glycerin has evolved into an everyday shoe that you can take out on easy days to long runs. Our women testers preferred the Glycerin 23 over the Ghost 18 because of the shoes’ fit. Several testers reported hot spots in the Ghost 18’s bunion-prone area. The Glycerin 23, on the other hand, was praised for its broad platform, soft and plush knit upper, and ample wiggle room in the toebox.

“The shoe is cushioned in a way that makes me want to do all my long runs in them,” mentioned tester and Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá. “It doesn’t drag as some cushioned shoes do, but feels responsive. My go-to comparison of a cushioned shoe is the Saucony Echelon which I love for walking/hiking, but which I cannot do long miles in because the shoe drags, makes me work too hard. In comparison, the Glycerin is plushy but responds well to my moods and the corresponding pace changes.”.

Sources indicate that the shoe has Brooks’s DNA Tuned midsole foam, which was introduced in the even cushier Glycerin Max. The experience running on DNA Tuned is just like Černá described: plush, supportive, responsive, ideal for running long.

One of our women testers described the Ellipse v1 as “nearly perfect.”.

Newly introduced Balance’s intent with the shoe was to provide a high-cushioned, trampoline-like bounce experience for recreation. It’s the kind of shoe you can wear for daily training, while you lace up in it for a casual, conversationally paced group run. The Ellipse was specifically made to make runs easier.

In a recent development, fresh Foam X is dialed in to produce a foamy, high-rebound ride with reliable shock absorption. It’s a ride that makes me look forward to lacing up the Ellipse and taking it out for whatever kind of run my heart desires on the spot. The tweaked foam makes running in the soft, springy shoe feel like a treat.

According to recent reports, “The best word to describe the cushion is plush,” said tester Laura Parks. “It has the extreme cushion sensation of a Hoka Bondi without feeling the weight.” She described the ride as unlike any she’s had running in other Fresh Foam X models.

It has been revealed that we’re still in the process of testing the Clifton 11, but the team is already loving the shoe weeks into testing. Everything we love about Hoka—plush cushioning, cozy fit, responsive midsole—is usually encapsulated in each iteration of the Clifton. The 11 is no exception. It was a hard follow after the ClifTEN, but the Clifton 11 makes runs feel effortless, thanks to the compression-molded EVA midsole foam, which provides high rebound and a comfy platform that pillows your foot.

It has been revealed that the shoe has Hoka’s Meta-Rocker geometry to promote smooth transitions. Sidewalls make the fit snug but not too narrow as the Hoka Bondi 9.

According to recent reports, the Clifton 11 is also excellent for run/walking because of that cushioned support and rocker geometry. These elements make the Clifton reliable at any pace.

According to recent reports, the Bondi 9, one of Hoka’s plushest daily trainers, is somehow cushier and sleeker with this patch. Hoka added 10 mm to the midsole—but this shoe is no chonk. We even tested it sprinting on the treadmill; the supercritically foamed EVA provides high energy return and soft support. But we especially like using the shoe for run/walking and recovery.

“The Bondi 9 delivers great protection with an amazingly smooth roll,” noted tester Tiffany Volpe. “I can see why there is so much hype behind the Hoka and [why it’s called] the Queen of Cushion. I felt like I was sitting down in the midsole. I felt locked in with ample protection especially in the tongue and collar.

“I found the Bondi a perfect recovery day shoe and one that I reach for when I just want to head out for a long slow run to clear my head.”.

The shoe was also rated high in stability among testers, and they appreciated the reflective, as well.

According to recent reports, runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate boldly dubbed the Adizero Evo SL Shoe of the Year merely a month into 2025. That sentiment is upheld and shared; the shoe is Best Overall on our list of Best Running Shoes. For $150 (and frequently on sale), just above the cost of the New Balance Ellipse, you could also say it’s Best Value. And because of its secret sauce, Adidas’s Lightstrike Pro midsole, which is featured in the brand’s super shoes, you could also say it’s Best for Speedwork, too.

Sources indicate that one woman tester gamely raced in the Adizero Evo SL, and experienced excellent results. “The coolest thing about these to me was the weight and cushion,” remarked that tester, Caroline Lennon. “It was a perfect balance of being light and springy but still feeling well-cushioned and supported. They were so comfortable at all paces and let me feel faster than I was anticipating. They felt best at a harder effort. My 5K race was surprisingly fast given that there was no carbon plate!”.

It has been revealed that breaking: A Nike shoe with Hoka-plush cushioning. The Vomero 18 is unlike any Nike we’ve tested. It has a dual-density midsole with 46 mm of ZoomX and ReactX foam, which puts this shoe in the super trainer category. What you get is a bouncy, soft ride that makes long runs an energized quest instead of a Saturday (or Sunday) morning slog.

Industry observers note that “I didn’t expect to love this shoe as much as I do!” noted Associate Health and Fitness Editor Kristine Kearns, a self-described loyal Brooks Ghost fan. “I wasn’t sure if I would like the Vomero 18 because of how much heel cushioning there is, and how it kind of elevates me forward in that way. But it turns out the shoe provides so much stability, even on the side.”.

Industry observers note that the source of the stability Kearns is referring to: the wider platform. Nike collected input from women testers, who wanted a wider fit in the midfoot. The result is a more accommodating foot shape that provides midrun support.

The Endorphin Elite 3 makes good with super adjustments after a strong reception with the Endorphin Elite 2. Several testers loved the previous model’s aggressive bounce, becoming inspired to race in it at their next marathon. Others, like me, had difficulty troubleshooting the squishy TPEE foam. It was volatile, pogo stick-like bounce that required mastering before you went all out on this somewhat unstable super shoe.

Saucony tamed the shoe this go-around. That pogo stick bounce is still there, but the ride is more stable with a connected heel and midfoot (not the slightly decoupled heel that made it more likely to turn your foot inward navigating sharp turns). The PwrTrac outsole also adds more support by providing grippy traction.

Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 Review.

The Adrenaline GTS 25 is pumped with even more foam for a comfier, more supportive ride. Brooks added 1 mm of DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and 3 mm in the forefoot, resulting in a slightly higher stack height, lower heel drop, and more responsive ride.

It has been revealed that dense guide rails on the lateral and medial sides of the shoe act as bumpers to help with ankle and knee alignment while running. The support aids overpronators and late-onset overpronators alike.

“One of the shoe’s best features is the sense of security it provides,” said tester Kylie Rodriguez. “The Adrenaline series is known for its stability, and this model is no exception. I felt confident and secure on every surface, from slick sidewalks to uneven dirt paths.

“This blend of comfort, stability, and a lightweight feel makes the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 a fantastic and reliable choice for any runner looking for a do-it-all shoe. It’s a solid, dependable performer that won’t let you down. Another solid key component to the shoe was the cupping support the heel gave my strong heel striking steps even more confidence and support.”.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

We’re still getting in Torin 9 feedback, but it’s safe to say early on that the shoe is a worthy follow-up to the Torin 8. When Altra was founded in 2009, its core values were balanced zero-drop cushioning, an accommodating toebox for toe-splaying, and a women-specific fit. The brand has evolved with a 4mm-drop shoe line but its values haven’t changed.

According to recent reports, the Torin, basically the Ghost version of a zero-drop shoe, is a terrific cushioned entry into running a no-drop shoe. Dual-density foam provides a moderate but supportive bed of cushioning to help you transition into zero-drop running. Runners with wide feet and bunions will also appreciate Altra’s wide toebox, which not only allows your toes to wiggle but also helps with your biomechanics (squeezed toes help you run faster, mentioned no one ever).

The updated outsole is Vibram XS Dura, which is grippier than the rubber on the Torin 8. I like how the shoe can dabble off road and not have to worry about falling face-first when I traverse onto a trail—which is rare.

The lululemon shoe team has made it its mission to produce women-specific trainers since the release of the brand’s first running shoe, the Blissfeel, in 2022. Their latest model, the Wildfeel, provides the same comfy, secure fit with a responsive, high-rebound ride off-road.

The shoe has men’s and women’s editions, which are tweaked to support each sex’s anatomical differences and distinct biomechanics. For instance, the forefoot of the women’s shoe is slightly more flexible than the men’s to complement the shorter toes, longer arch, and shorter instep typical of women’s feet.

It has been revealed that our testers appreciated the Wildfeel’s flexibility and overall comfort. It’s a good choice for runners upcoming to the trail who want more of a hybrid option that can take on some technical track.

“I loved the flexibility of the Wildfeels!” said tester Jenny Stump. “I am primarily a road runner. These felt comfortable enough that I could do some easy miles on the road as well as tackle some trails with uneven surfaces. All the trail runners I have previously tried felt more stiff and had such a thick sole that I wouldn’t even want to warm up on the road with them.”.

According to recent reports, what I love most about the Experience Wild 3 is that it’s a trail shoe that feels like a road shoe. The fit is accommodating in the midfoot and toe area—Altra is known for its spacious toeboxes that allow your toes to splay—and the collar and tongue are padded and cushioned.

It has been revealed that the Altra Ego P35 foam is responsive on the trail and provides a nice balance of support and ground feel. Another win for me, the mostly road runner: the shoe is incredibly flexible. No stiffness or hot spots that cause my feet a world of hurt the first couple of runs before they’re broken in.

Industry observers note that the shoes have gaiter attachments to provide even more protection and a toe sweep. The drop is a low 4 mm, which isn’t as intimidating as going full zero (though if you’re game, the Lone Peak 9 is a good place to start).

The shoe is also available as the Experience Wild 3+, which has a Vibram Megagrip outsole. It’s a little more expensive at $165. If you want tackier grip, go for it. But the 3.5mm lugs on the MaxTrac outsole suit me and fellow testers just fine on slush, mud, and icy snow.

It has been revealed that women’s feet have distinct structural differences than men’s feet. From shape to proportions to biomechanics, all of these things significantly impact shoe fit and comfort. For example, while men’s feet typically present a more uniform width from heel to forefoot, women’s feet tend to be wider in the forefoot relative to the heel. Any lady who has felt their toes get squished as their heel slips right out of the shoe knows this concern.

According to recent reports, recognizing these anatomical differences, and responding to the hoards of women runners clamoring for something better, running shoe manufacturers have (finally) started to incorporate more gender-specific design elements into their products. This means crafting shoes with distinct features tailored to the unique shape and biomechanics of women’s feet. For instance, a women’s running shoe might feature a wider toebox to accommodate the broader ball of the foot, while a narrower heel counter secures the back of the foot and prevents slippage.

Additionally, the materials used in the heel construction might differ between men’s and women’s versions to account for variations in where we strike our foot when we land. Women and men obviously have different centers of gravity—especially when we’re pregnant—and that changes how we strike and the wear pattern of our soles.

Brands are not just shrinking and pinking the shoes anymore. Their aim is to enhance performance and prevent running-related aches and pains. A shoe that fits properly and supports the foot’s natural movement can improve running efficiency and reduce the risk of common running-related injuries, such as blisters, plantar fasciitis, the pedi-ick black toenails, and shin splints.

Sources indicate that researchers have also found that, because women tend to have wider hips than men, women’s feet are more likely to strike the ground toward the outside of their shoe soles. The inward rolling of the foot, called pronation, that results from this explains why more women are believed to overpronate than men (aka, walk a bit duck-footed.). Some women’s running shoes account for this increased tendency with stability features in the sole, such as guide rails and medial posts, to provide more support.

This list includes what we regard as the best shoe in its category. But there are still plenty of other shoes for you to choose from.

For the plushest ride and more foam underfoot, check out the Best Cushioned Running Shoes.

If you’re an overpronator or think you need more support, take a look at the Best Stability Shoes.

And if you want more of a selection of non-road shoes, visit the Best Trail Shoes.

No matter the distance or your shoe preferences, there’s a great shoe for you on our lists.

What’s the size difference between men’s and women’s running shoes?

If you prefer wearing men’s running shoes, size down 1.5. For example: A women’s size 10 would equal a men’s size 8.5.

When should you change out your running shoes?

Running shoe shelf life is dependent on the runner. Some runners wear down their shoes after only a couple weeks, others have their shoes well past several months. The standard mileage on everyday trainers is 350 to 500 miles, 250 to 300 for lightweight shoes, and 100 to 250 for racing or minimalist shoes.

Sources indicate that if you don’t keep track of mileage, a good rule of thumb is switching out shoes twice a year. For racing shoes, two to three races.

How do you clean your running shoes?

It has been revealed that you can put your shoes in the washing machine with some detergent, set on cold. Never put your shoes in the dryer—it will melt the glue and make them degrade faster.

Sources indicate that instead, remove the insoles and allow them to air dry. Stuff wads of newspaper inside your shoes and leave them to sit for a couple hours so the paper can absorb the moisture.

Garmin’s Best Cycling Radars Are Discounted for Black Friday—Here’s How the RearVue 820 and RTL515 Compare, and Which Is Best for Your Rides

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that cycling radar entirely changed my bike rides. After a speeding pickup passed dangerously close to me on a ride in June 2025, I installed a radar system on my road bike. Since getting a radar, I have ridden over 7,500 miles on paved and gravel roads, and I’ve had a radar mounted on my bike for almost all of them—I cannot imagine riding without it. It’s the best safety upgrade I’ve made in more than three decades of riding and something every road and gravel rider should try.

Industry observers note that for Black Friday, Garmin—the market leader in cycling radar—has its two top-performing Varia radar systems on sale. This includes the benchmark RTL515 and the latest RearVue 820 released earlier this year. Both are exceptional radar units, and our top-tested models—but which one is best for you, or as a holiday gift for a cyclist in your life?

SHOP MORE GARMIN DEALS SHOP MORE GEAR DEALS.

Garmin Black Friday Radar Deals.

Above: Test Editor Dan Chabanov digs into all of the details in this video.

Recent findings suggest that all cycling radar systems work essentially the same. The radar unit emits pulses of electromagnetic radio waves that bounce off vehicles approaching from behind before returning to the device. Using the reflected beams, the device calculates and tracks vehicles’ distance, direction, and relative speed, and sends that tracking data to your cycling computer. The head unit then provides an audible warning and graphically displays vehicles’ relative location and speed, giving you time to react accordingly. Most devices also integrate the radar with an LED taillight to alert drivers to your presence.

Sources indicate that what separates good radar units from bad ones is the proprietary algorithms each brand uses to tune sensitivity and detection for their respective devices. A good radar consistently provides clear warnings of approaching vehicles, but bad ones can provide frequent false alarms, or worse, fail to warn of an approaching vehicle.

In the year and a half since I started using a radar light on my rides, I’ve ridden a dozen radar systems from nine brands. Several work well and I use them on my bikes, and a few of them were duds. However, of all of the cycling radars we’ve tried, none are as consistently reliable as Garmin’s Varia models.

Picking the Varia model that’s best for you (or a rider whose safety you care about) depends on a few factors. Both are excellent units, but why overpay for tech you can’t use or don’t need on your rides?

It has been revealed that the RTL515 is the benchmark cycling radar system, and we judge all others against it. The 515 works more reliably than any other radar we tested—Other systems might have longer battery life, weigh less, or pack a brighter light, but none are as well-rounded or as easy to use as this Garmin. It detects vehicles up to 153 yards away, and its 65-lumen flash is visible to drivers from 1.2 miles.

According to recent reports, the 515 packs up to 8 hours of battery life per charge, and weighs 72 grams (without a mount). It connects to most cycling computers featuring Bluetooth or ANT+ compatibility, but Garmin’s Varia radar phone app is also stellar. If you ride with your phone on your bar, it can serve as a display, and it can deliver audio notifications through headphones even if you’re not listening to music or a podcast.

In a recent development, garmin’s newest cycling radar improves on the Varia RTL515’s greatness. Compared to the 515, the RearVue 820 has more battery life (up to 15 hours), a brighter flashing light (100 lumens), and greater vehicle-detection range (up to 191 yards). Plus, the 820 adds a brake-light feature that increases rear light intensity as you slow.

In a recent development, crucially, the RearVue 820 incorporates features found on no other radars (from Garmin or any other brand). While other radars often drop vehicles when they slow down behind you, the 820 tracks vehicles traveling at your same speed; it’s a handy feature you don’t know you need until you try it. Additionally, if you use a Garmin Edge X40- or X50-series computer, the radar tracks a vehicle that changes lanes behind you. It also demonstrates icons to indicate each vehicle’s size (small, medium, or large).

Industry observers note that the RCT715 is basically the RTL515 with a rear-facing camera. However, it is larger, heavier, and has a shorter battery life than the 515. It’s so heavy (148 grams) that it requires a proprietary mount. The camera also greatly reduces battery life—in continuous video mode, it might not last through long rides. However, the 715 is worth considering for bike commuters, riders who advocate for better cycling infrastructure, or those who want peace of mind.

6 Budget Running Watches That Deliver Accurate GPS, Long Battery Life, and Much More

📅 21 May 2018 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • I’ve spent the last several years testing running watches, from the $800 flagships with topographical maps and training-readiness scores to the ones that do almost nothing except tell you how fast you’re going.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Basic” has become an insult, and I’d like us to cut that right the heck out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I’ve spent the last several years testing running watches, from the $800 flagships with topographical maps and training-readiness scores to the ones that do almost nothing except tell you how fast you’re going. Both have their place.

Recent findings suggest that “Basic” has become an insult, and I’d like us to cut that right the heck out. A basic running watch isn’t a cheap, crappy watch—it’s a watch that does what it was meant for. Pace, distance, splits, a lap button you can hit with sweaty or frozen fingers, a battery that won’t quit at mile 20, and a screen you can read no matter how tired. That’s the job. These do the job.

They’re also—and this surprises people—what a lot of very fast runners wear. Stand near the front of a starting corral sometime and count the watches that cost less than the shoes. Elites don’t need a wrist device to tell them they’re tired. They need accurate splits.

In a recent development, if you’re new, that’s the biggest thing you need. Nothing kills a running habit faster than forty metrics you don’t understand that insist you’re doing it wrong. Same goes if you’re kitting out a kid for their first track or cross-country season: buy the simple device. It’ll survive the school bus, the mud, and the whole season. And they’ll learn to run by feel, which is the entire point. My first Garmin was essentially a pace-watching brick on my wrist and I still managed PRs. Here’s what I’d actually put on your wrist.

In a recent development, our Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate tested the Pace 4 and came away calling it a fast, accurate, lightweight GPS watch that nails the basics without charging laptop-level prices. The Coros Pace 4 adds a sharp, always-on AMOLED display and significantly improved battery life over the Pace 3, offering up to 31 hours in max GPS mode (about 24 with the screen always on), all while keeping the case compact and comfortable on the wrist.

It has been revealed that it tracks advanced run-specific metrics like running power, ground contact time, and left/right strength balance: That might not be necessary for latest and casual runners, but they are useful measurements for training. (There’s a reason why RW Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen named it “Best Value” in our overall Best Running Watches guide.).

GPS performance is a standout, with dual-frequency technology delivering smooth, reliable tracks even in neighborhoods and city environments that can throw cheaper chips off course. Dengate also highlights the new voice log feature, which lets you record post-run thoughts that automatically transcribe into the Coros app, making training logs easier to maintain.

Sources indicate that at 40 grams with the silicone band (32 grams with nylon), the watch feels barely there in daily use and workouts, though Dengate dislikes the finicky digital dial—especially with gloves—and finds notification text too small to read easily mid-run. For runners who value turn-by-turn, full-color maps, the Pace 4’s breadcrumb-only navigation may be a limitation, but for most no-frills runners wanting accurate tracking, solid battery life, and a modern screen at an entry-level price, it is a compelling choice.

Look, I’ve spent more money on a pair of running shoes than this watch costs. And, honestly? That’s a little embarrassing for the shoes. At $170, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium is wildly outperforming its price tag, and in the words of Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate, if you can find better (for the price) I’ll eat it.

It has been revealed that for new runners, this watch is a gift. There’s a whole training library that walks you through what a tempo run or a fartlek actually is, instead of assuming you already know. You get pace, cadence, heart rate zones, running power, and form metrics like ground contact time, which is stuff I did not have on watches costing three times as much. It also has free offline maps with turn-by-turn navigation, so you can leave your phone in your pocket. The cheapest Garmin with offline mapping is over $700.

Sources indicate that the recovery metrics are right up there with Garmin and Apple: Training load, VO2 Max, readiness recommendations, sleep and HRV tracking that’s detailed enough to make you rethink that 5 p.m. Diet Coke. It nudges you toward rest days with a little less guilt than Garmin.

According to recent reports, the nitpicks: The user experience needs polish—do not disturb is fiddlier than it should be, and the four buttons are sensitive. I’ve paused mid-run more than once with an errant sleeve. Still, for the money? Nothing touches it.

At just around $300, the Polar Pacer has some great training specific features that make it especially useful for competitive runners training on a budget.

In a recent development, its built-in running program can help you create a training proposal to get ready for a 5K, 10K, half marathon, or marathon. Using the Polar Flow app, you can select your race type and date (or the name of the race) and it will create specific workouts to follow within the app that are synched to your watch to follow along. It also provides comprehensive training insights after intervals and long runs, and tracks your long-term fitness trends outside of training.

There are also niche, but useful features like fueling and hydration reminders, and “Training Load Pro,” which monitors strain and recovery. As someone who isn’t great at taking cues from my body when it’s time to take a break, having an active reminder was helpful. (And something you can usually expect in an affordable running watch.).

In a recent development, although I generally liked Polar’s hardware and software design, I felt that Polar could have used the space of its 1.2-inch MIP display a bit more effectively. Much of the text was small, and the screen had lots of unnecessary white space that could have been used to support more specs, or at least a larger font.

I also found it a bit unintuitive that the “red” button was used for intervals, rather than a start/stop button. It ended up working out great–it’s a helpful button–but there was a bit of a learning curve.

For race runners who want support to help them train, but may not be able to afford a coach or training program, the Pacer feels about as close to having a coach on your wrist as possible at this price point.

The Garmin Forerunner 70 is Garmin’s new entry-level running watch, priced at $250, and it’s a great pick for beginners.

It has a 1.2-inch AMOLED touchscreen, which is the same panel tech found on watches costing twice as much, so it looks and feels more premium than you’d expect at this price. More importantly, it includes Training Readiness and Training Status, features that used to be reserved for watches costing $400 or more, plus an on-device Quick Workouts generator and free Garmin Coach aims for 5K, 10K, and half-marathon training—no subscription needed.

The five buttons make it easy to navigate menus, and it’s light and comfortable for daily wear. Battery life is boss too: they say it’s up to 13 days in smartwatch mode and 23 hours in GPS mode, but in real life? You’re getting a full week. It skips extras like multi-band GPS and NFC payments, but for a fresh runner focused on building a habit and understanding their training, that’s an easy trade.

Before I switched to a “proper” running watch, I started my wearable tech journey by tracking runs on an Apple Watch. I trained for my first marathon using one, and I actually still wear an Apple Watch SE between runs because of its effective multi-sport fitness tracking and quality of life features like setting voice-activated timers.

Though the Apple Watch is generally beloved, we generally steer runners towards brands like Garmin and Coros, which offer more robust tracking features and better battery life, often at lower prices than Apple’s generalist counterparts. That noted, Apple Watches still work well for casual runners, tracking the basics and giving you lifestyle features that you won’t find on other watches in this price range.

To keep it to $300 with GPS and cellular, we recommend the smaller of the SE’s two sizes, 40mm, which translates to a 1.57-inch display. (The larger 44mm version starts at $280 without cellular, though you can sometimes find it for less.) Both versions are far larger than any of my other basic recommendations, which is great if you have a larger wrist or need a large screen for visibility. I personally like the smaller version, which keeps the watch light but still easy to read.

Apple Watches also generally feature a wider range of wrist band options, first- and third-party, and the SE’s bands come in two sizes: If comfort has been an matter for you, this watch gives you the best chance of finding something that feels good.

Apple offers two related apps that utilize your run data–the fitness focused Apple Fitness and the more metrics-minded Apple Health. Fitness allows you to create workouts and segments for training, while charting deep metrics. You can see a lot of information at a glance, too, including time elapsed, heart rate, rolling mile (pace over the last mile), average pace, and distance. That remarked, I didn’t love the way Apple organized my workout data, you need to search by date rather than just checking an activity log. (Of course, you can always switch to Strava or Nike Run Club if you don’t like the system.).

If you have a child who is starting to exercise and wants to track their steps like mom and dad, the Garmin Bounce is a special smartwatch designed for kids that covers basic fitness tracking and serves as a controlled way for parents to keep tabs, both via texting and GPS tracking.

In a recent development, the Bounce is designed for kids, which is to say that it’s built to withstand them. It’s durable and water-resistant with an IP68 rating, so it can go anywhere with them. The battery lasts up to two days, minimizing the chance that it’ll run dry on them. It also has a colorful UI that encourages kids to engage with the watch and their metrics, and activities and games to help get them moving.

In terms of tracking, the Bounce falls short of my usual standards for tracking: It just shows time and distance. For a kid–not a teen or even a tween, but a kid–that’s about as much as they can handle or care about. That data syncs with the Garmin Jr. app, which parents can access remotely.

It’s worth noting that both the parenting and games features have elements that require mobile WiFi (LTE) support, so you will likely want to add it to your mobile data plan, which will add about $10/month to your monthly bill.

Overall, this is a great way to help kids start to move around more and start thinking about the concept of exercise.

Every watch on this list costs $300 or less. That’s the line I drew, and I drew it on purpose: you shouldn’t have to spend a car payment to find out whether you like running.

According to recent reports, I’ve spent my running career strapping these things to my wrist—testing, logging miles, and digging through what’s actually worth buying right now. What made the cut are watches that nail the fundamentals: speed, heart rate, and location, tracked with reasonable accuracy. (If the gap between 155 and 156 bpm matters to you, you need a pricier watch or, better yet, a dedicated HRM. For everyone else, this is plenty.) From there, they earn their spots with battery life that won’t leave you hunting for a charger, multi-sport modes, advanced biometrics like blood oxygen, and built-in coaching programs.

According to recent reports, here’s the part nobody says out loud: a basic watch is the best way to figure out what you actually want. It reveals you real data, real proof that the hard work is working. And by the time you’re ready to shell out for something flashier, you’ll know exactly which features you really need.

Industry observers note that at the bare minimum, an affordable running watch needs to track your pace, heart rate, route, distance, and time—with at least moderate precision, and displayed in a way you can read at mile 9 when your eyes are glazing over. It should have GPS, so you can map your routes and find your way home, and it should be accurate.

Sources indicate that but basic doesn’t mean bare-bones. Plenty of watches in this range monitor more nuanced heart rate data, like your body’s ability to use oxygen during exercise (VO2 max). Most throw in sleep tracking and multi-sport modes, and many will synthesize your training data into insights that can help you get faster.

In a recent development, spend more and you’ll get mid-tier and high-end watches with features that are nice to have but almost never essential: bigger and more precise sensors, LTE and WiFi support, contactless payment, onboard music storage. Worth knowing: some of the most elite runners in the world train and race in shockingly basic watches. The watch doesn’t run the miles. You do.

Sources indicate that checking your stats mid-run on a sunny day is miserable if the display is small and dim. The best running watches use an AMOLED display which is the same tech found in high-end smartphones and it has brighter colors and deeper contrast, so your numbers stay legible in full daylight.

According to recent reports, an AMOLED screen isn’t a guarantee at $250, but that doesn’t mean you’re stuck squinting. Several watches I recommend use a transflective Memory-in-Pixel (MIP) display, which trades vibrant color for battery efficiency and stays highly visible outdoors. Pixel density matters just as much as the panel type, as does maximum brightness, measured in nits.

Most running watches have an auto-off backlight to conserve battery, but the screen should snap on the instant you raise your arm. You should never be standing there waiting for your own watch.

Size-wise, basic running watches run small. They’re roughly 1 to 1.6 inches. A bigger screen makes it easier to see your route map and stats, and gives you room to fit more data on screen if you customize your workout display.

Every smartwatch brand makes a companion app for iOS and Android that stores and analyzes your run data. Because the watch display is tiny, your phone is almost always the better place to adjust settings, rearrange screens, and build workouts.

In a recent development, if you have an iPhone, you already know Apple Fitness. Garmin, Coros, and Polar all offer companion apps with similar functionality, though some are meaningfully easier to live with than others. And any running watch worth buying should support the massive third-party apps like Strava and Runna.

Aside from Apple’s watches, even the budget-friendly models I recommend only need charging every week or so, and they juice back up fast. The best of the best go over a fortnight on a single charge.

Keep your expectations calibrated, though: manufacturer battery estimates are best-case scenarios, and your watch probably won’t hit them. Real-world battery life varies charge to charge, and your mileage depends on, well, your mileage. Continuous GPS tracking during workouts is the biggest drain by far. You can switch features off to stretch the time between charges, but a good watch gives you plenty of run time either way.

Recent findings suggest that A good running watch should feel light enough that you forget it’s there. At this price you rarely find something heavy and bulky, but check how it sits on your wrist before you take it out for miles. Some of my picks come in multiple sizes, which helps if you have smaller or larger wrists.

Recent findings suggest that make sure the band is highly adjustable and can feel secure without being too tight. And remember that many watch bands are replaceable, so if the stock strap isn’t working for you—comfort-wise or style-wise—you have options.

Recent findings suggest that known as a “social network for athletes,” Strava has become increasingly popular since its launch in 2009. By connecting your running watch to the app, you can upload your runs to the platform for your “friends” to see and give each other “kudos”. The app also tracks PR for different distances and frequent segments that you can get badges for.

It can be an easy way for you to keep all your running data in the same place, especially if you’re using different brands of running watches to track your runs. Plus, you can unlock more features, such as advanced training metrics, with the full paid membership.

What heart rate do I need to hit to get faster?

Sources indicate that according to Mayo Clinic, runners should aim for a target heart rate zone of 70- to 85 percent of their maximum heart rate to improve speed over time. This is also known as Zone 2, which some runners tout as the ultimate training metric. A running watch can help you figure out your max heart rate and will allow you to monitor your heart rate during and after the run.

Do basic running watches track distance and heart rate accurately?

For both mapping and logging distance, smartwatches rely on a Global Position System (GPS), which uses satellites to precisely track your location. The quality of your specific watch’s tracking can vary, both based on the quality of the GPS system and on environmental factors like tall buildings and crowds.

That mentioned, the quality of GPS tracking in smartwatches is quite high across the board: Nothing’s perfect, but you can expect your location to be accurate to within a few feet, and your movement to be captured precisely.

Running watches are set to connect with US GPS systems, but you can also opt to connect with other systems like Galileo (European Union) and GLONASS (Russia) to try to improve your accuracy, something I recommend for those experiencing disruptions.

Industry observers note that for heart rate, smartwatches rely on optical heart rate sensors that use light (those green beams coming out of the bottom of your watch) to measure blood flow changes in the skin's capillaries and determine your heart rate. They are fairly accurate, generally to within a few beats per minute (BPM). That said, a dedicated heart rate monitor that you strap to your chest will generally provide more accurate readings.

Sources indicate that cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

Tech Report: I Rode My Road Bike Where the Pavement Ends to Find Out How Much Gravel It Could Handle

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, just as the seasons change, so do riders’ preferences of which types of riding are preferred.
  • According to recent reports, many of us have tried to take our road bikes on gravel, and there are steps you can take to get the most out of that underbiked gravel ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, just as the seasons change, so do riders’ preferences of which types of riding are preferred. For some, the season for taking the road bike on the local roads starts to fade as temperatures get colder and the gravel trail that parallels the road gets more appealing every degree cooler. It’s time to turn the road bike onto that gravel path.

According to recent reports, many of us have tried to take our road bikes on gravel, and there are steps you can take to get the most out of that underbiked gravel ride. After a recent lunch ride, the question was asked, “how much gravel can you take a road bike on?” Since gravel means different things to different people the easy answer is, it depends, but I wanted to stress test my road bike to find out.

I remember an old-school bike technician I used to work with told me, “you can ride any bike on anything if you are light on the bike and find the right line.” While that may be true, I wanted to find out how I could most comfortably take my road bike on everything that is off-road.

After taking my road bike where it was not designed to go, I learned some limitations as well as some simple part swaps to get the most versatility out of a road bike. Below I’ll touch on those limitations that I found and give you the most impactful changes you can make to your road bike before taking it on gravel. As Doc says to Marty McFly in Back to the Future, “Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.”.

In a recent development, the bike I decided to do the testing on is my Trek Madone, and I’ve had 700x28mm Pirelli P Zero Race tires pretty much since I’ve built up the bike. Those are by far my favorite road tires for all-around road riding—they’re fast, grip well through turns, and are surprisingly durable for performing so well.

Even though I love those Pirellis for road riding most of the year, I knew I would want to have extra rubber when I’m chattering along through some of the chunkier gravel I’d be testing on. I decided to swap out my tires for a set of the Continental Grand Prix 5000 in 700x32 mm. The maximum tire width on the Gen 8 Trek Madone is 32mm, but these Continental tires only measure just over 30mm because of the internal rim width on the stock Bontrager wheels. I could probably bump up the width a bit more, but I decided to keep the 32mm just in case I knock the wheels out of true during the stress testing.

Going wider with your tires adds an extra bit of compliance and more contact patch—both will help your ride quality when you take your road bike out on gravel. Part of the trick with going wider and bumping down your tire pressure is to make sure your tires are set up as tubeless. Setting your tires up tubeless allows you to run a lower tire pressure without the risk of pinch flats.

In a recent development, when you take your road bike on gravel, new bar tape can help by decreasing a little bit of the vibration. As you ride, most bar tapes compress a bit from the constant pressure of your hands. Some tapes may even start to unravel in sections where you keep your hands a lot—we used to see this a lot when customers couldn’t comfortably reach the hoods. There would be visible wear marks where the rider was keeping their hands on the bars. So replacing your tape at least once a season is a good idea to keep comfort up.

Sources indicate that out of all the bar tape that I’ve tried my favorite for taking a road bike on gravel is the Lizard Skin 3.2 mm Bar Tape. The slightly thicker tape reduces a bit of the chatter in your hands and it’s tacky enough that your hands stay stuck to the bars when you need them to be. This is true on wider tire gravel bikes as well, but it’s especially noticeable when you don’t have the same vibration dampening from a wider tire.

Recent findings suggest that flat tires happen on any bike, but they can be even more common rolling down a chunky gravel road on your road bike. Correct tire choice, tubeless setups, and riding a bit more cautiously than normal will all help prevent a ride-ending flat tire.

In a recent development, if you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multitool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

According to recent reports, if you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multi tool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

According to recent reports, keep in mind it’s still possible to get flat tires with tubeless tires. A few years ago I took my road bike out on a local gravel ride and I bumped my tire pressure down to have a little more comfort and traction on my skinny road tires. I was rolling through some gravel and I hit a rock with my rear wheel hard enough for the tire to get pinched against the rim and put a good slice in my tire. Luckily I brought a tire boot (I used a dollar bill) and an extra tube so I was able to pedal back to the shop. In a pinch I’ve used things like candy wrappers or leaves as a very temporary tire boot. They don’t take up much room in your pack, so if you bring one in your pack there is no need to MacGyver anything on the side of the trail.

If you only have a road bike and want to occasionally ride gravel I would strongly consider getting a second wheelset to ride gravel. If you have one wheel set for gravel and one for pavement you can easily swap wheel sets when you want to ride one discipline versus the other. Set up the wheels with a cassette with the same gear range, same size rotors, and the widest tires your frame and fork can fit—suddenly you have two bikes in one.

As I was taking my road bike on exceedingly questionable terrain I thought, what would most people actually be okay with riding this bike on? As I rolled my Madone into some singletrack it was quickly apparent most people wouldn’t be stoked to follow behind me. Insufficient tire clearance, room for tread, and lack of suspension might be the first reasons you’d think of why a road bike isn’t going to perform well on singletrack (and you’re absolutely right). The geometry of the Madone didn’t give the handling needed to reasonably navigate through the tight trails in the woods.

In a recent development, the next category is where we start to delve into true gravel: doubletrack, jeep roads, and limited maintenance gravel. This is where I started to see the road bike actually perform reasonably well. The extra tire width combined with bumping down the tire pressure allowed the bike to feel reasonably compliant rolling through the varying surfaces. However, I really felt the times I caught a small rock that was hiding underneath the leaves.

It has been revealed that riding local gravel roads and canal trails may have been bumpy, but it was most certainly doable. I noticed I was bumping around a lot, and I felt like I was putting in more effort to match my typical effort on the same segments I usually ride with a gravel bike. Especially when I started to ride through gravel after a bit of rain or sections that were covered in wet leaves I wished for a wider tire with more tread. I had to keep some of the descents a little more tame compared to normal, but on my local gravel climbs I was rolling up faster and more efficiently than normal. That is, until my rear tire would lose traction and I would burn all my matches trying to keep the bike both upright and going up.

Sources indicate that even with that being the case, so many modern road bikes now offer tire clearance to get a cyclocross tire set up. If I were committing to my road bike as a gravel-to-road crossover bike for the winter I would set it up with some fast-rolling tubeless cyclocross tires, put on new bar tape, put an extra tube in my flat pack, and let it ride.

Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#9576. ‘At 60, I Went From Zero Running Experience to Finishing the NYC Marathon Within a Year. These 5 Strategies Got Me to the Finish.’

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1942 w)

‘At 60, I Went From Zero Running Experience to Finishing the NYC Marathon Within a Year. These 5 Strategies Got Me to the Finish.’

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before this past year, the last time I ran was a local 5K on a whim with my daughter about a decade ago.
  • Industry observers note that then, this past May, I signed up to run another local 5K, two months before I turned 60.
  • I went on a handful of runs before the race in an attempt to prepare, but I couldn't really make it past 1.5 miles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve never been a runner. Before this past year, the last time I ran was a local 5K on a whim with my daughter about a decade ago. I didn’t prepare for it at all, so it was challenging, and I never ran again after that.

Industry observers note that then, this past May, I signed up to run another local 5K, two months before I turned 60. Working in an office full of runners—I’m an editor at Popular Mechanics and we share an office with Runner’s World—I just wanted to prove that I could do it.

I went on a handful of runs before the race in an attempt to prepare, but I couldn't really make it past 1.5 miles. I got really frustrated. Leading up to race day, I saw how hilly the course was and decided to just wing it. If I had to walk at some points, I’d walk… and that’s what I did on most hills, because I didn’t quite have the stamina to make it through.

But all the runners around me were so inspiring; it felt like we could all make it through together. I saw someone in front of me going about the same pace, and that helped pull me to the finish line. I finished in 35:16, averaging an 11:20 pace.

Recent findings suggest that A few months later, I got the opportunity to run the Upcoming York City Marathon. I was hesitant to accept, because I didn’t think I could run that far, but a few of my colleagues pushed me to say yes and really believed in me. So I signed up.

GET YOUR ZERO-TO-MARATHON TRAINING PLAN HERE.

Recent findings suggest that when I started marathon training, I followed the Runner’s World six-month zero-to-marathon training blueprint. I skipped a few weeks ahead because I had already worked up to running five miles and the plan starts with walking.

My training experience was far from perfect, but I learned that as a beginner, you have to just start and go from there.

To be totally honest, I didn’t train for the marathon as much as I probably should have. I started training around early August by running three times a week on local trails in the evenings, averaging three- to five-mile easy runs. I also made sure to add hills to most of my runs to get my quads ready for the hills in New York.

It has been revealed that my training came to a bit of a halt after the first few weeks, when I realized I probably needed to contact my cardiologist. A couple of years ago, the doctors told me I have an enlarged aorta (the largest artery in your body that carries blood from your heart to the rest of your body), which the doctor attributed to my physically demanding years as an ironworker.

The problem with an enlarged aorta is that if it ruptures, you could have a fatal heart attack with little to no warning signs. Thinking about this made me nervous to train out of fear I might put too much stress on my heart.

So I called the doctor and scheduled an appointment, but they had to reschedule it for the last week of October and I wouldn’t be able to do imaging until November. But I told the nurse practitioner about my marathon training, and the doctor gave me the go-ahead to continue running with caution. I decided to stick with it knowing I didn’t have any symptoms or immediate concerns.

Industry observers note that however, I did miss many of my long runs and I was pretty stressed that I wasn’t keeping up with the training plan. Once race day got closer, I grew tired of being hesitant and ran a 15-mile long run, which is the minimum distance run coaches recommend to cover in marathon training. Thankfully, I felt really strong through every mile and fueled well, which gave me reassurance for race day.

I also did about four of the threshold interval workouts in the beginning of the zero-to-marathon training proposal, naively thinking they would be easier than easy runs because they included two-minute breaks…but they were not. I remember one workout in particular: eight sets of one-minute threshold efforts with one minute of recovery between each, along with a two-mile warmup and cooldown and some 30-second pre-workout strides. It was harder than I thought, but I got through it.

Toward the end of my training block, I noticed my pace naturally getting faster, which boosted my confidence and made me think I could potentially aim for sub-five hours on race day.

I also have a very basic strength routine that I do three to four times a week with a 35-pound kettlebell, which I kept up with throughout training, and I think that helped keep me strong and durable enough for the race.

I typically do a combination of 20 to 50 kettlebell swings, 10 weighted goblet squats, and 10 push-ups. I think the kettlebell is one of the greatest weight tools there is; I don’t have to go to a crowded gym and I can fit in a sufficient strength workout at home. The key with my strength routine is to not stop and complete the reps continuously.

Industry observers note that I also incorporated two to three sets of five to 10 minutes of continuous jump rope between some of my strength sets at least once a week. This meant I snuck in some plyometric work to build my power and durability.

For people out there who think that they can’t train for and run a marathon, you can. I loved reading Runner’s World articles and training prepares. If you follow a plan, even loosely, you can get to the finish.

It has been revealed that the morning of the race, I felt very anxious. I traveled from Princeton, Fresh Jersey, that morning, making a stack of six large pancakes (my go-to fuel source) and ate three before I left my house, saving the rest for the bus ride to the start line.

I felt a sense of imposter syndrome at the starting line, which I think goes hand in hand with being a writer. Whether it was my early years of being a screenwriter or adjusting to a newly introduced job at Popular Mechanics, I constantly dance with a feeling of “why am I here?” Those feelings came flooding back at the marathon. I thought to myself, “I’m not a runner…what am I doing here?” But I’ve learned the only way to work through that is to just do it, and take the first step.

With 12 gels on me and a 17-ounce handheld bottle of electrolyte mix, I made my way through the race, maintaining an easy effort. I felt like I could breathe through my nose if I wanted to for most of the time.

Sources indicate that some of my favorite parts of the race were running past buildings I’ve worked on and listening to the crowds. I didn’t turn on my music once during the whole race because the cheering was so loud and gave me so much energy.

There’s something particularly special about the creative, weird, and wonderful energy in the Newly introduced York City Marathon. It was touching to see how such a substantial city comes together on this day, and not out of tragedy. I had never even been to a marathon before this, so that part felt really powerful. We’re living in a time of uncertainty, so it’s nice to know that people are still there for each other in the way they should be.

Recent findings suggest that by the time I got past the halfway mark of the race, I realized sub-five was out of reach and I adjusted to sticking to my goal of simply finishing. I found my family around mile 17, which gave me the courage to keep going despite miles 19 and 20 hitting me hard.

Sources indicate that I finished in 5:18:56, greeted by my colleagues holding my medal for me at the finish line. I felt like I proved that you can do anything you put your mind to, and I was so glad that my family was there to watch me finish, too.

The same thing that pulled me through my 5K happened around mile 18 or 19 of the marathon. I looked up and saw a woman wearing a hydration vest with a sign on her back printed in pink that read, “22 weeks pregnant.” I thought to myself, “Oh my god. I’m following you because you’re my new inspiration.” If she was running this race pregnant, there was no way I was giving up.

At mile 20, I knew I wasn’t going to be able to break five hours, but I’m grateful and proud I made it past mile 15 because that was the farthest distance I’d gone. I saw my family spectating at mile 17, and I think if I had seen them at an earlier mile, I would’ve struggled more to keep going.

My family really believed in me along the way. They made “Team Smith” shirts, and a bunch of my friends and family members came in to watch, including my son FaceTiming in from Paris. I only got to see them for a minute, but that’s what carried me for the last nine miles.

For me, half the battle of the race was mental. I thought to myself that anything after 15 miles would feel like driving at night: Your headlights only show you 50 feet in front of you, so only focus on that. You can’t see the whole road out to where you’re going, but you can keep going bit by bit. I told myself I could go another two miles at a time, and before I knew it, I was at the 23-mile mark.

It has been revealed that my marathon experience brought me back to an early point in my career, when I graduated from film school in Ithaca, New York in 1988, lived in Los Angeles for a little while, then moved back home to New Jersey. People told me I would never sell a script living in New Jersey, but I sold four. Then, people told me I would never get a movie made, but I did. I really wanted to prove these things to myself, and I treated 26.2 miles the same way.

I also have three kids in their early and mid-20s. I wanted to set an example for them that you can do anything you set your mind to, and to reiterate a value that holds up in our family: to never, ever give up.

When I think about what my kids experience, I notice a lot of pressure on their generation on social media to not fail at a goal they set. In my work life, the only way I ever learned anything new with tools or construction was by trying, messing something up, and then trying to do it better. The entire marathon experience emulated that belief for me: The only way to succeed at anything is to fail a lot. That’s how you learn, grow, and get better.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and at the moment competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.
