#9574. 6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1488 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that to dial in your training, it’s notable to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides.
  • In a recent development, the formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr.
  • Over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that to dial in your training, it’s notable to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides. The catch? The most common formula for calculating max heart rate is not very accurate.

In a recent development, the formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr. William Haskell and Dr. Samuel Fox in 1970, and it wasn’t necessarily validated by research and involved data from a wide mix of people, including those with heart disease and smokers. As a result, the formula tends to overestimate max heart rate for younger people and underestimate it for older adults.

Over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age). However, it’s still a rudimentary system—like, “might as well use an abacus as a bike computer” rudimentary, states Cherie Miner, M.D., a sports medicine specialist in Birmingham, Alabama. “It’s been the standard for years, but there are a lot of variables that can throw off your max heart rate.” Some of those variables: how fit you are, how hot it is, and how much stress you’re under.

Sources indicate that because of these variables, there are also a lot of myths surrounding max heart rate. Here, we debunk some of the most common ones so you can get to know your heart, and use your metrics to train efficiently.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve got to admit: This is equally horrifying and comical. But you can rest easy because it won’t actually happen.

Industry observers note that “Most people have one to two minutes at their max heart rate—highly-trained athletes may have more,” Miner says. Expect to see your performance suffer very swiftly if you try and maintain your max heart rate for more than just a short burst. Fortunately, years of evolving to survive prevents us from actually killing ourselves.

The old-school formulas assume that it is the same, but Golich says it’s much more nuanced than that. Max heart rate is largely untrainable and determined by genetics—some of us have hearts tuned like humming birds’ while others have the slow-and-steady type.

According to recent reports, although not perfectly accurate, age-based formulas give athletes an easy and accessible way to find a rough baseline of their max without undergoing rigorous (or sometimes dangerous, in the case of a sedentary person) testing. That said, The American College of Sports Medicine suggests age-based formulas with a lower standard deviation, for example, the Gelish equation: 207 minus (0.7 x age) or Tanaka: 208 minus (0.7 x age).

It has been revealed that no matter which way you calculate it, your max heart rate is not an indication of performance, Golich claims. “If your max is 200, and someone else’s is 190, it doesn’t mean one of you is the better athlete.” In fact, Golich has worked with numerous talented athletes at both ends of the spectrum.

It has been revealed that it’s good to remember that everyone’s max heart rate does drop as they age—but again, that doesn’t mean you’re losing fitness. Regular training and good nutrition will affect performance more than the fact that your max heart rate is now slightly lower than it was three years ago.

In reality, it’s not your max heart rate that determines your fitness level. Being able to hold your max heart rate for longer and longer sessions is what’s key.

In a recent development, heart rate is a reaction to work being done, not a measurement of actual work. For example, Golich says that if you ratchet yourself up to 200 watts (wattage measures your cycling power) for three minutes, for the first minute, your heart may tick along at 170 beats per minute (bpm). By minute two it may be at 180 bpm, and by minute three you could be pushing 189. But you’re doing the same amount of work the whole time: 200 watts.

Recent findings suggest that if you were to ride for three minutes with the intention of maintaining the same heart rate, things would look different. Say you ramped up to 180 bpm to start—you might ride at 200 watts for the first minute, but you’d likely have to drop your watts to sustain that heart rate for minutes two and three.

Golich claims he prefers to have his clients train with power meters or using rate of perceived exertion (RPE)—a personal appraisal of how hard you feel you’re working—rather than heart rate.

“There are a lot of grey areas with heart rate,” he says, adding that being overheated, under-fueled, or even just hopped up on caffeine will throw your heart rate numbers off for the day.

According to recent reports, furthermore, the number displayed by your heart rate monitor or the screen on a gym treadmill may not be accurate. Sure, using a computer is certainly more accurate than the 220-minus-age formula, but Golich adds that because these devices take measurements every few seconds, they’re probably not dead-on.

If you really want to know your true max heart rate, an EKG is one way to go or a cardiopulmonary exercise test for even more accurate measurements, both of which require a visit to your doc or a lab.

Also, if you think that unless you’re hitting your max heart rate on every ride, you’re not working hard enough, here’s your license to chill. Max heart rate workouts should be done sparingly, Miner claims, since the ultra-high intensity can lead to injuries, extreme fatigue, and other symptoms of overtraining.

Plus, there’s merit to working in many different heart rate zones—from increasing your base fitness with low-intensity sessions to pushing the boundaries at your lactate threshold, and even tipping into some anaerobic work. If you only have two speeds—hard and harder—you’re doing yourself a disservice.

Heart attacks, while rare, happen to athletes at all different workloads. Even so, cardiologist James Beckerman, M.D., says you’re slightly more at risk when working at very high intensities.

Industry observers note that “This is likely related to a combination of high heart rate, higher blood pressure with exercise (which is normal), and higher levels of catecholamines (hormones produced by the adrenal glands),” he says. “For people without heart disease, exercising at higher intensity is generally safe.”.

If you’re someone with heart disease or who has exhibited risk factors, however, it’s a good idea to talk to your doctor about safe heart rate ranges for exercise and even get a stress test, he notes.

Sources indicate that you’re not mistaken—your max heart rate for cycling really may be different than your max for another sport. Again, this is indicative of how variable heart rate is, Golich says.

Activities that are load bearing—like running—will generally push your heart rate higher, because you have to do more work to overcome gravity. Cycling, because it has the mechanical assistance of the bike, will generally produce a lower max heart rate. And swimming, which happens in a pool with zero-impact, may be lower still—since the water is keeping you cool, Golich says, heat will be less of a factor in raising your heart rate.

Recent findings suggest that what exactly is heart rate reserve? According to Miner, heart rate reserve is the difference between maximum heart rate and resting heart rate.

Sources indicate that your heart rate reserve can actually be a good measurement of how fit you are overall. “A higher heart rate reserve indicates better physical fitness,” she states. That’s because, unlike maximum heart rate, a lower resting heart rate is associated with better fitness. “If your resting heart rate is lower, then your heart rate reserve will be higher,” Miner says.

Tamanna K. Singh, M.D., is a board-certified adult clinical and sports cardiologist and RRCA-certified run coach. She earned her medical degree from Boston University School of Medicine and completed her Internal Medicine Residency at Boston Medical Center. She completed her Cardiovascular Medicine fellowship at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Latest York, New York and her specialty training in Sports Cardiology at Massachusetts General Hospital. She is right now the codirector of the Sports Cardiology Center at Cleveland Clinic in Cleveland, Ohio and assistant professor of medicine at the Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine of Case Western Reserve University. To date, she has held several council roles with the American College of Cardiology (ACC). As a sports cardiologist, Dr. Singh provides cardiovascular care for professional, competitive, and recreational athletes and describes herself as an advocate for safe participation in sports. Media and print contributions include the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Time Magazine, and others. Outside of her profession, she enjoys running marathons, hitting the weights in the gym, playing sous-chef to her wonderful husband while cooking plant-based meals, and playing with her four beautiful dogs.

#9573. After Hitting Rock Bottom, an Army Veteran Went for a Run With a Proposal to End His Life. Then He Heard a Familiar Military Command He Couldn’t Ignore.

After Hitting Rock Bottom, an Army Veteran Went for a Run With a Proposal to End His Life. Then He Heard a Familiar Military Command He Couldn’t Ignore.

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that editor’s Note: This story contains a mention of suicide.
  • Jeremy Hurtt woke up that winter morning in 2014, and after staring at the ceiling for a few minutes, headed out for a run, thinking it may be his last.
  • Industry observers note that he headed toward the spot where the run—and everything else—could end.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that editor’s Note: This story contains a mention of suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or self-harming behaviors, call or text 988 to get help from the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Jeremy Hurtt woke up that winter morning in 2014, and after staring at the ceiling for a few minutes, headed out for a run, thinking it may be his last.

Industry observers note that he headed toward the spot where the run—and everything else—could end. An overpass above an interstate in the town of Benton, Arkansas, a mile from the house he had been crashing in for the past few weeks, sleeping on a cold floor, getting by on the generosity of a friend. Money had troubled Jeremy for years. He did odd jobs around town for a few bucks but mostly was bumming $10 and $20 from friends just to get by. He was 34 years old, with nothing in the bank, no home, no car, not even a driver’s license. All these little indignities, piling up, had started to bury him.

And then there were the memories, too.

According to recent reports, since finishing a deployment in Iraq in 2008, there’d been lots of days when Jeremy felt down, depressed—and seemed different from the playful, clownish, upbeat guy his Army pals and others had come to know. “He was no longer good-time Jeremy,” one friend states. “He was withdrawn, reclusive.” But he never seriously thought about hurting himself. Until that morning when the indignities were too many, and his mind couldn’t stop wondering why he was still alive and better people weren’t.

In a recent development, the overpass was a destination he had crossed before. On walks and runs when he was up for it. At that early-morning hour, semitrucks would be rushing below. He, on the other hand, wasn’t rushing, running at his usual 8- to 9-minute pace, which let his mind race ahead. Running was something he had done occasionally, a means to an end after his return home from Iraq, a way to stay somewhat fit. That morning, running was the means to get where he needed to go.

He thought of what would happen if he decided to jump. About the driver whose vehicle would likely strike him once he landed on the road. He didn’t want to cause another person pain. He knew from his time in Iraq the pain that comes with sudden death. But even this good intention couldn’t deter him from running ahead.

He gave little thought to what might happen if he didn’t jump.

Industry observers note that he neared the overpass. A short way to go. The sound of semis intensified. Just a little farther. A railing on the overpass to climb over. The poor driver. One more step.

Industry observers note that and then he heard something else. Words in his head.

If you’ve been in the military, you know Charlie-Mike. You may have heard the call, the command. Jeremy followed it often when stationed in Iraq in the mid–to-late aughts. It was a time when improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and explosively formed penetrators (EFPs) got mentioned on the nightly news as often as sports scores and tomorrow’s forecast. When American troops tried to end chaos in a country exacerbated by American miscalculation.

According to recent reports, charlie-Mike is military code: Continue the Mission. Move forward. In the face of adversity. No matter what.

There was no shortage of adversity in Iraq, which the U.S. invaded in 2003. By the time the U.S. Central Command unveiled the final withdrawal of troops this past September, more than 4,300 American troops had been killed. Jeremy Hurtt served there for 15 months, during the 2006–2008 surge. What he saw and heard, and those he met and those he lost, remain fresh in his mind. He and his troop—Alpha 3/61—were fired upon often; sometimes they stopped until they heard the command. Like the memories of friends who didn’t come home from their deployment, he’s never forgotten Charlie-Mike.

Sources indicate that at that moment atop the overpass, Charlie-Mike dominated his thoughts—pushing out all others. It triggered, he says now, “a moment of clarity.” Everything is a mission. “You’re not done,” he recalls thinking that morning. “You’re not done until you get to where you’re supposed to be.” To him, that meant he couldn’t stop running—or living.

Jeremy ran until he was back at his friend’s house. He had a plan, one he put into action a couple of days later. And as the plan unfolded in the weeks and months that followed, the running intensified. Longer and longer distances. Not fast miles, just miles.

But as much as he’s run in the years since that January morning, Jeremy has never outrun what ultimately brought him to the overpass in the first place.

According to recent reports, jeremy Hurtt comes from Harrison, Arkansas, a town in the Ozarks. When he was a kid, the town had maybe 9,000 residents. “It’s major,” Jeremy, now 47, says with a slight chuckle. “There’s not a town that size for 90 minutes in any direction. Growing up, my cousins called me a city boy because I was from Harrison.”.

In many ways, it had the comforts—and trappings—of the South. Like nearby Bull Shoals Lake, filled with smallmouth bass that made for easy fishing. Jeremy’s dad, a semipro fisherman, showed him all the tricks. Come the fall, football ruled. University of Arkansas Razorbacks, with their wishbone offense. When he wasn’t watching them on TV, Jeremy played ball himself. Even though he was barely 5 feet when he got to high school, he earned a spot as a wide receiver and safety on the school’s team. But for all the fun, at home his mom, Frances, kept priorities in order. “She was definitely one of those Bible-thumpin’ Southern Christian Baptists,” claims Jeremy’s older brother, Jason. “We were raised in the church, and we always had that voice in our head, even when she wasn’t around.”.

After high school, Jeremy followed many of his classmates to the University of Arkansas. He liked being away from home, living in the bigger city of Fayetteville, far from his mother’s rules. He was social, made friends easily, and bonded with many over his love of the Razorbacks. He attended games, as well as the pre- and postgame tailgates. He could go out on a Saturday night, and Friday and Thursday, too. The parties and the drinking came easy for the garrulous kid from Harrison. But his grades suffered, and by the end of his freshman year, his time in college had ended. Jeremy, who friends say was one of the smartest guys they knew, was “asked not to come back” for year two.

In a recent development, that summer, back in Harrison, he kept drinking, hanging out, working a dead-end job at a local newspaper. It was leading nowhere, and that didn’t sit well with Frances. One night he returned home to some tough talk. “My mom basically came to me,” he remembers, “and was like, ‘You’ve got a decision to make; you’re not going to sit here forever. You’re gonna figure out what you’re doing next.’” She’d already done some groundwork for him, talking with a local Army office. Jeremy followed up with a recruiter, thinking it would “get her off my back.” Instead, he was tantalized by prospects of a steady paycheck and career options following his service time. And, the recruiter told Jeremy, it was peacetime. There was no war to worry about. Jeremy enlisted right away and within days was headed to basic training.

It was September 1998. Peace wouldn’t last forever.

These days, Jeremy Hurtt loves to run hills. He’ll track his runs, aiming to hit 2,000 feet of elevation gain during a 13-miler. The effort calms him, lets him think. “The feeling of pushing yourself,” he says, “and trying to improve yourself.”.

Running and hillwork weren’t always his forte, though, especially in boot camp where, as a college dropout, he was learning what discipline was all about. “I never was a huge running fan,” he claims, “and I hated hills. I just couldn’t stand it, you know? I’d get halfway up a hill and just want to quit.”.

After basic training, he was first stationed in South Korea and then assigned to a communications role in Washington, D.C. Some days he worked in the Pentagon. Life was good. He made friends with the other enlisted soldiers, who got to know Jeremy as the quick-witted guy from the Ozarks. The one who’d send his buddies off-color emails to get a chuckle or impress them by demonstrating how to download music for free. “I was always trying to make people laugh,” he says. They loved hanging out with him, especially after a cocktail or two. “He was a really smart guy, really funny, and he definitely enjoyed the world he was in,” says Dillon Cunningham, who was stationed with Jeremy at the time. He pauses a moment. “And then, you know, 9/11 happened.”.

Jeremy was not in the Pentagon on September 11, 2001, when a hijacked American Airlines plane crashed into the building, killing the 64 passengers on board and 125 military personnel and civilians; he was doing fieldwork a few miles away. Amid the horrors and chaos of the events unfolding, it would take days before he could contact his mother and tell her he was okay.

Until 9/11, Jeremy’s path in the Army had gone according to plan. “My idea was [not] to go anywhere near combat,” he notes. But the terrorist attacks that took nearly 3,000 lives changed his mind. One of his grandfathers had served in World War II. Jason, his brother, was already stationed in Turkey with the Air Force. Jeremy no longer wanted to serve within the relatively safe confines of his communications posting, testing radios and satellite switches. In 2003, he asked to be assigned to a cavalry unit so he could prep for deployment. He was 25 years old. “It was just a feeling that this is the moment for my generation,” Jeremy says. “I wanted to be directly involved in whatever came next.”.

Industry observers note that it would take three years before Sgt. Jeremy Hurtt learned what next involved—and how it would test him like no hill ever could.

As fall arrives in the Ozarks, the Buffalo River, where Jeremy and his friends used to raft in the summer, is still just deep enough for one last excursion. And the Arkansas Razorbacks are back on the field, offering once more a promise to their diehard fans.

In a recent development, but in the fall of 2006, Jeremy was in Iraq and missed all that. Home was 7,000 miles away—and somehow felt even farther. On his first full night in Baghdad, a rocket struck his barrack. It didn’t explode, and no one was injured, but Jeremy now had firsthand experience of combat life. “It wasn’t like that all the time,” he says. But it was clear to him that “there are people who want me dead. They are going to try to kill me.”.

For much of his time, Jeremy and his troop were on security detail. They patrolled sectors in Sadr City and East Baghdad, scanning rooftops and street corners, searching for “high-value targets” to capture or kill. “There’s some combat; occasionally people shoot at you,” he states. “It’s a lot more common for them to try to blow you up.”.

He recalls just one of many incidents. One afternoon in 2007, Alpha 3/61 was southwest of Sadr City. They were in six armored vehicles, Jeremy with his M240 machine gun on lookout in the third Humvee. Without warning, an EFP, the most lethal form of homemade explosive used against Coalition troops during the war, tore through the backside of the lead Humvee. The warhead narrowly missed Sgt. Matt Haeffner, Jeremy’s roommate, who sustained a concussion in the blast.

As Haeffner recalls, Jeremy was one of the first in his troop to check on him. “We’ll be friends forever because we shared crazy moments like that,” notes Haeffner, who was awarded a Purple Heart following the EFP attack. “My wife calls it trauma bonding.”.

Not all of Jeremy’s friends in Iraq made it home. Sgt. Eric Snell, a father of two, was killed during a small-arms fire in Baghdad. He was charismatic, Jeremy remembers, a former pro baseball player with the looks of a model. And there was Sgt. Alexander Fuller, who died when his Humvee struck an improvised bomb. “His wife was pregnant with their first child,” Jeremy notes. Jeremy knew both Snell and Fuller from his earliest days in the cavalry. And then there were the eight men from his troop who died in a vicious battle in Afghanistan. That was hard on Jeremy, who, by then, had finished his deployment and was back in Arkansas, a world away from the fighting.

Sources indicate that the distance added to his sense of guilt. Should he have re-upped for another tour and gone with his former troop to Afghanistan? Why did Snell and Fuller die, and not him? Why did the dumb drunk, as Jeremy thought of himself, get to live and those men did not?

“I always thought it’s a trade that anybody would have made. If you could trade me for Fuller and he gets to see his daughter grow up—I think people would make that trade,” Jeremy says. “And keep Snell around for his kid; that trade would make sense.” He pauses for a second. “To me, it just always seemed like a cruel joke—those people didn’t get to experience their lives, and I was still here.”.

So he’d keep asking himself, “Why should I be alive when better people weren’t?”.

Back in Arkansas, Jeremy didn’t forget what he saw and what he was missing. He couldn’t find much work but found plenty to drink. Within a year of returning home, his weight went from 170 pounds to 230. In Iraq, he ran occasionally, when the situation allowed, sweating in the desert heat. So when he got prodded by friends to enter a local weight-loss competition, he turned to running to peel the pounds away. “I was running up and down hills and in the heat and humidity of Arkansas,” he says, “so it came off pretty swiftly.”.

In a recent development, bringing order and routine to other parts of life proved more challenging. For a time, he returned to the University of Arkansas, starting fresh. He tried majoring in broadcasting but never made it to graduation. He found a variety of part-time jobs, including production work at an ESPN radio affiliate. Nothing stuck. A girlfriend came and went. Alcohol was the only constant.

Fireworks on the Fourth of July or at a football game made him edgy. He’d drive through an underpass, see trash on the side of the road, and wonder if it was concealing an IED. He’d suddenly remember Snell. “He was my favorite soldier ever and got killed the day I went on leave,” he says, his eyes watering. He waits a moment. “That all rolled up into the guilt, everything, I felt for a lot of years afterward.”.

Recent findings suggest that friends and family noticed a different Jeremy from the one they knew before deployment. “I remember linking up with him a few times, catching up, and it was like a shell,” Dillon Cunningham recalls. “He was there, but there wasn’t anything solid in there. You could swiftly tell he was not operating at the specs we used to expect from him.”.

Once they began to notice the changes, his friends and family began to worry.

Twenty-two. It’s a number “that really sticks heavily in most military guys’ heads,” Jason says. For nearly a decade, 22 referred to the number of deaths by suicide among U.S. military veterans each day. Several suicide prevention organizations have 22 in their names. The number is on flags and tattoos to promote awareness. Various versions of a 22 Push-Up Challenge ask participants to do 22 daily push-ups for 22 days. Even though the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs downgraded the number of suicides to 17.7 per day in 2024, 22 remains code for those in the know.

Jason worried his brother might become a statistic.

“The power that the brain has when you get yourself in certain situations—if you don’t have those people to talk to, you do just fall down a drain,” Jason says. “And the unfortunate thing is, so many people don’t know who to talk to. A perfect example is Jeremy; he lost his buddies. Those may have been the guys he talked to and that he felt good with. Well, they’re gone, and so he starts going down that drain.”.

Recent findings suggest that jason became Jeremy’s lifeline. On that morning in 2014, when Jeremy didn’t jump from the overpass, he got back to his friend’s house and called his brother, who was living outside of St. Louis, several hundred miles away. He didn’t talk about his suicidal thoughts, but asked for help finding work, getting back on track. Jason didn’t hesitate. He got Jeremy a job on his crew that worked on upgrading cell towers. He’d be on the road a lot, and the hours would be unpredictable, but the work would be steady and bring in a paycheck—and a group of coworkers to be around. And after his shifts, Jeremy could go for a run, which he often did, in the same pair of basketball sneakers he wore to work.

Jeremy never sought professional counseling, but he suspects he was suffering from PTSD. Getting psychological help is not something many veterans choose to pursue, his brother states. “When you come home, and you go talk to someone that has the sheepskin on the wall,” Jason says, “they say they know how a brain works. [But] you start talking to them, and there’s a major disconnect. These people have no idea what you’re talking about.”.

According to recent reports, jeremy found a different kind of help, a different way to cope. The simple act of putting one foot in front of the other that brought clarity to his mind like nothing else. It interrupted the repetitive negative thoughts rumbling in his head. “So many troops find things to soothe their pain—if that’s gentlemen’s clubs, beer, drugs, whatever,” notes Jason, who now works as a helicopter pilot for the FAA. “Jeremy was smart enough to channel that into running, and running was that savior for him.”.

Jeremy started paying off debts. With the technical skills acquired from his past communication job, he eventually got a job with a manufacturer doing software testing. By 2018, he had saved enough to buy a place in a wooded, secluded area back in the Ozarks. Hills were nearby. That was when his love for accumulating elevation kicked in. He entered some races—he’s run the Little Rock Marathon three times, with a PR of 4:55:58—but preferred running solo.

And on those solo runs, he could finally start processing what he lived through in Iraq.

It has been revealed that jeremy has never mentioned his run to the overpass to Jason or Matt Haeffner or Dillon Cunningham. In fact, the only person he’s told is his wife, Stacie. They met online before his deployment to Iraq and stayed in touch for nearly a decade. In 2014, they reconnected. Stacie was living in Nashville at the time, and Jeremy was in the area working on a cell tower job. They went on a few dates, kept texting and calling when Jeremy’s job was done and he was back in Arkansas. Then, at the end of 2019, when Jeremy was living alone in his house in the woods, he texted Stacie that he wanted to be more serious. “He had been running,” she remembers, “and he was like, ‘I really think we’re supposed to give this a real shot.’ I was like, ‘Okay, let’s figure this out.’” She packed up and moved to Arkansas. “We were engaged in a few months,” she indicates with a smile.

And by 2021, they were married. Friends from around the country came to the wedding. They saw the Jeremy they remembered from before Iraq. Sort of. The night before the wedding, a group of Army friends got together in his house. The laughter was flowing, and so were the drinks. But before it got too late, Jeremy told his buddies he was headed to bed. “You can imagine military guys—we were like, ‘Oh, come on, man. You’re getting married. Screw that,’” Dillon says. “And he was like, ‘I gotta run a half marathon in the morning. I run a half marathon every Saturday.’” On the morning of his wedding, Jeremy ran, showered, and made it to the ceremony with time to spare.

It has been revealed that this past June, Stacie and Jeremy welcomed a new member to the family. Baby Josephine. She keeps Mom and Dad busy, so Jeremy has cut back on running. He might get a short one in during the workweek. Come the weekend, though, Stacie gives him the green light and lets him go long. And at an 11-minute pace, he runs his half marathon.

Sources indicate that “I don’t think it was trivial that I ran to that overpass,” he indicates, sitting in the den of their home outside of Houston, where they moved just before Josephine was born. “There’s something that happens in a run where, like, I have breakthroughs and insight. And I think that’s what happened that day. The mile I took to run to that overpass gave me just enough to be in a moment. It all kind of clicked into place.” Jeremy waits a second. He thinks back a dozen years. “I was—excuse my frankness—bullshitting away the opportunity. I had to be here, in this experience of being alive.”.

Recent findings suggest that just then, Josephine starts stirring. Jeremy Hurtt has to go. He has a mission to get back to.

Charles Butler, a former editor at Runner's World, now teaches journalism at the University of Oregon. With Matt Long, he wrote The Long Run: A Upcoming York City Firefighter's Triumphant Comeback from Crash Victim to Elite Athlete.

In a recent development, the RearVue 820 (Garmin’s latest cycling radar) sets a newly introduced bar for on-bike radar systems. It improves on the Varia RTL515—our longtime benchmark, which is also on sale—with increased detection range, same-speed vehicle tracking, longer battery life, and a brighter taillight. Plus, when paired with a newer Garmin cycling computer, the RearVue 820 will track the lane location and size of approaching vehicles.

Still using your phone to track your rides? A cycling computer is a safer, more accurate way to navigate, display key riding metrics, and capture data from devices like heart rate monitors and power meters. Garmin’s Edge 540 packs computing power, battery life, and function into an 80-gram package. It’s a great upgrade for any road, mountain, gravel, or fitness rider.

According to recent reports, wahoo’s Elemnt Bolt 3 is a favorite of our editors and test riders for its small size, accuracy, and ease of use. The Bolt features a 2.3-inch full-color display, 20-hour battery life, and an 85-gram weight. For simple operation and a lower price, the Bolt uses buttons instead of a touchscreen.

Recent findings suggest that keep your hot drinks warm on cold winter rides. CamelBak’s Podium bottles are popular among gravel and off-road riders due to their open/closed twist-lock cap. I love its simplicity and clean looks—it doesn’t look out of place, even on high-end race bikes.

It has been revealed that “Flat pedals win medals” is an age-old bike saying. They’re intuitive, compatible with almost any shoes, and you never have to worry about unclipping too late. OneUp’s Composite Pedals are lightweight and durable—plus they’re available in two sizes and six colors.

It has been revealed that lazer’s Tonic Kineticore helmet performs much better than its $80 MSRP suggests—and at $60 (25% off), it’s a steal. Lazer offers the Tonic in four sizes, and four color options are on sale. It’s a solid pick for any road or gravel rider.

In a recent development, wahoo reinvented indoor training when it released its original Kickr in 2012. Now on its sixth generation, the Kickr remains our top pick for high-performance indoor smart trainers. The Kickr is super accurate, folds easily for storage, and is stable during workouts. The latest version adds WiFi connectivity, which enhances connection speeds during Zwift rides and races.

It has been revealed that garmin’s Tacx Neo 2 sits at the top of the performance-trainer pyramid. However, most indoor cyclists don’t need its pricey features. The Tacx Flux 2 has a large 7.6 kg flywheel with up to 2,000 watts of resistance (more than enough for almost any rider). It also simulates gradients up to 16%, to replicate the toughest climbs in virtual cycling worlds such as Zwift and Rouvy.

WOMEN’S QUEST TIGHTS - $110 $82.

The AmFibs also have an extended cuff, so cold air doesn’t get into your gloves or jacket.

Rapha makes excellent, high-performance cycling apparel. However, it tends to be too pricey for many riders. With proper care and washing, the bibs will last you several seasons.

We love these shorts because they’re great for hot summer rides and sweaty indoor workouts in the dead of winter. Plus, they have thigh pockets to hold your cell phone or snacks while you ride.

Recent findings suggest that if you log a lot of time on the trainer, it’s worth refreshing your shorts regularly; worn-out shorts are a recipe for discomfort. The extra sweat from indoor rides breaks down the chamois faster than outdoor miles and leads to saddle sores. At this price, you should grab a pair (or two!) before they sell out.

On its own or paired with a light vest, this fleece grid jersey breathes well and keeps you from becoming sweaty and cold. On colder days, wear the Attack Thermal under a windproof jacket to keep your core insulated and cozy.

It has been revealed that A test editor favorite for years, Smartwool’s socks are light—but not too light—and have the right amount of compression to keep your feet snug without feeling squeezed. When I find socks I love, I buy a pair every time they go on sale— you can never have too many cycling socks!

For riders who only go full coverage when absolutely necessary, this waterproof cycling cap will be right in their wheelhouse. It offers extra protection from rain, sleet, and wind without added bulk. It’s thin and fits comfortably under a cycling helmet.

If you’re new to winter cycling, you need a thin hat like this one for cold days. It goes under your helmet while keeping your ears and forehead covered. And if you’ve been riding through winters for years, you probably need a new one anyway—that crusty old hat you bought a decade ago has definitely seen better days.

I’m Anti-Fitness Tracker—But Google’s Fitbit Air Changed My Mind

  • According to recent reports, I loathe running watches.
  • Fitness trackers combat most of my grievances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, I loathe running watches. They bastardize one of the most lasting examples of single-function elegance—the wristwatch—and turn it into an omnipresent reminder that your health is declining in some way at all times: too fast, too slow, not enough rest, not enough quality sleep, you’re 34 only in years—your body is a wheezing 78, etc. I’m aware of my mortality and run to forget it.

Fitness trackers combat most of my grievances. They don't offer real-time notifications, and many don’t even have screens. However, many are also obtrusive, have subscription fees to see the full scope of health data, or are just ugly. The Oura Ring messed with my grip on pretty much every lift while strength training, and though the Whoop Band is covert (but still bulkier than I’d like), you’re on the hook for a 12-month subscription. Both devices also cost well over $200. It's steep for something I want to use only while lifting or running, not in my civilian life.

It has been revealed that I wanted to try Google’s Fitbit Air after reading how simple it was to use. After weeks of testing, it’s stayed out of the way, gives me the health metrics I want, and is priced right at $100.

The Fitbit Air gives me heart rate, steps, and estimated calories burned through the paired Google Health app. It has a simple interface that lets me go as deep (or not) as I want in data, and it's delightful to use. I only use it for fitness, but you can also track food and water intake.

Recent findings suggest that I wanted a fitness tracker to record running, lifting, and the occasional rowing or cycling workout. I’ve run four marathons and one half marathon, relying only on my phone and Strava to tell me how far I ran, how long it took, and pace breakdowns. Running is how I turn on, tune in, and drop out. A running watch would have me constantly worrying about my pace or anxiously waiting for a notification that my heart rate has gone above Zone 2. I want heart rate data from my runs, but I don’t want it to bother me in the moment.

Linking the Fitbit Air to Strava was easy and straightforward. I’m still used to manually starting a run in the Strava app, but the device automatically detects them and loads the data into the Google Health app. It also tracks lifting sessions, giving me an idea of cardio load and time spent in different heart rate zones. I’ve only needed to charge it once in about two and a half weeks, but I don’t wear it every day.

Sources indicate that the Fitbit Air is so pleasantly small and lightweight that I forget I’m wearing it. I don’t even clock it on runs, and it doesn’t hinder gripping dumbbells or the handlebars on my spin bike and rowing machine. I’m using the Performance Loop wristband that it comes with and see no need for another—it’s comfortable, inconspicuous, and easy to adjust. Call me shallow, but how a fitness tracker looks is generally where they lose me. The device reads more like a wristband from the night before or a NATO strap of a field watch; I’m fine with either interpretation. If people ask, I say it’s a Kabbalah bracelet.

Sources indicate that the Fitbit Air tracks heart rate variability, blood oxygen, skin temperature variation, sleep stages, and irregular heart rhythm alerts for atrial fibrillation. You can also upgrade your Google Health membership to Premium for adaptive AI coaching that breaks down health metrics and suggests workouts. These are features more expensive fitness trackers tout, and I’m not interested in them. I’m not using the device to its full potential. That’s the beauty of the Fitbit Air—capable tracking that lets you tap into the info you want without bombarding you with data.

#9568. Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X Review (2025): Assault’s Best Bike Yet?

Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X Review (2025): Assault’s Best Bike Yet?

📅 15 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines presently offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity.
  • In a recent development, here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike.
  • In a recent development, at Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines presently offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity. Popular in the CrossFit community, this fan bike consists of a belt-driven system and a heavy-duty steel frame, making it a great tool to build both endurance and strength.

In a recent development, here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike. We put it through hours of strenuous cardio workouts to see if it could take on the challenge. In this Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X review, we’ll highlight our results, how well the bike ranked in testing, and how it compares to other fan bikes.

In a recent development, at Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment. We have a product testing team that has put hundreds of machines through the wringer, using them for everything from gentle warm-ups to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workouts. Many of our staff members are home gym owners themselves and use these products nearly every day.

With the knowledge we’ve gained over the years, we created a proprietary scoring system that we used to rank the AssaultBike ProX in various categories. Not only did we evaluate how the bike performed on its own, but we also compared it with nearly 30 other exercise bikes to see how it stacked up against the competition.

Sources indicate that from the founders of the AssaultRunner (one of the best treadmills to train with), the Assault Bike ProX is made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat that helps keep it corrosion-resistant and capable of standing the test of time. It is a top-tier fan bike that can provide a brutal workout for any athlete.

In a recent development, in addition to its tough and durable frame, it incorporates a belt-driven system for a quiet, smooth training experience. It also requires less upkeep than chain-driven systems, which should come as a relief to busy individuals who can’t be bothered with complicated maintenance protocols.

At the time of writing, the Assault Bike ProX costs $899. Fortunately, there is also an option to finance it at around $82 a month through Affirm. For comparison, the Assault Bike ProX is more expensive than the AssaultBike Classic at $699 but cheaper than the Concept2 BikeErg, which costs around $1,100.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX also provides free shipping, which is a big deal for equipment this size. Buying an air bike from another brand could set you back another $100 in shipping costs.

All of the above considered, we’ve rated this bike 4 out of 5 stars for its shipping rate, finance options, and value.

The Assault Bike ProX weighs 125 pounds, has a max user weight of 330 pounds, and boasts a heavy-duty steel frame with a corrosion-resistant black powder coating finish. We love this type of frame and finish because it means less maintenance over time.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also similar to what you would see with the Rogue Echo Bike, which has a black powder coating and almost looks like it was built from scraps of a heavy-duty squat rack! But the Assault Bike ProX isn’t as bulky as the Rogue Echo Bike, making it more compatible with small spaces, which our product testers enjoyed. For comparison, the ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high, while the Echo Bike is 55 inches long, 29.5 inches wide, and 52.25 inches high.

The Assault Bike ProX provides a wide padded seat that can adjust to 11 different heights and six different directions either forward or backward. These adjustments were the same on the Assault Bike Pro, which the ProX replaces. The rubber handles on the ProX help you maintain your grip and keep your hands comfortable throughout the workout as well.

This fan bike also comes with footpegs at the base of the handlebars for you to place your feet. This gives you the option to do an upper body-only workout, which is great for injury recovery or arm day.

Based on the quality and construction of the Assault Bike ProX, we rated it 5 out of 5 stars.

Industry observers note that we gave the AssaultBike Pro X 5 out of 5 stars for delivery and assembly because of how straightforward it was to build. The bikes arrived at our testing facility 75 percent built, so all we had to do was attach the LCD console, pedals, handlebars, seat post, and saddle. Assault Fitness provides all the tools needed to build your air bike, and it should take roughly 35 to 45 minutes.

In a recent development, when testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a smoother and quieter ride than what we’ve experienced with other air bikes, like the Titan Fan Bike or the AssaultBike Classic. This is predominantly thanks to the belt-driven system. A belt-driven system requires less maintenance than a chain-driven system, but it is also harder to use. When you pedal, the steel fan wheel generates resistance based on your effort. The harder you pedal, the more resistance is applied.

However, once you stop pedaling, the fan wheel will stop moving, requiring more effort to get it started again. This might be tough if you’re not prepared for a high-intensity workout. Due to this, we gave the Assault Bike ProX a 4 out of 5-star rating for performance.

The Assault Bike ProX’s LCD monitor provides seven built-in training programs and a competition mode for those ready to take on the challenge. Through the Assault Fitness App, which we’ll review below, there is also an option to follow instructor-led programs or create customized workouts.

Recent findings suggest that all in all, we give it a 3 out of 5 star rating in this category. The included workouts aren’t as robust as what you’d see in a more interactive bike like the Peloton. However, we do appreciate having them and think they can be valuable for people who may not know where to start.

While the AssaultBike Classic was only compatible with the Polar T34 heart rate chest strap, the Assault Bike ProX is compatible with other brands, like Garmin. You can link a heart rate monitor through the bike’s Bluetooth features. However, you need to purchase a compatible one separately, which is why we only rated it 4 out of 5 stars here (though to be fair, this is common for most exercise bikes).

The Assault Bike ProX comes with a five-inch by eight-inch monitor, which is a common size amongst other fan bikes. This high-quality LCD monitor is powered by four AA batteries, which Assault includes with your purchase. The console is great for tracking stats such as calories, distance, heart rate, speed, watts, and RPM. It also connects to the Assault Fitness App.

Industry observers note that our product testers loved that it could track power output in addition to distance and speed, which is a great measure of energy expenditure to quantify workout intensity. The Rogue Echo Bike monitor doesn’t provide feedback such as watts and RPM on its monitor, which gives the Assault Bike ProX the edge.

All things considered, we’ve given this bike 5 out of 5 stars for its display and tracking capabilities.

When testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a ton of conveniences. First, the air bike requires no electric outlet, and we loved being able to use it anywhere. This feature is also a welcome benefit for commercial CrossFit gym owners, as you don’t have to worry about your members tripping over power cords.

Other conveniences include a device holder and a water bottle holder. Some fan bikes like the Titan Fan Bike also include these conveniences. Others, like the Rogue Echo Bike, don’t (though they are available to purchase separately). We always appreciate it when a brand throws in little extras like this. They allow you to have all your workout essentials within reach. Plus, you don’t have to worry about potentially placing multiple orders or paying extra shipping fees to get them.

Overall, our product testers rated the conveniences 4 out of 5 stars. The only reason we docked a point is that we wish the bike came with a wind guard to prevent cold air from blowing in our faces when training in a cold garage. There is one available on the Assault Fitness website, but you have to buy it separately for an additional $39.

The Assault Bike ProX is a part of the Assault Fitness line of exercise machines that operate using the Assault Fitness app. The app was one of our product testers’ favorite features.

Free to download from the App Store and Google Play, the Assault Fitness App provides you with a multitude of instructor-driven workouts. You can do these workouts on your own or compete against other athletes virtually. Many of the workouts also integrate other types of equipment, such as dumbbells and kettlebells, to help you get more well-rounded programming.

While we enjoyed the app, we only gave it 4 out of 5 stars. As of this writing, it’s not available on the most recent version of Android. Athletes with newer Android phones may not be able to use it.

Sources indicate that the Assault Bike ProX is Bluetooth-enabled. We don’t necessarily consider Bluetooth connectivity a standout feature, as dozens of cardio machines we’ve tested now come with it. But we’ve also tried inexpensive cardio equipment that doesn’t have this feature, and even Assault Fitness’s classic AssaultBike lacks Bluetooth capabilities. As such, we rated the ProX 5 out of 5 stars here.

Recent findings suggest that when comparing other fan bikes we tested, the Assault Bike ProX generated less noise due to its belt-driven system. The belt-driven system operates more smoothly than chain-drive systems such as those on the Schwinn Airdyne. A noisier system can make it tough to perform workouts at home, especially if you train early in the morning or late at night when others are sleeping.

That mentioned, no fan bike will be completely silent, so you should still expect some noise as air travels through the flywheel. Due to this, we give the noise level of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

Sources indicate that the Assault Bike ProX offers some portability, thanks to two small transport wheels at the front. To move it, all you need to do is tilt it onto its wheels to help glide it across the floor. However, although it might be easy for some athletes to move this fan bike, others might struggle to relocate it because it weighs 125 pounds. Based on these findings, we give the portability of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX has a three-year non-wear parts warranty and a seven-year frame warranty. The three-year non-wear parts warranty doesn’t cover normal wear and tear on parts like the seat, pedals, and handle grips. This may seem like a drawback, but in our experience, this is common in warranties on other brands’ fan bikes. But the length of Assault’s warranty is longer compared to Rogue, who only offers a two-year warranty on their Echo Bike, and Titan, who only offers a one-year warranty on their fan bike. We gave the warranty of the Assault Bike ProX 5 out of 5 stars for this reason.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high. Compared to the classic AssaultBike, these dimensions are one to two inches bigger in each category. If you’re between the two, we definitely recommend measuring carefully to ensure you choose the one that will best fit your space.

The Assault Bike ProX is a fan bike, meaning it builds resistance based on how much air you recruit in the fan wheel as you work. The harder you pedal, the more air resistance is applied, making your workout more challenging.

In addition to air resistance, the ProX uses a belt-driven system, meaning it only operates when you begin to pedal. If you stop pedaling, the machine stops moving. This makes it harder to operate compared to a chair-driven system, like what you’d see with the AssaultBike Classic.

Industry observers note that the weight capacity of the Assault Bike ProX is 330 pounds. This is more than the Classic bike, which holds 300 pounds, but less than the Elite, which holds up to 350 pounds.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX can accommodate most body sizes with 11 different height settings and six front-to-back settings. These adjustment levels are relatively standard based on what we’ve seen on other fan bikes. However, some competitors like the Rogue Echo Bike only have five front-to-back seat settings.

Because the Assault Bike ProX does not require an electrical outlet, you can transport it wherever you want to go —outdoors or indoors. The monitor, however, does require AA batteries to operate.

Recent findings suggest that at first glance, it seems the Assault Bike ProX and Rogue Echo Bike have many similarities. When you analyze them more closely, you’ll find that there are several key differences between the two.

Below are the dimensions of both fan bikes:.

Even though the Rogue Echo Bike is bulkier in material and dimensions, it has the same 330-pound weight capacity as the AssaultBike ProX. Both of these fan bikes are also powered by movement, so no electrical outlet is needed. Further, weighing in at 123 and 125 pounds, respectively, the Rogue Echo Bike and the Assault Bike ProX are equally portable, especially given they both have wheels.

According to recent reports, finally, both products use belt-driven mechanics, providing a smooth and quiet riding experience. But the Assault Bike ProX gives more metrics on the monitor, such as watts and RPM. This feature alone could make or break your decision, depending on how notable tracking is to your training.

The Assault Bike ProX comes in with a strong 4.6 out of 5-star rating on the Assault Fitness website. Many users claim that it is super easy to set up, requires low maintenance, and is a favorite piece of equipment in their home gyms. Customers also praise its sturdiness and its ability to handle a tough workout.

It has been revealed that one user mentioned that the left peg became loose during their workout. Another buyer mentioned that the Assault Bike ProX was very noisy and didn’t think it was as stable as other reviews might suggest — note, however, that complaints like this are in the minority.

Sources indicate that after extensive research and testing of the Assault Bike ProX, we can say that this air bike is worth it. Made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat, it can take on the toughest workouts. It’s ideal for anyone looking for a full-body, high-intensity interval training machine for improving both endurance and strength.

The smoother and quieter experience you get with the Assault Bike ProX is thanks to the belt-driven system integrated into the design. Although this system might require more effort to operate, this bike can still be a great purchase for everyone from CrossFitters to health and fitness enthusiasts.

The Assault Bike provides a great workout, combining air resistance and a belt-driven system for a tough cardio and muscular endurance workout. You can use both the foot pedals and the arm handles to get a full-body workout. Or you can just use the arm handles to work out your upper body exclusively.

The Assault Bike Pro X is a belt-driven system. The fan bike only works when you operate the pedals and/or handlebars. The belt-driven system also offers a smoother and quieter workout.

The AssaultBike alone may not aid fat loss if you’re eating too many calories. However,  it can provide a strong enough stimulus for an intense enough workout to help you burn more calories and hit multiple health and fitness goals.

Sources indicate that because the AssaultBike Pro X requires a full-body effort and utilizes a belt-driven system, you could potentially build a small amount of muscle by using it consistently. However, resistance training with implements like dumbbells or barbells (and following a diet that supports muscle growth) will be your best bet if you want to pack on as much muscle as possible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mike Clarke got his viral Fresh York City Marathon moment, getting cheered on by none other than Ariana Grande herself, but his appearance in the November 1 race has now earned him a yearlong ban from New York Road Runners events.

The organization confirmed to Runner's World that Clarke used a counterfeit bib to enter the marathon, a violation of its Code of Conduct and Rules of Competition. NYRR mentioned it learned about the incident through multiple sources and has barred him from competing in its races for the next year, although he has the opportunity to appeal.

"When individuals fraudulently enter our events, they jeopardize everyone's safety," a NYRR spokesperson said in a statement provided to Runner's World. "These acts are egregious and are antithetical to supporting the sport of running and its community.".

Recent findings suggest that according to reporting by the New York Post, Clarke wore a duplicate of a bib (No. 4207), which had been assigned to Nicolas Bourot, a French banking executive.

Industry observers note that bourot had spent a decade trying to secure entry into the NYC Marathon, and finally got his chance this year, finishing in 3:23:23—only to discover that another man appeared in race photos under his name and bib number. Fortunately, it didn’t affect Bourot's official finish time.

"It's not fair for all the runners," Bourot told the Post, noting how difficult it can be to earn a spot in the race.

Clarke's participation in the race attracted plenty of attention online, particularly after footage of him high-fiving the Grammy Award-winning artist near the finish line blew up on social media. One of his Instagram videos has surpassed 6 million views, while another is approaching half a million.

Industry observers note that clarke acknowledged to the Post that he wasn't officially registered, claiming the bib number held sentimental significance because of a friend who had died and that he didn't realize it had been assigned to another runner. When explaining the decision to participate anyway, he told the newspaper via text:.

Sources indicate that “At the end of the day they can call it unfair or cheating the system but for me it was to push my limits while running for this goal and have fun while doing it. [And] after [the] race, I received a medal but gave it to a kid afterwards haha!”.

Sources indicate that sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that trying the latest and greatest running shoes is an expensive hobby, but sometimes you get lucky and find a bargain on top-tier kicks. Today is one of those days: You can score the Adidas Hyperboost Edge, the brand’s latest super trainer, on sale for up to 25 percent off.

The Hyperboost Edge is on sale at Adidas for $160—that’s 20 percent off its $200 MSRP. The shoe is on sale in both men’s and women’s in several colorways, and plenty of sizes are in stock (for now). Adidas has the best size and colorway selection, but you can also find this shoe for just $150 in men’s at Nordstrom.

Recent findings suggest that the Hyperboost Edge is a big shoe with bold engineering, and it’s designed for long training runs up to marathon length or even longer. It features a towering 45mm stack height, and the midsole is made with pelletized PEBA, which Adidas calls Hyperboost Pro. There’s no midsole plate or other stiffening tech, just a thick block of this soft, exceptionally bouncy foam. It’s topped with a durable Primeknit upper (more on that in a moment).

In a recent development, overall, RW testers and editors loved the Hyperboost Edge. Editor Amanda Furrer called it “near perfect” and noted it’s a “go-to long-run shoe.” Its pillowy, responsive ride helped her shave a full minute off her usual pace on a 10-mile run. And it’s not just for plodding through high-mileage workouts, either: Testers mentioned it feels so great, you can even wear it casually.

“It’s responsive enough for easy mileage, durable enough to handle regular training, and comfortable enough that you could leave it on all day without thinking twice,” mentioned tester Dee Koutsourais.

The upper, however, did cause some problems, namely blisters and hot spots across the top of the foot. It’s an unfortunate drawback to such a high-performance shoe, but even so, the Hyperboost Edge still earned a 2026 Shoe Award for its unique tech and sublime ride. It sets a upcoming standard for super trainers.

Now’s the perfect time to try it: Snag your pair for up to 25 percent off at Adidas or Nordstrom.

Michael is a freelance writer with years of experience covering gear and the outdoors for Runner's World and other publications; when he's not writing, he's usually biking, hiking, and running in the mountains around Los Angeles, where he lives.

Tech Report: The Arizona Experiment!

📅 02 Nov 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.
  • Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.
  • According to recent reports, eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

According to recent reports, eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many new experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly big change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a new life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

So on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

Looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

We’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

A major part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole fresh life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here. It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

So What Are You Going to Do in Arizona?

Sources indicate that the exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:.

Is There a Bigger Picture To All This?

It has been revealed that okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart new people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

Industry observers note that by throwing myself into a newly introduced community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,.

Sources indicate that “Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”.

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

According to recent reports, that means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a fresh job that gives you a better work-life balance.

According to recent reports, the biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

But even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

The spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining new Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

In a recent development, further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

Sources indicate that to summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

Interested in stopping by for your own Mini Culdesac Experiment? They have a few short-term rentals available at rather reasonable rates (less than nearby hotels) – check em out at book.culdesac.com.

What will you do with your car?

Industry observers note that I’m bringing the car just as a convenient electric moving truck to carry two people and four months of living supplies. Once I get there, I’ll find a safe place to park it offsite and live the full car-free lifestyle of Culdesac, much like I do when I’m here at home. I typically only use cars to carry really heavy stuff or for trips to other cities and states, but it’s even easier to accomplish this in Tempe with its location right on the light rail and with their onsite bike, scooter and even car sharing lots.

In a recent development, my place in Colorado is presently set up as a two bedroom house on the main floor, plus an apartment with a separate entrance on the walkout lower level. When I’m at home, I use the whole thing as one home – the apartment just makes a great place to host a fairly constant stream of visiting friends. But for the winter I’m hoping to rent out one of these spaces to a friend or trusted acquaintance who will take good care of everything, while I leave the other section free for the occasional visits I’ll be paying to this area over the winter. Aside from keeping an eye on the place, it will be a great way to practice the age-old Mustachian technique of making money while taking vacations!

What Happens at the End of March?

Industry observers note that as it stands, I have no intends beyond this point. I’ll head back to Colorado for my home base, but with this being a newly introduced phase of life I’ll be layering on new adventures. Aside from the two mountain properties that I’ve been helping to build out, I may end up with an MMM Mountain Retreat of my own someday. Conclusion: ongoing thoughts on the Culdesac experiment are here: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/.
