The Best Smith Machine for Your Home Gym in 2025

📅 04 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, other than the almighty treadmill, there may not be a piece of equipment more synonymous with commercial gyms than the Smith machine.
  • However, you don’t need a gym membership to enjoy its benefits.
  • With options spanning from traditional Smith machines to all-in-one home gym solutions, you might feel a bit overwhelmed about which direction to go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, other than the almighty treadmill, there may not be a piece of equipment more synonymous with commercial gyms than the Smith machine. Boasting tremendous versatility and functionality, this muscle-building tool is popular among lifters of all experience levels.

However, you don’t need a gym membership to enjoy its benefits. While it may have not been a home gym staple years ago, the Smith machine has become a must-have for many fitness enthusiasts. Offering added protection without a spotter for your bench presses, back squats, deadlifts, and other strength exercises, the Smith machine is a wise investment for those trying to build the ultimate garage gym.

With options spanning from traditional Smith machines to all-in-one home gym solutions, you might feel a bit overwhelmed about which direction to go. Luckily for you, our team of expert product testers did all the due diligence necessary to separate the cream from the crop. From analyzing the build materials to testing the smoothness of the bar path to assessing the value, we took the time to dissect each element in order to narrow down our list to just five.

In addition, we got some valuable insight from Mauro S. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness, on the benefits and what factors to consider when you’re shopping for a Smith machine.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any fresh supplement or exercise regimen.

Industry observers note that if you’re searching for a multifunctional Smith machine that’s compatible with a ton of attachments, the Force USA G15 is the machine that can truly do it all — albeit at an expensive price point of around $5,500. However, there’s a reason it earned 4.5 out of 5 stars for versatility from our top product tester: you can perform a wide variety of exercises by taking advantage of all of its functionality.

Recent findings suggest that tipping the scales at nearly 1,000 pounds, the G15 combines a functional trainer, half rack, and Smith machine into a single, sturdy unit. Measuring over 6 feet wide, over 4 feet deep, and about 7 feet tall, the G15 earns a 4-star footprint rating. While there are more compact options, it’s still a good option for folks with limited space, especially considering the versatility you get.

Offering dual 289-pound weight stacks that keep it well-anchored, the G15 also scores 4 out of 5 stars for durability and construction.

“This thing is like a tank,” our tester indicates. “Once it’s assembled, it’ll basically be stuck in place.”.

Unfortunately, our tester wasn’t as impressed with the cable pulley material. Asthey’re made from nylon instead of aluminum, they don’t move as smoothly and won’t be as durable as their metal counterparts.

Something that separates the G15 from many competitors is its ability to go from a 2:1 or 4:1 pulley ratio. This gives you the ability to make the weight feel like half or a quarter of the actual weight. While our tester would prefer a 1:1 ratio for more effective resistance, he claims the 2:1 or 4:1 ratios “will be adequate for most people working out from home.”.

It has been revealed that the G15 comes with a lengthy list of attachments, including J-hooks, safety spotter arms, multi-grip dip handles, a multi-grip pull-up bar, band pegs, and a low row footplate. If you want to unlock even more training possibilities, the $700 G15 Upgrade Kit includes three additional strength training stations, three functional attachments, a TV mount, and four storage shelves.

Two knocks against this ultra-versatile machine: assembly and value.

Although some of the parts arrive pre-assembled, our assembly expert recommends budgeting “at least 20 man hours” to get the G15 fully put together. And if you want to leave it to the professionals, you’ll need to pay an additional $800.

At nearly $6,000 on its own, the G15 certainly isn’t made for budget-conscious shoppers. Our top product tester gave it 3.5 out of 5 stars for value, noting that Force USA could use better quality components, cables, and accessories, including one of the key parts of this premium-priced unit: the built-in barbell.“The knurling is super passive and not going to allow for an adequate grip for the user if you were to go heavy on any Smith machine movements,” he explains.

Want to crush a full-body workout with a single piece of equipment? The Titan Fitness Smith Machine can be the all-in-one solution that allows you to train your upper body, lower body, and core in a safe, effective manner.

Is it as versatile as the G15? No. Is it far more affordable? Yes.

According to recent reports, for less than a third of the price, you can still get an excellent workout experience from the $1,7000 Titan Smith Machine. One of our more seasoned product testers used it for a variety of strength training sessions, highlighting how impressed she was by the smooth glide of the barbell and the angled design. In addition, this Smith machine is counterbalanced so you don’t have to support the entire 45-pound barbell like you do on other machines. Beginners will appreciate this, as the bar only feels like 15 pounds.

Unfortunately, like Force USA, Titan left our team wanting more out of the knurling.

“It’s fine for a Smith machine, but it’s definitely not the most grippy bar,” our tester notes.

On the other hand, this machine earns high marks for its ergonomics. Our tester rated it 4 out of 5 stars in this category. She found the single-axis, angled design helped improve her muscle activation during lower-body weight training exercises like Smith machine squats and lunges.

Most importantly, she felt completely secure using this Titan machine. Not only was there no wobbling or shaking, but the bar moved smoothly, leading her to give a 5-out-of-5 rating for stability.

According to recent reports, “This is a super stable machine; there was no give to it even when we were using heavy weights,” our tester says. “This was ultra-smooth.” While Titan priced this machine fairly, we’d like to see a better warranty. A one-year policy falls well short of what we expect from most brands. Plus, if you want to return a piece of equipment, you must pay the return shipping costs and a 20% restocking fee. That results in a disappointing customer experience score of just 2 out of 5 stars.

According to recent reports, don’t want a standalone Smith machine? Bolt Fitness has a space-saving solution in the form of the Storm Series Stinger Smith Machine Attachment. Compatible with any 3” x 3” frame using 1” hardware, this universal attachment can seamlessly integrate with your existing squat or power rack, opening the door to even more training possibilities.

According to recent reports, we rate this Smith machine attachment a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers 12 different positions totaling 60” of vertical adjustments. That means you can quickly go from a steep incline bench press to a Romanian deadlift, making your workouts more efficient, too. Plus, we also like that this attachment has a 43” built-in multi-grip pull-up bar, giving you the ability to develop your vertical pulling strength and endurance.

Industry observers note that bolt also earns solid marks for construction, earning 4 out of 5 stars in this key category. However, our chief product tester warns not to expect quite the same level of craftsmanship as some better-known brands.

“You won’t see the same quality welds or powder coats from Bolt as you will from Rogue or REP,” he says.

It has been revealed that like several other nominees on this list, our tester was also disappointed with the Smith bar’s knurling. The passive knurl pattern won’t give you a particularly stable grip, especially when using heavier weights.

“You definitely won’t mistake this for an Olympic barbell,” our tester indicates.

In a recent development, as for the price? At around $1,100 this is on the expensive side for a Smith machine attachment. For example, the Bells of Steel Smith Machine Rack Attachment is much more affordable at $800. We rate it a 3 out of 5 for value, especially since you already need a rack to use it. Otherwise, expect to invest a significant chunk of change to get a fully functioning setup.

Just because you can’t afford to splurge on something like the G15 doesn’t mean you can’t find a Smith machine that fits within your budget. If you don’t have a ton of financial wiggle room, the RitFit Smith Machine is the most affordable option that earned our stamp of approval.

As our top product tester puts it, “If you’re looking for a Smith machine and you’re on an ultra-budget, this is it.”.

Industry observers note that at about $500 on Amazon, this machine is less than a third of the price of the Titan Fitness Smith Machine and less than a tenth of the cost of the G15. Of course, it’s not the most durable option on the market, but it offers sufficient versatility at a very attractive price point to earn a near-perfect value rating of 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Dubbed the “sleeper pick” by our tester, he notes that “the low price covers so many sins.”.

Industry observers note that before we dive into some of RitFit’s shortcomings, let’s highlight some of the strengths of this machine. First, we rated it 4 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers built-in low row and lat pulldown capabilities using a plate-loaded cable pulley system that holds 165 pounds. The RitFit Smith Machine also comes with several attachments, including a pin-on landmine row and two multi-purpose pull-up handles.

Sources indicate that secondly, it has a compact design that makes it suitable for home gym setups with limited  space. It also weighs just 140 pounds, making it easier to move than other options on this list.

Industry observers note that however, our tester had several callouts about the RitFit Smith Machine that deserve mentioning. With cheaper build materials and a lightweight design, it didn’t prove to be as stable as he would have liked, earning just 3.5 out of 5 stars for both construction and stability. Needless to say, this isn’t the best option if you want to lift heavy weights. Still, considering you could pay around the same price for a high-quality Olympic barbell, the RitFit Smith Machine is a solid option if you’re on a limited budget.

Sources indicate that imagine if you could turn your squat rack into a Smith machine in a matter of minutes. That dream can be a reality if you’re willing to invest around $700 on the VTS Lite Rack Attachment from Bulletproof Fitness, a lesser-known fitness equipment manufacturer that’s caught our attention.

Recent findings suggest that while we haven’t gotten our hands on this attachment just yet, it’s hard not to get excited about the concept and execution by Bulletproof. The Versa Trolley System (VTS) Lite allows you to convert your squat rack into a Smith machine using your own barbell. The rollers are made from UHMW plastic, an ultra-durable material we’ve seen used on other racks. This attachment only weighs 15 pounds, making the VHS Lite a more user-friendly alternative than the full-sized VTS, which weighs in at 24 pounds. From a construction standpoint, we feel comfortable giving the VTS Lite 4 out of 5 stars.

In a recent development, in addition, we like that Bulletproof offers a wide range of options to accommodate different racks. You can choose between a 3” x 3” pair, a 2” x 3” pair, or a 2” x 2” pair. You also can choose different hook sizes based on the diameter of your barbell. This optionality, along with the added exercise variety you get from using the attachments, earns a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility.

Set to be released in May 2025, we’re excited to see this product in action. If you want a more streamlined solution than getting a standalone Smith machine, this is an attractive space- and money-saving solution. Based on the price and versatility, we give it a value rating of 4 out of 5 — though it could go higher once we get our hands on it.

As Smith machines have become more popular among the home gym community, we’ve ramped up our efforts to test ones from a variety of brands. This has allowed us to develop a thorough evaluation process that examines a number of key factors that impact your workout experience.

With options ranging from standard Smith machines to all-in-one trainers with cable machines, here’s what we assess during testing using a 1-5 scoring system:.

What makes a Smith machine such a valuable training tool? If you’ve ever used one, you already know there’s added peace of mind knowing you have built-in support. Here’s an overview of the different benefits of utilizing this popular piece of equipment.

It has been revealed that unlike when you use a barbell and squat rack, the Smith machine provides a fixed bar path. This can help reduce the risk of injury and ensure a stable lifting environment.

“The Smith machine helps the athlete feel supported and gives them greater control and stability when performing an exercise,” states Mauro M. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness.

In particular, fresh lifters can benefit from starting out on a Smith machine so they can focus on their form while being supported by the machine.

In a recent development, “Maintaining correct form is key for avoiding injuries and maximizing the effectiveness of your workouts,” states Dr. Christopher Mohr, PhD, RD. “Beginners might benefit from working with a personal trainer initially or taking a beginner class to learn proper techniques.”.

Industry observers note that the guided motion and added stability of a Smith machine makes it an ideal training tool for those returning from injury or anyone with mobility issues. It encourages proper form and can be a safer way to increase your strength and joint stability before moving on to free weights.

Recent findings suggest that maietta recommends starting with lighter weights to get a feel for the range of motion before progressing. “The fixed range of motion is not for everyone, so be sure to speak with your local fitness professional and listen to your body and joints if you feel any discomfort or pain during the planned movements,” he claims.

According to recent reports, if you prefer to work out alone or don’t have a training partner available, the Smith machine can act as a “spotter” for you. These machines offer an extra layer of safety, as you can easily rack the bar or set the safety spotters to a specific point that will keep you out of harm’s way.

In addition, this advantage allows you to safely follow progressive overload, a proven method for increasing muscle size and strength.

“This continual challenge helps your muscles grow stronger,” indicates Mohr. “It’s important to start with manageable increments to prevent injury.”.

It has been revealed that you won’t find many machines that offer as much versatility as the Smith machine. Want to train legs? You can knock out squat and lunge variations. Want to grow your chest and shoulders? Grab an adjustable weight bench and work on your bench press and overhead press without having to worry about keeping the bar stable. A high-end option like the Force USA G15 gives you the ability to perform cable exercises like cable crossovers, chest flys, and overhead triceps extensions.

“The Smith machine can be seen as the Swiss army knife of the weight room since it allows for several strength training exercises in its fixed vertical path, ranging from squats to overhead pressing movements,” claims Maietta.

In a recent development, what should you consider when choosing a Smith machine? Based on our experience as equipment experts and dedicated lifters, here’s what we recommend:.

It has been revealed that consider the machine’s footprint when determining if it is a good fit for your needs. One benefit of Smith machines is all-in-one trainers are available to consolidate the space needed for multiple workout stations.

Many of the home gym Smith machine options on this list are designed as all-in-one trainers designed to provide multiple workout functions with one convenient machine. The machine can include stations for a power rack, functional trainer, low-row attachment, chin-ups/pull-ups, dips, suspension trainers, and more.

Recent findings suggest that smith machines offer pulley systems with varying weight ratios, including 1:1 and 2:1. A 1:1 ratio means the weight you load is the exact weight you lift. A 2:1 ratio means you lift half of the weight you load. For instance, with a 2:1 ratio, if you load 100 pounds, you lift 50 pounds.

Some Force USA Smith machines, including the G15, allow users to easily switch between 2:1 and 4:1 ratios, which is helpful when people of various skills use the same machine.

Weight capacities vary depending on the functions offered by the machine. The weight capacities on this list start at 300 pounds. Be sure to confirm the machine’s weight capacity can accommodate your needs..

In a recent development, if you are looking for versatile strength-building home gym equipment to achieve a full-body workout, a Smith machine can help you achieve your goals. Since the 1950s, this game-changing machine has allowed gym-goers to work out safely without a spotter. Today, there is a wide range of consumer options, allowing you to experience the benefits of the Smith machine in the comfort of your own home gym.

According to recent reports, smith machines all perform similar functions, but there are different types of Smith machines available. For instance, some Smith machines provide a vertical path for motion, while other Smith machines provide a slightly angled path. Some Smith machines may be limited to the Smith machine function, while others are designed to be all-in-one machines with multiple stations for different exercises. Smith machines vary based on the manufacturer.

Yes, you can deadlift on a Smith machine, but whether you should depends on your skills and ability.Maietta suggests thinking through the following questions before performing moves on a Smith machine:-How is your range of motion?-Do you have the proper form or mobility to perform these compound moves?If you do not know, Maietta suggests working with a local fitness professional who will be able to help coach you and correct your form if necessary.

Yes, you can build muscle with the consistent use of a Smith machine. Smith machines are considered a good strength and muscle training option for beginners or those without a spotter. However, the drawback is motion is limited to a specific vertical (or slightly angled) path. For sports-specific muscle building, some experts prefer free weight exercises.

Industry observers note that yes, you can squat with a Smith machine. Safety features such as hooks and stoppers can help provide extra protection. Again, be mindful of your abilities and consult with a fitness pro if you are unsure of how to do this safely and with proper form.

Tech Report: The Ultimate Life Coach

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.
  • In a recent development, you’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises.
  • But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.

In a recent development, you’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises. And then to put thousands of hours into everything else I value as well: family, health, friends, adventures, building stuff, and even writing the occasional blog post. No complaints about any of this.

But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.

To most people, this sounds like a dream come true. Especially if you combine total freedom with plenty of money, life is just a non-stop blissful playground of self actualization, right?

Industry observers note that well, maybe, but maybe not. In reality, the answer depends on who you are.

Freedom and money reveal a person’s true strengths and weaknesses, and the result is a spectrum with “Unlimited drugs and booze on the couch” at one end, and “Create and manage a series of nonprofit foundations which employ thousands of people to research and invest in medical advances and clean energy” at the other.

For most of my journey so far, I seem to have found the balance pretty naturally. My Dad job was very intense for the first decade, but somehow I also had time to build and restore quite a few houses in the neighborhood, take plenty of intense trips to interesting places, give some talks and make some videos, and still write a few hundred blog posts.

But in these last few years, I have started slowing down, and it has become more and more difficult to wrangle and focus myself to get these things to happen as often.

Instead of constantly bouncing around the construction site building cool things, or falling into laser focus on the keyboard finishing an article that I just had to share with you, I found myself retiring to the couch earlier and earlier each afternoon, seeking distraction on the phone and wishing I had the energy and focus to do those other more enjoyable things.

So I fought back, by learning more about health and wellness. Trying to study and train my way into more energy and focus and motivation. And you’ve seen some of the results here, in articles I’ve shared about daily habits, steering clear of excessive comfort, and more.

And all of these things really work, IF you take the knowledge and actually put it into action. And therein lies the problem:.

Sources indicate that I kept learning effective new things, and successfully incorporating them into my life. They would work for a while, but gradually my brain would invent various excuses to stop doing them consistently, leaving me with plenty of knowledge but far too little accomplishment to show for it.

Until finally, just a few months ago, I realized that I had been sabotaging my own progress by turning my biggest life advantage into a disadvantage:.

I have been using my freedom too much – in order to avoid doing things that I didn’t feel like doing.

It has been revealed that see, freedom is great if it frees you from leaving your children at 5am so you can drive an hour through a traffic jam to sit in an office building for nine hours. But that same freedom goes to waste if you then just plunk the kids down in front of a playlist of cheap cartoons while you lounge in the corner to scroll Facebook all day.

It has been revealed that you need to use it to do things that are even more valuable than the job you just quit. And if you can’t do that, you might as well just keep the damned job.

This is what I was doing, while lying about it to myself. I would focus on the easy things which are still good for me, like taking care of the house or hanging out with friends who live nearby. But I avoid doing the harder things – which for me means the things that require more planning, energy or focus. Even though these are the things that allow me to lead the life I enjoy most.

Let’s use workouts as an easy example. I already know that on a minute-for-minute basis, this is the single most effective thing almost anybody can do with their time because it drastically improves every other area of life. But despite knowing this, I was still following this pattern:.

“I want to get in a really good weight training workout today.But I don’t feel like doing a workout because it’s hard.So I’ll try to grease the wheels for myself so it’s easier to achieve. I’ll pick the perfect time of day when the weather is nice, and my energy level is high. I’ll set up my gym in advance the night before.And when that golden moment of perfect conditions hits,I’ll hit the gym!“.

According to recent reports, but between you and me, that moment didn’t always come. Some weeks I’d achieve it 2-3 times, some weeks I’d get “busy” and make excuses like “well at least I walked a lot today”. Some days I would complete a great workout, but when recording it in the journal I’d see that the previous one was over a week ago.

And the results of this lackluster effort were exactly what you’d expect: lackluster fitness.

Recent findings suggest that then something changed and I learned that there’s a much better way to get those workouts done. It’s by replacing the long, meandering, frankly wussypants dialog above with this one:.

Industry observers note that I want to work out today.I don’t feel like it.^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

I’m using workouts as an example because this is the behavior I managed to change most successfully, but the exact same technique applies to everything else that you or I want to do, but fail to do regularly.

The key is learning to watch over yourself like an Eagle and identify that exact moment of hesitation.

And then instead of using it as a trigger for excuses, you use it as a trigger for action.

It’s so counterintuitive at first, but then obvious in retrospect. Hesitance feels shitty in the moment, and it really can ruin your life if you listen to it too often. But the ultimate solution is usually to run directly towards, rather than away from, the stuff you don’t want to do.

So really, Hesitation can be the ultimate life coach.

Using Extremely Badass People as Fuel.

Recent findings suggest that as part of writing this article, I shared the idea around with friends to test it out first. And I was initially surprised to get mixed results. About half of them could relate with me: they felt they were underachieving in life and wanted to do more. The other half though I was crazy: these people feel they are already doing too much, raising multiple kids and managing multiple businesses and training for ironman triathlons in the mountains.

In a recent development, the overachievers go through life nicely buzzed but often stressed. When hearing them describe their schedules, I was absolutely not envious. At the same time, they weren’t impressed with my schedule either because it’s too easy. We could both benefit from making adjustments towards the center.

Impressive overachiever friends are one thing, but the thing that really flipped the switch for me was hearing a podcast interview with our planet’s most extreme example of driving yourself beyond your former limits, David Goggins.

I learned about his life story with a mix of awe and horror. Severely beaten as a child, he grew up with a looming wall of psychological demons and challenges, but his reaction was the unique part: he has been driven to compulsively seek out and overcome extreme hardship, not just to unimaginable levels but hundreds of times beyond that.

From pushing through several near-death experiences just to qualify for a Navy SEALS career, to breaking his own legs, heart and lungs from the constant exertion of things like running 240 miles over four days without sleeping, to setting a world record of 4025 bar pull ups over 24 hours (shredding his hands to look like ground beef in the process), the man does things I would never have thought are even close to possible for a human.

And that flipped a switch for me, by putting my own incredibly easy, under-achieving life into perspective.

Because while I absolutely do not want any part of the Goggins life, and I would gladly live my life never having run more than 10 miles at a single stretch, I do find it incredibly helpful to learn that pretty much all of our barriers are entirely mental, not physical or placed upon us by the outside world.

Recent findings suggest that sure, we do have different starting points and different amounts of luck. But instead of thinking of life like this:.

I now realize that things are more like this:.

And that’s a really empowering way to think about life, that feels like the sky has opened way up.

It has been revealed that so the podcast was just an introduction. I wrote down the particularly concise quote “You already fuckin’ know what to do.” on a piece of cardstock, stuck it to my bathroom mirror, and started acting on it immediately.

Suddenly, I was able to hit the gym every single day because I had two ways to approach it: wanting to put in a workout, and not wanting to put in a workout, either of which became a trigger to work out immediately.

And of course, once I finally put in the effort, it started working. Even though I’ve been sorta into this type of training since I was a teenager, I have mostly floated along on a plateau for years. But with this change in attitude, I gained ten pounds of lean weight over the first four months, returning to the strength and flexibility that I had at age 25, and every single joint in my body feels like it has been upgraded to a study, well oiled spring.

I also used the “catch yourself at the moment of hesitance” trick to get myself to run instead of walk more often (over 20 runs since I got back to Colorado last month), get over to the MMM-HQ coworking space for more work and socializing visits, and even to sit back down at the computer to write this post for you. While I’ve found that too much blogger work (and internet “success”) is a bad thing, there is still a right level that works for me. But it takes a lot of discipline to be willing to do it, because of all the other easier and more thrilling activities I could be doing with this same stretch of time.

It has been revealed that for me, fully internalizing this one powerful piece of inspiring profanity has been transformative. But I still find that returning regularly to the well makes all this work even better. So I downloaded both of the Goggins audiobooks and worked through them in little chunks on my morning walks over the period of a month. Then I moved on to Peter Attia’s Outlive, and Jocko Willink’s Extreme Ownership.

It has been revealed that while the intellectuals fret about the perils of “Bro Science” or the “Toxic Masculinity” of today’s tribe of health podcasters and question their motivation, I simply absorb the messages that work for me and discard the rest. Find people who make you reach a little higher, and feed on their energy.

It has been revealed that and for me, being exposed to successful, strong, athletic people who squeeze a lot of work out of themselves is a big source of inspiration. It helps me do more with my day, which is exactly what works for me right now at this phase of life.

And I wish you more of what works for you too!

What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again.
  • Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward.
  • Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, notes Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.

Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.

Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, notes Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.

Keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try fresh fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy says. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”.

If you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?

Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

GET YOUR MAINTENANCE LOOKS HERE.

First, it’s key to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.

Recent findings suggest that “The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” claims Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.

Then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy claims. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.

This tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy says.

Andrew M. Jones, Ph.D., professor of applied physiology at the University of Exeter in the U.K., puts the minimum effective dose of maintenance running slightly lower—at 50 percent—though after about four to six weeks at half the volume, runners will likely start to see “more significant deterioration,” he claims, specifically of race-specific endurance. (Running economy may be more resilient.).

That’s not necessarily a bad thing (and allows you to focus on other goals; more on this soon), and 50 percent is enough to preserve a foundation to allow you to pick up at the beginning of a 16-week marathon training plan with relative ease.

Greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in Latest York City, agrees and provides this example: Say a runner finished Berlin on September 27 and plans to run London on April 24. After time off, he’d have them work back up to 50 percent of their mileage by October 25, then hover in the 50 to 60 percent of mileage range until early January when their London block would start in earnest.

Sources indicate that retaining intensity during the maintenance phase is arguably more crucial than frequency and duration, per Jones. “It’s impossible to give a minimum effective dose [for intensity] but ideally by week two [after a marathon] they’d get back to the pre-marathon training intensity but with lower volume,” he states, which might be lower duration and/or frequency of quality running. “Intensity is the key stimulus.”.

To hit this stimulus, Sheehy and Laraia both like to have runners add in strides (e.g., four to six 30- to 60-second strides as part of an easy run) before doing more intense speed workouts that could make their way back into the weekly schedule about a month after a race.

Sheehy provides an example of a speed workout he likes to include during the maintenance phase:.

Industry observers note that “The upcoming race pace is something I know they can achieve that is apparent in previous race results and workouts; not some aspirational wish pace,” Sheehy states. “This will give them the confidence they need or maybe a wake up call, but it makes for a great starting point, and allows us to calibrate their easy paces and use the lower volumes to let their body (and heart) adjust to the new norm.”.

Industry observers note that sheehy cautions against swapping out runs that make up your maintenance mileage for other cardio, as it is notable to maintain the specificity of running if you want to maintain running fitness. But he often adds in an indoor cycling day during his offseason on top of four or so days of running. If you dropped down your running frequency, an aerobic cross-training workout can support your fitness maintenance. Plus, it gives you a mental break, Jones says.

Laraia states one case where swapping maintenance miles for other cardio could make sense would be when runners come off a fall race injured or worn down and simply need a break from running so much. “Running is always going to be the best option because running is the sport, but if an elliptical or a bike is going to make you miss [running] enough to want to do it again, let’s start there,” he says.

Industry observers note that the maintenance phase is also a great time to focus on strength training, Jones claims. Sheehy agrees, suggesting aiming for two to three days a week. You can do more volume (either via an extra day or more sets/reps) during this phase, but it’s still important to include one true rest day in your plan, Sheehy says.

Industry observers note that strength work helps to build neuromuscular capacity, improve power that can translate to speed, and strengthen your tendons and ligaments for the upcoming season, especially if you focus on heavier lifting. “Let’s get comfortable with the extra load and then let’s see if it makes running better and more efficient,” Laraia states.

GET YOUR STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

Laraia says signs that you may have pulled back too much include a higher-than-usual heart rate during runs or paces that feel harder than normal.

In a recent development, still, it’s probably better to lose a little bit more running fitness in the offseason than to push yourself too hard, he indicates. The former is going to put you in a better position to start a newly introduced training block in the spring, compared with the latter, which could lead to burnout and could set your next training cycle back.

Recent findings suggest that “Realistically, you’re going to be better off taking the extra day versus trying to push through something if you’re early in a block or just trying to maintain fitness,” Laraia indicates. “I’d rather you be 100 percent recovered for every run versus in the build,” where it might make sense to go into a run feeling a little depleted.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that what's your FI number?
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Recent findings suggest that the S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Average Annual Return Since 1957.

Lowest S&P 500 ETF Expense Ratio.

Largest U.S. Companies Included.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that the S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

According to recent reports, the index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a firm is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

According to recent reports, an S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

It has been revealed that warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has stated: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals.".

The top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

The lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

BlackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, released in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

According to recent reports, schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment plans.

Investing in an S&P 500 fund takes less than 15 minutes:.

Sources indicate that for retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your blueprint. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

In a recent development, the total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:.

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $25,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

In a recent development, S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

The most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard indicates that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly claims to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right.".

Open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Sources indicate that transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Industry observers note that automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

If you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

According to recent reports, VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

It has been revealed that either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

In a recent development, as little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

Sources indicate that the S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

Recent findings suggest that S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

S&P 500 index funds are the single most key building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

#9477. Latest Update: Forgotten 7,000'ers: Changtse

Latest Update: Forgotten 7,000'ers: Changtse

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Changtse is a rarely climbed peak in Tibet in the Everest massif, flanked by the Main Rongbuk and East Rongbuk Glaciers, and linked to the world’s highest mountain by the North Col.
  • Modern Chinese mapping lists Changtse at 7,543m, though older sources cite figures up to 7,583m.
  • Because of Changtse’s connection to the classic northern approach to Everest, early mountaineering parties repeatedly crossed its flanks long before treating it as an independent objective.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Changtse is a rarely climbed peak in Tibet in the Everest massif, flanked by the Main Rongbuk and East Rongbuk Glaciers, and linked to the world’s highest mountain by the North Col. With a prominence of only 497m, Changtse is subordinate to its parent peak.

Modern Chinese mapping lists Changtse at 7,543m, though older sources cite figures up to 7,583m. The Changtse Glacier flows north into the East Rongbuk system, and some geographic surveys note a glacial lake on the glacier near 6,216m, ranking it among the world’s highest.

Changtse and Everest. Photo: Wikipedia.

Because of Changtse’s connection to the classic northern approach to Everest, early mountaineering parties repeatedly crossed its flanks long before treating it as an independent objective.

In 1924, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine became the first climbers to set foot on Changtse. They climbed the East Ridge while scouting camp locations during the British Everest expedition.

During the 1935 British Mount Everest Reconnaissance Expedition led by Eric Shipton, the team divided to scout possible climbs before targeting Changtse. Bill Tilman and Edmund Wigram considered the peak’s Northwest Ridge but deemed it impracticable and crossed north of Changtse to Camp 2.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Michael Spender and Charles Warren established high-altitude survey stations, and Shipton and Dan Bryant explored the West Rongbuk Glacier. Shipton’s primary goals were to photograph Everest’s upper sections and gather data on monsoon snow behavior. Despite deteriorating weather and waist-deep snow, they established three high camps.

It has been revealed that on August 21, 1935, Shipton, Tilman, Wigram, Bryant, and Warren debuted an attempt on Changtse. They climbed to within 460m of the summit before dangerously deep, soft monsoon snow forced them back. They spent a freezing night at high camp. Then, confronted by unstable slopes and buried tents, they abandoned their summit attempt.

Moving down the East Rongbuk Glacier on August 23, the climbers reunited with Spender, who had completed his difficult survey work, and headed toward the Kharta Changri Pass.

Sources indicate that base Camp of the 1924 Everest expedition. Photo: Royal Geographic Society.

In 1952, during the British Cho Oyu Expedition, Edmund Hillary, George Lowe, and three Sherpas illegally crossed the Nup La Pass into Chinese-controlled Tibet after abandoning their Cho Oyu climb.

Sources indicate that the group traveled to the North Side of Everest, exploring the East Rongbuk Glacier and visiting pre-war British base camp sites. Subsequently, they pushed up the Changtse Glacier for a direct attempt on Changtse’s summit. They reached 6,600m before a lack of food and supplies forced them to turn back. They returned over the pass to meet up with Shipton.

Sources indicate that on October 3, 1982, Dutch climber Johan Taks, a member of the Dutch Everest expedition, climbed Changtse without a permit and against the wishes of his expedition leader. Contemporary Dutch accounts described him setting out alone after being ordered not to, returning later that day to announce success.

Industry observers note that changtse from the upper slopes of Lhakpa Ri. Photo: Himalayanwonders.com.

Eleven days after Taks’ unauthorized solo push, on October 14, 1982, the first official ascent of Changtse was achieved by members of a German party.

It has been revealed that the German Alpine Club team, co-led by Eduard Geyer and Hansjuergen Tauscher, approached the mountain via the East Rongbuk route. The expedition included climbers Paul Braun, Thomas Dunsser, Martin Engler, Walter Ernst, Rudolf Frick, Andreas Heckmair Jr., Ludwig Hoesle, Peter Lechart, Udo Zehetleitner, and Wilfried Zink.

According to recent reports, the team drove from Lhasa and established their Base Camp near the final moraine of the Rongbuk Glacier at 5,105m. From there, they pushed up Everest and Changtse without the help of high-altitude porters. The climbers relied on their own strength and a team of six yaks to establish Camp 1 at 5,601m on October 2, followed two days later by Camp 2 at 6,096m, at the foot of Changtse’s long northeast ridge.

According to recent reports, to get higher, the climbers first had to climb a difficult 610m snow-and-ice slope mixed with exposed rock. They established Camp 3 at 6,400m, sheltered behind a protective rock spur. Above this point, they fixed ropes along a steep slope on a wide ridge that curved first north and then sloped east. On October 13, they successfully placed Camp 4 high on the ridge at 6,903m.

Sources indicate that on October 14, Zehetleitner completed the first official ascent, climbing via the four-kilometer northeast ridge, starting from the junction of the East Rongbuk and Changtse Glaciers. Two days later, on October 16, Braun, Frick, Hoesle, and Engler also topped out. They listed Changtse’s height as 7,550m.

Everest and Changtse. Photo: Himalayanwonders.com.

Industry observers note that in May 1983, the first Chilean expedition to Everest was already stretched thin by high altitude and extreme logistics when internal friction pushed the team over the edge. Among the climbers was 25-year-old glaciologist Gino Casassa, who had been temporarily sidelined by altitude sickness and was sent down to Base Camp to recover.

Industry observers note that as his health improved, Casassa grew restless under the strict commands of his expedition leader, Gaston Oyarzun. Forbidden from taking unnecessary risks, Casassa instead fixed his sights on Changtse. At 3:30 am on May 14, Casassa secretly slipped out of camp alone, starting an unauthorized solo attempt up the mountain’s long northeast ridge — the same route used by the Germans.

Sources indicate that moving rapidly in the subzero darkness without a permit, radio communication, or backup, he gambled everything on a lightweight style. By 3:30 pm, he was just 10m below the summit. However, the upper sections of the ridge deteriorated into unstable snow cornices and deep powder. Casassa narrowly escaped disaster when the snowpack fractured and slumped 4.5m beneath his boots, threatening to trigger a massive avalanche down the face.

Refusing to retreat, Casassa bypassed the unstable ridge by traversing directly onto the steep, exposed north face. He finally reached the summit at 5:00 pm. After a difficult descent in the dark, he reached Camp 2 at 11:00 pm, exhausted and dehydrated.

Industry observers note that back at camp, his unexpected return sparked outrage rather than celebration. While Casassa was on the peak, his teammates were managing a high-altitude medical emergency, and his unauthorized disappearance had caused immense panic.

Because the climb lacked official Chinese permits, it also carried diplomatic risks for future Chilean expeditions. The Chilean Mountaineering Federation officially expelled Casassa, concluding one of the era’s most astonishing solo feats with immediate controversy.

According to recent reports, in May 1986, a massive Chinese–Japanese expedition (17 Japanese and 19 Chinese climbers) targeted the mountain. After establishing an Advance Base at the confluence of the Changtse and East Rongbuk Glaciers, they pushed up the Changtse Glacier and the northeast ridge.

Industry observers note that on May 10, 16 climbers reached the summit. Among them was Tibetan climber Gunsang (also spelled Guisang), who became the first woman to summit Changtse. A second wave of eight Chinese climbers topped out the following day, while the remaining Japanese climbers withdrew to assist a teammate suffering from high-altitude sickness. According to the Himalayan Database, Gunsang remains the only woman to summit.

Ed Webster’s photo on August 26, 1986, during his first attempt on Changtse’s Northeast Ridge. Two days later, he established a new route, solo via the Southeast Face. Photo: Ed Webster.

Later that same summer, American mountaineer Ed Webster arrived to attempt a bold, lightweight climb.

Sources indicate that on August 26, 1986, he initially turned back from 7,163m on the right side of the face because of dangerously thin snow over brittle shale. After just a single rest day, he introduced another attempt on August 28 and established a landmark latest route up the southeast face.

Sources indicate that starting from an Advance Base at 6,126m near the foot of the North Col, Webster climbed the lower, highly avalanche-prone sections in total darkness to capitalize on the stable nighttime freeze. He navigated a prominent snow gully between two massive rock buttresses, traversed the upper face, and connected with the German northeast ridge route to reach the summit alone in a 15-hour round trip.

According to recent reports, in September 1987, an Australian expedition led by Robert Turner arrived at the East Rongbuk side of the mountain. On September 29, despite punishing high-altitude winds and deteriorating conditions, Turner and Glen Nash reached the summit. They climbed via a central couloir to the left of the north face icefall. This completed a line that was closely related to a route scouted by a Japanese team the previous year.

Industry observers note that changtse attracted global attention in late summer 2016 because of two remarkable solo ascents. Jordi Tosas of Spain reached the summit via the east ridge on August 27, and Kilian Jornet followed on September 11, via a variant line up the northeast face.

The total number of Changtse summits remains low, at around 60. The standard line remains the northeast ridge.

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (592 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Everest Climbers Return to West Ridge With One Member Less

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On their second venture up Everest, the Russian team is aiming to progress further along the West Ridge.
  • Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will climb one of the longest routes of Everest, with no supplemental oxygen, no support team, and no clear idea about the exact line they will follow.
  • Kondrashkin recently posted details about their previous ascent to the Lho La and the beginning of the ridge last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On their second venture up Everest, the Russian team is aiming to progress further along the West Ridge. This time, they will be a team of just three: Natalya Belyankina was airlifted out yesterday due to health problems.

Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will climb one of the longest routes of Everest, with no supplemental oxygen, no support team, and no clear idea about the exact line they will follow.

Kondrashkin recently posted details about their previous ascent to the Lho La and the beginning of the ridge last week. As he noted, their route skirts below gigantic hanging seracs. They felt safe traversing the area on the way up because they saw no avalanche debris. However, after they reached the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide col, the boom of a falling serac below them reminded them of the risks.

On the following morning, the climbers approached the first part of the West Ridge.

“[It was] a sharp ascent to the ridge: first, on a 50˚ snow slope and, higher up, more than 100m of 60˚ glacial ice,” Kondrashkin recalled. “Then, climbing over a slight snow cornice, we emerged onto the ridge.”.

Shipilov and Vasiliev climbed further up a rocky outcrop, looking for both the most suitable line and a potential campsite on the ridge. They also photographed the sections ahead. As Kondrashkin and Belyankina watched from below, “It felt like we were looking at it from the very foot of the mountain, just how enormous it is,” Kondrashkin wrote about Everest’s upper half:.

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Serguey Kondrashkin.

The team returned to Base Camp the following day, finding a better route that involves less time under the hanging seracs.

It has been revealed that since then, they have been resting and preparing for the next foray up. However, the rest was not enough for Natalya Belyankina, who was already suffering from a bad case of Khumbu cough.

Natalya Belyankina in the helicopter back to Kathmandu today. Photo: Natalya Belyankina.

According to recent reports, “It’s a real pity,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote today. “Natasha did so much to make this expedition happen, but it’s impossible to continue in this condition.”.

Vasiliev then confirmed that Kondrashkin, Shipilov, and he are heading up again today for about a week.

Industry observers note that the Russians are the only climbers right now on an 8,000m peak, and their goal is among the most ambitious on Everest in years. They intend to climb the mountain entirely on their own, without supplemental oxygen, in a light style, via the West Ridge.

On Pete Poston’s graph of Everest routes, the Yugoslavian route is #5 in pink, and the 1963 U.S. route is #2 in green.

Sources indicate that the West Ridge of Everest has been climbed just three times, each via different variations, all of them epic and sometimes tragic expeditions. Climbing the West Ridge involves two possible routes. First, an endless climb along the ridge from Nepal like the 1979 Yugoslavian team did (Andrej Stremfelj, Nejc Zaplotnik, Stipe Bozic, Stane Belak-Srauf, and Ang Phu Sherpa).

In a recent development, second, they could cross into Tibet at some point and continue up the North Face via the Hornbein Couloir. This route retraces the steps of Americans Tom Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, who started up the normal route to Camp 2, then joined the West Ridge and crossed to what became known as the Hornbein Couloir to the summit in 1963.

#9467. Alaska to Patagonia, One Summit at a Time

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (553 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Alaska to Patagonia, One Summit at a Time

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since 1972, Alaska to Patagonia has been a classic cycling route of 30,000km or more.
  • According to recent reports, the 23-year-old endurance athlete is not only pedaling the distance but also climbing the highest peak in each of the 35 countries he passes through.
  • Sources indicate that northern lights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since 1972, Alaska to Patagonia has been a classic cycling route of 30,000km or more. At any given time, several ambitious cyclists are attempting it. But no one is doing it quite like Tobias Renggli of Lucerne, Switzerland.

According to recent reports, the 23-year-old endurance athlete is not only pedaling the distance but also climbing the highest peak in each of the 35 countries he passes through. And although it’s part of the marketing rather than the adventure, the imagery so far — shot both by Renggli and by a film production group he belongs to called the Black Forest Collective — is stunning for such a difficult journey.

Sources indicate that northern lights. Photo: Tobias Renggli.

Despite his age, this is not Renggli’s first adventure. In 2022, at the age of 18, he cycled all 44 European countries within seven months, climbing the highest peak of each and camping every night. In 2024, he climbed the highest mountains of all 26 Swiss cantons in about three weeks.

Subzero cycling. Photo: Tobias Renggli.

According to recent reports, renggli began in April from Deadhorse, Alaska, on the shores of the Beaufort Sea — still deep winter at that latitude, though the long Arctic days had returned. Pedaling 1,200km in temperatures as low as -30˚C, he made his way to Talkeetna, then skied in for eight days while pulling a sled.

He then summited 6,190m McKinley with his occasional partner, Heli Hofmann — the first party atop the peak this year, which meant they had to break trail through the deep snow. It took them 36 days.

According to recent reports, next, it was onto 5,959m Mount Logan, Canada’s highest peak. Again with Heli Hofmann but no guide, they summited in late June. This time, they were the last party of the year to summit Logan.

Renggli then cycled with another friend to Vancouver, took a two-week break after covering 3,000km and summiting two of the hardest peaks he would encounter, then continued alone through the U.S. Typically, he cycles 100 to 160km per day, with some shorter days.

In Seattle. Photo: Tobias Renggli.

In a recent development, unlike most Trans-America cyclists, he chose to take Baja California rather than mainland Mexico. Crossing Baja was more difficult than expected. He described temperatures exceeding 40°C and a 120km stretch toward Loreto that he began with only two liters of water.

In Death Valley. Photo: Tobias Renggli.

Sources indicate that later, near Ciudad Insurgentes, thunderstorms flooded the roads. At night, he carried his bicycle through a fast-moving, thigh-deep flood while vehicles turned back.

Renggli had intended to take no motorized transportation, only sailboats when confronted with water — he also wants to climb 12 high points in the Caribbean. However, this is such a massive undertaking that he’s not being too strict on himself. Although he skied into Denali, for example, he flew back out to Talkeetna. And from La Paz in Baja, he caught the ferry to Mazatlan on the mainland and continued from there.

Details have been sparse since Baja, but Renggli recently crossed into Guatemala. Presumably, he climbed 5,636m Pico de Orizaba before leaving Mexico and is now headed to 4,220m Volcán Tajumulco, Guatemala’s highest peak. He has been on the road for 202 days.

Reggli’s route and current location.
